# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Barony:** Chiefly Lower Dunluce; partly Carey
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **County:** Antrim | **Province:** Ulster
- **Post town:** Bushmills (also contains a portion of Dunserverick)
- **Political status:** Part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland throughout 1780–1870; County Antrim remained in Northern Ireland (UK) after 1922

**Religious denominations confirmed:** Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian, Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian), Wesleyan Methodist, Roman Catholic. Billy parish had meeting houses for all three Protestant dissenter groups plus the established Church of Ireland, and Catholic mission access centred on Coleraine.

**Key events affecting records:**

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Tool coverage note

`place_search` returned no results for any variant of "Billy, County Antrim," "County Antrim, Ireland," or plain "Ireland," so `collections_search`, `volume_search`, `external_links_search`, `place_population`, and `wiki_place_page` all produced zero results — those tools require a resolved `standardPlace`. `wiki_read` attempts for the Billy Civil Parish page and most Ireland topical pages (Civil Registration, Census, Land, Probate, Military, Naming Customs) returned a generic placeholder rather than the actual articles. All claims below are sourced to one of those. Gaps are noted rather than filled from memory.

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Barony:** Chiefly Lower Dunluce; partly Carey (source: Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **County:** Antrim
- **Province:** Ulster
- **Post town within parish:** Bushmills; also contains a portion of Dunserverick
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Province of Ulster; part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland throughout 1780–1870
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no results (tool limitation); figures not available from these tool runs. Consult the General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI) or the PRONI for demographic data.
- **Economy:** The parish contains Bushmills, later known for whiskey distilling; agricultural and coastal economy typical of north Antrim. No economic figures returned by tools.
- **Ethnic composition:** County Antrim was predominantly Protestant in the north; in 1861 the Church of Ireland and Presbyterian churches together accounted for sixty percent of the Northern Ireland population as a whole, with Catholics at approximately forty percent (source: Ireland Church Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).
- **Religious denominations confirmed by tools:** Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopal); Presbyterian; Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian); Wesleyan Methodists. Roman Catholic. The parish had meeting houses for Presbyterians, Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists (source: Billy Civil Parish wiki).
- **Key historical events:** Catholic Emancipation Act 1829 (directly affects when Catholic parish registers commence in rural areas); Great Famine 1845–1852 (falls within the target period and dramatically affects emigration records and gaps in registers); introduction of all-Ireland civil registration 1864.

## Boundary changes

- Billy parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride (source: Billy Civil Parish wiki). That union was dissolved before the target period. Records created under the union may be filed under Billy or under the successor parishes — check all five.
- The civil parish boundary was partly in Barony of Carey and partly in Lower Dunluce. Land records and some administrative records may be indexed under either barony.
- After 1922, the six counties of Ulster (including Antrim) remained in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. The Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) was established as the archive for these counties; the National Archives of Ireland in Dublin holds pre-1922 national records affecting all of Ireland. Both repositories must be consulted for this period (source: Ireland Church Records wiki).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date at the national level:** Civil registration was introduced across all of Ireland on 1 January 1864 for births and deaths; the FamilySearch Ireland Church Records wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) states: "Before civil registration was introduced in 1864, Church records provide the primary source." The exact start date for non-Catholic marriage registration and any earlier local provisions are not stated in the tool results returned in this run; the researcher should verify this against GRONI (see Repositories below).
- **What exists within the target window:** Civil registration overlaps only the final six years of the 1780–1870 period (1864–1870). For 1780–1863, no civil vital records exist; church registers are the only primary vital record source.
- **Where held:** General Register Office Northern Ireland (GRONI), Oxford House, 49–55 Chichester Street, Belfast BT1 4HL; https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/. Indexed copies accessible through IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/) for some record types (note: the Ireland Church Records wiki states IrishGenealogy.ie covers "County Kerry, western and northwestern County Cork (Cork City excepted), and most of the City of Dublin" — County Antrim coverage on that portal was not confirmed by these tool results; verify directly with GRONI).
- **Gaps:** The entire 1780–1863 period has no civil vital registration.

### Church records

This is the primary record class for 1780–1870 in Billy parish. The FamilySearch Billy Civil Parish wiki page lists church record stubs for Catholic, Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends, and Others sections — but all sections are empty in the wiki (no register start dates or coverage dates are given). The researcher must consult PRONI's Guide to Church Records (see below) for specific register start dates for the congregations serving Billy.

#### Church of Ireland (Anglican/Episcopal)

- **Denominational context:** The Church of Ireland was the established church throughout this period. Church of Ireland records began in 1536 nationally, but two-thirds of all Church of Ireland parish registers in Ireland were destroyed in the 1922 fire at the Public Record Office in Dublin (source: Ireland Church Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).
- **What survives for Billy:** Not confirmed by these tool results. The researcher must check (a) the RCB Library's List of Parish Registers to see whether Billy's registers survived the 1922 destruction, and (b) PRONI, which holds surviving original registers and microfilm copies for Northern Ireland parishes.
- **Where originals are held:** RCB Library (Representative Church Body Library), Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735; Tel: +353 (0)1 492 3979; Email: library@ireland.anglican.org; Request a search: https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy; List of surviving parish registers: https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf
- **Where microfilm/digital copies are held:** PRONI (see Repositories below). PRONI's Guide to Church Records lists what is available.
- **Online:** Church of Ireland diocesan marriage license bond indexes 1630–1845 are at FamilySearch Catalog (https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/217297); the broader index to Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds 1623–1866 is searchable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3460239 (indexed, images, free).
- **Language:** English.
- **Digitization level:** Register survival unknown pending RCB Library check. Online marriage license bond index: indexed + images (FamilySearch, free).

#### Presbyterian

- **Denominational context:** Presbyterian settlement in Ulster dates from the 17th-century plantation; Billy parish had meeting houses for Presbyterians. The average starting date for Presbyterian registers in Ireland is 1830, though numerous registers date from the 1600s (source: Ireland Church Records wiki).

- **FindMyPast:** Ireland, Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-births-and-baptisms; Non-Conformist Marriages: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-marriages; Non-Conformist Congregational Records: http://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-congregational-records (paid subscription).
- **Digitization level for Billy specifically:** Not confirmed from these tool results; check PRONI's Digitised Church Records portal (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1).

#### Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian)

- Billy parish had a Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house (source: Billy Civil Parish wiki). Covenanter records are covered under the broader non-conformist collections at FindMyPast and may be indexed at RootsIreland. Specific register dates for the Billy Covenanter congregation are not available in these tool results; consult PRONI's Guide to Church Records.

#### Wesleyan Methodist

- Billy parish had a Wesleyan Methodist meeting house (source: Billy Civil Parish wiki). Methodist registers in Ireland are typically late; many begin in the 1800s. FindMyPast holds some Irish non-conformist congregational records. Specific dates not available from these tool results.

#### Roman Catholic

- **Diocesan context:** In the Roman Catholic divisions, Billy parish forms part of the district of Coleraine (source: Billy Civil Parish wiki). Coleraine is in County Londonderry; the relevant RC diocese is not named in these tool results — the researcher should confirm whether the relevant registers fall under the Diocese of Derry or the Diocese of Down and Connor before searching catalogues.
- **When registers typically begin:** Most rural Catholic parishes in Ireland did not begin keeping registers until Catholic Emancipation in 1828 (source: Ireland Church Records wiki). For Billy, which is a rural north Antrim parish, registers before 1828 are unlikely to exist; this is unconfirmed for the specific Coleraine district congregation.
- **Online:** NLI Catholic Registers — the National Library of Ireland has digitised and made freely available Catholic parish registers; search at https://registers.nli.ie/. Ancestry holds Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915 at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61039/ (subscription). RootsIreland (http://www.rootsireland.ie/) indexes Catholic registers for many parishes (paid).
- **Digitization level:** NLI portal: browse-only images (free). Ancestry: indexed + images (subscription).

### Census records

- `wiki_read` for Ireland_Census returned a generic placeholder; no specific census data was confirmed by tools in this run.

The 1901 and 1911 census returns survive complete and are freely available online at https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/ — those fall outside the 1780–1870 window but are highly useful for identifying families.
- No FamilySearch collections_search or volume_search results were returned for this place (tool limitation). The researcher should search the FamilySearch Catalog at https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog for "Antrim" and "census" directly.

### Probate and court records

- `wiki_read` for Ireland_Probate_Records returned a generic placeholder. No specific probate data was confirmed for this run.

Neither specific collection was returned by collections_search or volume_search (tool limitation) but the researcher can search for them through the FamilySearch Catalog.

### Military records

The researcher should check the British Newspaper Archive (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/) and the Irish Newspaper Archives (https://www.irishnewsarchive.com/) for Coleraine Chronicle and Ballymoney Free Press coverage of the Bushmills/north Antrim area during this period. ### Immigration and emigration records

- The Famine decade (1845–1852) falls within the target period and generated very large emigration flows from County Antrim, primarily to North America. Passenger lists for arrivals in the United States are held at NARA and indexed at Ancestry, FamilySearch, and FindMyPast.

- **School records:** Irish national school registers (post-1831) can record children's names, fathers' names, and religion. Surviving registers for County Antrim schools are held at PRONI.
- **Estate records:** Billy and the Bushmills area were historically within the estates of landed families; estate papers at PRONI may record tenant names and transactions. Check PRONI's eCatalogue under relevant estate names.

Both draw on microfilm made before some originals deteriorated; either can plug gaps left by the 1922 destruction (source: Ireland Church Records wiki).

7. **RootsIreland and the Ulster Historical Foundation are the primary indexes for north Antrim Presbyterian registers.** Because original Presbyterian registers remain with the local congregation and are not always accessible directly, these paid indexes provide the most efficient name search before requesting microfilm copies at PRONI (source: Ireland Church Records wiki, noting Ulster Historical Foundation at http://www.ancestryireland.com/).

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Schuylkill County was established in 1811 and is located in Pennsylvania, United States.

---

## Available Records

### Census Records
- **DGS 007621224 — U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1850–1860**
  - 412 images | **96% name-indexed** | **Full-text searchable**
  - This is the most accessible digitized source for this place and period
  - Also available on Ancestry: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/
- **1840 Census:** No county-level digitized volume was returned — a coverage gap; may require in-person access

### Church Records
- **DGS 004288771 — Lutheran Church Records, Schuylkill County, PA, 1840–1875**
  - 198 images | **0% name-indexed** | **Browse-only** | English and German
  - Must be browsed image by image; German-language content requires translation
- No volumes for other denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Catholic, Welsh Calvinist, etc.) were found online

### Probate Records
- **DGS 004812990 — Probate Records, Schuylkill County, PA, 1845–1880**
  - 286 images | 4% name-indexed | **Full-text searchable**
  - Plan to browse — most records are not accessible by name search alone
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994** (Collection 1999196): 3.2 million browse-only images, no name index

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No civil vital records collection was found for this county and period
- **Church records are the standard substitute** for this era
- Researchers should contact the county courthouse directly to verify what survives

### Military Records
- Covers the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and Civil War (1861–1865)
- Service records, pensions, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations held at **NARA**
- No Schuylkill County-specific military volume was found online

### Records NOT Yet Online
The following record types are likely only accessible in physical form:
- Civil vital records (births, marriages, deaths)
- Mortality schedules (1850–1880)
- Land deeds and property transfers
- County court records (naturalizations, civil suits)
- Tax records (1840–1870)
- Cemetery/sexton records
- Newspapers
- Non-Lutheran church records

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Federal census 1850–1860 (96% indexed); Probate 1845–1880 (full-text searchable); Lutheran church records 1840–1875 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | 1850 U.S. Federal Census – Schuylkill County | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse | Probate (Register of Wills), deeds (Recorder of Deeds), court records |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State-level records, county microfilm, military records |
| NARA (Philadelphia regional facility) | Federal census, military, passenger lists, pre-1906 naturalizations |
| Local historical societies | Local histories, newspapers, cemetery transcriptions |
| Denominational archives | Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized |

---

# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Somerset
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be confirmed from tool results in this session. Pulaski County is located in the south-central part of Kentucky.
- **Economy:** Agriculture-dominant during this period; subsistence farming and small-scale crop production typical of the Kentucky Appalachian foothills. Timber was also a local industry.
- **Religious denominations:** Before 1900, the largest religious groups in Kentucky were Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches (Kentucky Church Records wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records). These denominations were active throughout south-central Kentucky during the target period.
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861-1865) — Kentucky was a border state; local families were divided between Union and Confederate service, generating substantial military records on both sides. A records disaster struck the courthouse in 1871, destroying some county records within the target period.

## Boundary changes
Pulaski County boundaries have been stable since formation in 1798. No boundary changes during the 1840-1880 target period are noted in tool results. Any events before December 10, 1798, would appear in the records of Lincoln County or Green County, the parent jurisdictions.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates (county level):** Birth and death registration: 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910, with poor compliance throughout. Marriage: from county formation (1799). Per the Kentucky Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records), statewide birth and death registration did not begin until 1911, with general compliance by 1917; statewide marriage registration began in 1958.
- **What exists within 1840-1880:**
  - Marriage records at county level: continuous from 1799, held at the Pulaski County Courthouse
  - Birth and death records at county level: only for 1853-1862 and 1874-1878 — the years 1840-1852, 1863-1873, and 1879-1880 have no civil registration for births or deaths
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502) holds marriage bonds, original deeds, and court orders from county formation. Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA) in Frankfort holds microfilmed county records. Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics holds statewide records from 1911 onward.
- **Online:** FamilySearch has marriage bonds and consent forms for Pulaski County, 1799-1871 (per the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The 1871 record loss may account for this cutoff. Ancestry is noted as holding vital records indexes for the county.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration for approximately 30 of the 40 target years. The 1871 courthouse disaster destroyed some records within the target period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials), family bibles, cemetery records, newspaper death notices, and probate records naming decedents.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian were the dominant groups in Kentucky before 1900. Individual congregations were established throughout south-central Kentucky during the target period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, membership rolls, and church minutes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort (manuscript church records); Filson Historical Society, Louisville (Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records, primarily Louisville area); individual denominational archives (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville; Methodist conference archives; Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia); active local congregations.
- **FamilySearch online collections** (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records): Kentucky Church Records, 1818-1995 (index and images, incomplete); Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839-1960 (index only); Kentucky Marriages, 1785-1979 (index only); Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (index only).
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** The Pulaski County Historical Society holds the most comprehensive local collection of church records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). Contact them before assuming a congregation's records are unfindable.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — all five decennial censuses fall within the target period. Mortality schedules (listing deaths in the year preceding the census) exist for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880.
- **State census:** Kentucky took no state censuses (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy). No intercensal enumerations exist for this period.
- **Access:** Federal census records are available through FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Census records are indexed for name searches for all years in the target period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, court orders (civil and criminal), and naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record).
- **Date range:** Pulaski County probate records from 1801; court records from 1799.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (originals); KDLA (microfilmed copies).
- **Online:** FamilySearch has early will books for Pulaski County, 1801-1929, digitized (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). These overlap the full target period.
- **Note:** The 1871 courthouse disaster may have affected some probate and court records. The earliest record of earliest date in the Pulaski County wiki page places probate from 1801, suggesting pre-1871 records survived at least partially.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Kentucky is a state-land state using a metes-and-bounds survey system (not the rectangular township-range system used in federal land states).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Kentucky Land Office in Frankfort issued grants, warrants, surveys, and patents. Various grant periods apply to the 1840-1880 target window, including Old Kentucky Grants (1793-1856), Kentucky Land Warrants (1816-1873), and County Court Orders (1836-1955) (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Types:** Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents (Kentucky Land Office); deeds recording person-to-person transfers (county courthouse, from county formation 1799).
- **Where held:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort (grants/patents); Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort (additional land records and manuscripts); Pulaski County Courthouse (deed books from 1799, with the Pulaski County wiki page showing land records from 1799).
- **Online:** FamilySearch has Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants, and related records, 1700-1955. Ancestry holds Kentucky land grants and related records. The BLM General Land Office site covers federal land patents (note: Kentucky is largely a state-land state, so federal GLO coverage is limited).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts within/near period:** Mexican-American War (1846-1848); Civil War (1861-1865) — Kentucky was a border state with significant both Union and Confederate military participation.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and draft registrations at the National Archives (NARA). Kentucky state adjutant general records at KDLA.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service and pension records); KDLA (state military records); Fold3 (online database for military records).
- **Access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records online. NARA holds originals.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Kentucky cemeteries including those in Pulaski County. Sexton records and burial registers vary by cemetery and congregation.
- **Physical records:** Church burial registers (held by individual congregations or denominational archives); local historical society holdings.

### Newspaper records
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspapers including Kentucky titles. Check for Pulaski County / Somerset area papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), and community news fill gaps left by missing vital records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Note:** Pulaski County is an inland location far from ports of entry. No international border-crossing records apply. However, inland records remain relevant: declarations of intention, naturalization petitions, and certificates of citizenship were filed at local courts of record. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including Pulaski County's.
- **Naturalization access:** County courthouse (Pulaski County court records from 1799); NARA (post-1906 federal naturalization records).

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page notes Ancestry holds county tax lists. Tax records typically predate the target period from county formation.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (originals); KDLA (microfilmed copies); Ancestry (indexed).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for census records in years between enumerations and can track annual presence in the county.

### Other record types
- **Pulaski County Historical Society:** Holds vertical files organized by surname and the most comprehensive collection of church records and obituaries from local newspapers (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). Consult before assuming a record is unavailable.
- **Published local histories:** 19th- and early 20th-century county histories may transcribe early records or list founding families. The Kentucky Historical Society and University of Kentucky Special Collections hold these.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Will books 1801-1929 (digitized); Marriage bonds and consent forms 1799-1871; Kentucky Church Records 1818-1995; Kentucky Births and Christenings 1839-1960; Kentucky Marriages 1785-1979; Kentucky Deaths and Burials 1843-1970; Kentucky Land Office records 1700-1955 | Free |
| Ancestry | County tax lists; census records (federal, all target years); vital records indexes | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Kentucky titles | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (service, pensions, draft) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal census originals; military service and pension records; naturalizations post-1906 | Free/fee for copies |

**Coverage note:** The collections_search and volume_search tools both failed to resolve the Pulaski County place identifier in this session (both returned totalResults: 0 with empty standardPlace). The collections and volumes listed above are sourced from the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page and the Kentucky Church Records and Kentucky Land and Property wiki pages. A direct search of FamilySearch's catalog for this county returned 0 hits at both county and state level — this is treated as a cataloguing gap or tool limitation, not confirmed absence of digitized records, since the wiki pages name specific digitized sets.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from 1799; birth/death records for compliance periods | In-person or written request |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset, KY | Surname vertical files; church records collection; local newspaper obituaries | In-person; contact for hours |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort | Microfilmed county records; pre-1911 birth/death records | In-person or online request (kdla.ky.gov) |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort | Manuscripts, newspapers, land records, genealogical collections | In-person |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort | Land grants, original warrants, surveys, patents | In-person or written request |
| University of Kentucky Special Collections, Lexington | Local history publications, manuscripts | In-person |
| NARA (various locations) | Federal census originals; military service/pension records | In-person or reproduction request |

## Records NOT online
- Birth and death records for compliance periods (1853-1862, 1874-1878) exist only at the Pulaski County Courthouse or on KDLA microfilm; they are not confirmed as indexed in any online database from tool results.
- Post-1871 marriage records (1872-1880) are not covered by the FamilySearch marriage bonds series (which ends at 1871); these must be sought at the courthouse or KDLA.
- Most church records exist only on FamilySearch microfilm at the library or with individual congregations; the Pulaski County Historical Society holds the most comprehensive local collection.

The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy) states that a disaster destroyed some records in 1838 and again in 1871. The 1871 loss falls within the target period; which specific record series were affected is not detailed in the tool results. The FamilySearch marriage bonds series ending in 1871 may reflect this loss. Researchers should check whether the record they need predates 1871 and whether KDLA holds a microfilmed copy made before any destruction. Substitute sources for affected years include church records, the federal census, and newspaper notices.

**Where the Original Christ Church Marriage Register Is Held**

The original baptism, marriage, and burial registers of Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal, founded 1695 in Philadelphia) are held by the:

> **Christ Church Preservation Trust**
> 20 N. American Street, Philadelphia, PA 19106
> Phone: 215-922-1695

To view the original 1734 register — not a microfilm, not a transcription — you need to contact the Preservation Trust directly to arrange access. They control researcher access to the originals and can advise on current policies and hours.

---

**What's Available Online (Not the Original)**

FamilySearch has browsable (but not name-indexed) digital images of microfilm copies:

- **Film 1490578 / DGS 7615596** — Baptisms and burials, 1709–1800 (volumes 1–28)
- **Film 1490580 / DGS 7615594** — Marriages and burials, 1801–1900 (volumes 43–72)

Note: Neither of these listed films clearly covers colonial-era *marriage* records (pre-1801). The 1734 marriage register may not have been microfilmed separately, so confirming what's digitized would require checking with the Preservation Trust or FamilySearch directly.

The **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (1300 Locust Street, Philadelphia, PA 19107) holds a *published transcription* only — not the original you're looking for.

---

**A Note on 1734 Marriage Records**

By 1734, marriage practices were in transition — couples might have recorded banns, a license, or both. All of those entries would appear in the original register at the Preservation Trust.

**Bottom line:** Call the Christ Church Preservation Trust at **215-922-1695** to ask about researcher access and whether an appointment is required.

Here is the locality guide for the Alabama region around 1800:

---

**Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory), c. 1800 — Key Archives & Record Repositories**

The Alabama region around 1800 was legally the **Mississippi Territory** — statehood did not come until 1819 — so the most important thing to know is that records from that period are filed under the Mississippi Territory, not Alabama, and many survive only in paper form.

---

### Primary Repository

**Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery**
- Mississippi Territory censuses of **1801, 1805, and 1808**
- Territorial tax lists
- Early county deed, probate, and court records
- The earliest Alabama-coded collections generally begin 1803–1809

---

### FamilySearch Collections (Digitized/Indexed)
FamilySearch has **eight relevant indexed collections** covering:
- Church records
- Land records
- Court records
- Census substitutes
- Probate records
- Marriage records

Note: Most Alabama-coded FamilySearch collections start no earlier than 1803. For records right around 1800, the Mississippi Territory censuses and tax lists are the primary substitutes.

There are also **two browse-only digitized volumes** that must be paged through image by image (no name index):
- Court/land records, 1808–1819
- Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820

---

### Special Case: Mobile Bay / Gulf Coast Area
The Mobile Bay coastal area passed through **French, British, and Spanish** control before Americans took possession in 1813. Colonial-era records for that zone are held at:
- **Archivo General de Indias** — Seville, Spain
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** — France
- **Library of Congress** — Washington, D.C. (transcripts and copies)

---

### Next Step
To build a focused research plan, it helps to know which **specific county** within Alabama your ancestor lived in around 1800 — county boundaries changed frequently in the territorial period. Once that's established, a more targeted search sequence can be developed across land, probate, court, and church records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (ca. 1795–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory created 1817; statehood 1819. For the target period of around 1800, the territory was the Mississippi Territory (established 1798 from land ceded by Georgia and Spain).
- **Administrative center:** The Mississippi Territory was governed from Natchez (present-day Mississippi). After the Alabama Territory was split off in 1817, its capital was St. Stephens.
- **Parent jurisdiction at 1800:** Mississippi Territory, United States
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned from `place_population` for this period. According to Wikipedia, early settlement was concentrated around Mobile Bay; significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia accelerated after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, trade with Native nations (Creek, Cherokee), cotton cultivation beginning in the early 1800s, maritime trade at Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations occupied much of the interior. European-American settlers arrived from the Carolinas, Virginia, Tennessee, and Georgia. The Mobile area had a French Creole and Spanish Creole community from the colonial era. Enslaved African Americans were present throughout.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist and Baptist circuit riders were the primary Protestant presence in the interior settlements. Catholic parishes served the Mobile area from the French colonial period onward.
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory established 1798; Yazoo Land Fraud (affecting land titles); Creek War 1813–1814; Mobile captured by U.S. forces 1813; Alabama Territory established 1817; statehood 1819.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798: The present-day Alabama region was divided between Spanish West Florida (coastal strip including Mobile) and land ceded to the United States by Georgia.
- 1798–1817: The interior of present-day Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory. The southern coastal strip around Mobile remained in Spanish hands until 1813, when U.S. forces seized it.
- 1817: Congress split the Mississippi Territory; present-day Alabama became the Alabama Territory.
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood.
- **Important:** Records created before December 14, 1819 are records of a territory, not a state. Records for present-day Alabama from before 1817 are filed under the Mississippi Territory jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Alabama around 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not load (they returned only a generic page), so the exact statewide registration start date cannot be confirmed from tool results. Consult the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) for authoritative dates.
- **What exists for this period:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for ca. 1800.
- **Where held:** N/A for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the primary source for vital events. County marriage bonds and licenses began when counties were established — FamilySearch has 'Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950' (collection 1598408, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408), starting 1809. For 1800 specifically, this collection does not apply.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area, from French colonial period); Methodist and Baptist circuit riders in the interior settlements.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Catholic sacramental registers for Mobile begin in the French colonial era.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has 'Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950' (collection 1986396, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396), covering from 1803 — this is the closest online collection to the ca. 1800 period. Catholic records for Mobile may be at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives. French-era Catholic records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Language:** Catholic records in the colonial era are in French or Spanish.

### Census records
- **Mississippi Territory censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census is the first to include present-day Alabama (as part of the Mississippi Territory). No 1800 federal census was taken for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **FamilySearch collections:** 'Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890' (collection 2016756, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) begins 1810 — index only, no images. 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (collection 1927171, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) covers from 1792 and likely includes territorial Alabama records.
- **Access:** The Alabama 1810+ census substitutes are indexed. The territorial censuses at ADAH require in-person or correspondence access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, deed records, and court minutes.
- **Date range:** County-level records begin when individual counties were established. Washington County (formed 1800, one of the earliest Alabama counties) has deed and probate records from 1803.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Two browse-only volumes are available:
  - DGS 004512889: 214 images, Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: must be browsed image by image.
  - DGS 004512890: 96 images, Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: must be browsed image by image.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985' (collection 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) starts 1809 — partially outside the target window for ca. 1800 but overlaps by 1809.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (collection 1855293, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) starts 1799 and may include territorial Alabama court records.
- **Where held:** Original records are at the individual Alabama county courthouses and at ADAH.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range) system, as Alabama is a federal-land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. federal government issued land patents in the territorial period through the General Land Office. Colonial-era Spanish and British grants predate American control.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (from ca. 1803 onward), Spanish and British colonial grants (pre-1813 for Mobile area), county deed books (transfers after initial grant).
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (collection 1919694, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) starts 1798 and likely includes territorial Alabama land records — note this collection is indexed under Mississippi, not Alabama.
- **BLM General Land Office:** Federal land patents are searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish records of the Mobile District, including land grants, are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812; territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service records and pension files. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized military records including War of 1812 and early pension files. Territorial militia rolls may be at ADAH.

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides online cemetery coverage. For early 1800s burials, many graves are unmarked or the stones have not survived.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare or nonexistent for most of Alabama; church burial registers (where they survive) are the primary source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alabama newspapers begin after statehood (1819+). No Alabama newspapers predate the territory period in the target window. The nearest newspaper coverage for around 1800 would be Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital) papers.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for early Alabama newspapers post-1819.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay was the primary port of entry for the region. New Orleans (in Spanish, then French, then U.S. hands) also served the region.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, Spanish and French colonial censuses, naturalization records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal passenger lists. Spanish colonial census records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard including infants traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax records.
- **Date range:** Tax records begin when counties were established in the territorial period.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records. These are a critical census substitute for ca. 1800 when federal census coverage is absent.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary way to place a person in the Alabama region around 1800 before the 1810 federal census.

### Colonial records (Mobile area)
- **French period (1702–1763):** Colonial records including census returns and church registers are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **British period (1763–1780):** Records are at The National Archives (UK) and may be partially held at ADAH.
- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Alabama Church Records 1803-1950; Alabama Compiled Census Substitutes 1810-1890; Alabama County Marriages 1809-1950; Alabama Probate Records 1809-1985; Mississippi Territorial Land Records 1798-1907; Mississippi County Court Records 1799-1920; Mississippi Compiled Census Substitutes 1792-1890; 2 browse-only digitized volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810 onward for Alabama) | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including War of 1812, pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, territorial period onward | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers (Alabama papers post-1819) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Alabama for 1780–1820; these are the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The 4 Alabama-scope and 4 Mississippi-scope FamilySearch indexed collections are the complete returned set for each (4 each).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810; territorial and early county tax records; militia rolls; state and county records | In-person; some online finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| Alabama county courthouses | County deed books, probate records, marriage records from county formation dates | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives, Mobile, AL | Catholic sacramental registers from French colonial era onward | Contact directly |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias) | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial and early state records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial census, church registers, land grants for Mobile District | In-person or correspondence; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records 1702-1763 | In-person or correspondence |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 census is partially online through compiled substitutes) — held physically at ADAH
- Most territorial-era county tax lists — held at ADAH and county courthouses
- Most Catholic sacramental registers for Mobile from the colonial era — held at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives and on microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District — at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress; partially digitized separately
- French colonial records — at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- British colonial records — at The National Archives, UK
- Militia rolls and early territorial court records beyond the two digitized browse-only volumes at FamilySearch

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set for territorial Alabama was destroyed or lost. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890) being browse-only is a digitization/indexing gap, not a record loss. Coverage gaps in online collections (e.g., the Alabama collections starting in 1803 or 1809, missing the years 1798–1802) are gaps in digitization, not confirmed losses. Contact ADAH and individual county courthouses to determine what physical records survive for a specific county and period.

## Research tips
- **Search Mississippi collections for territorial Alabama records.** Around 1800, present-day Alabama was the Mississippi Territory. FamilySearch collections such as 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (collection 1919694) and 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (collection 1927171) are indexed under Mississippi but likely include records for the Alabama portion of the territory. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Use territorial censuses and tax lists as the primary locating tools for ca. 1800.** No federal census covered the Alabama region in 1800. The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 are the main enumerations; they are at ADAH in Montgomery. County tax lists from the earliest Alabama counties (Washington County formed 1800, Madison County formed 1808, etc.) are a critical supplement.
- **Identify which county existed at the time of the event.** Alabama was carved into counties as the territorial period progressed. Washington County (1800) was one of the first. Knowing the county of residence determines which courthouse and which series to search.
- **For Mobile area ancestors, the colonial records chain runs through three foreign archives.** Spanish records (1780–1813) are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. French records (1702–1763) are at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence. Microfilm of the French records is at the Mobile Municipal Archives. ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes exist for territorial Alabama.** DGS 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images) and DGS 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803–1820, 96 images) must be examined image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search.
- **Alabama is a federal-land state.** Land passed from the U.S. government to individuals via patents, not state grants. Search the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents from the territorial period onward.
- **FamilySearch Alabama-specific wiki pages returned only generic content.** The pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Census, and Probate did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey. Go directly to the Alabama Department of Archives and History website (archives.alabama.gov) for authoritative guides to Alabama record types and start dates.

- **Access:** The Alabama 1810+ census substitutes are indexed. The territorial censuses at ADAH require in-person or correspondence access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, deed records, and court minutes.
- **Date range:** County-level records begin when individual counties were established. Washington County (formed 1800, one of the earliest Alabama counties) has deed and probate records from 1803.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:** Two browse-only volumes are available:
  - DGS 004512889: 214 images, Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: must be browsed image by image.
  - DGS 004512890: 96 images, Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: must be browsed image by image.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** 'Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985' (collection 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764) starts 1809 — partially outside the target window for ca. 1800 but overlaps by 1809.
- **Mississippi Territory court records:** 'Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920' (collection 1855293, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) starts 1799 and may include territorial Alabama court records.
- **Where held:** Original records are at the individual Alabama county courthouses and at ADAH.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range) system, as Alabama is a federal-land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. federal government issued land patents in the territorial period through the General Land Office. Colonial-era Spanish and British grants predate American control.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (from ca. 1803 onward), Spanish and British colonial grants (pre-1813 for Mobile area), county deed books (transfers after initial grant).
- **FamilySearch collection:** 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (collection 1919694, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) starts 1798 and likely includes territorial Alabama land records — note this collection is indexed under Mississippi, not Alabama.
- **BLM General Land Office:** Federal land patents are searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Colonial land grants:** Spanish records of the Mobile District, including land grants, are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814; War of 1812; territorial militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal service records and pension files. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized military records including War of 1812 and early pension files. Territorial militia rolls may be at ADAH.

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides online cemetery coverage. For early 1800s burials, many graves are unmarked or the stones have not survived.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare or nonexistent for most of Alabama; church burial registers (where they survive) are the primary source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Alabama newspapers begin after statehood (1819+). No Alabama newspapers predate the territory period in the target window. The nearest newspaper coverage for around 1800 would be Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital) papers.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for early Alabama newspapers post-1819.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay was the primary port of entry for the region. New Orleans (in Spanish, then French, then U.S. hands) also served the region.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, Spanish and French colonial censuses, naturalization records.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal passenger lists. Spanish colonial census records are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard including infants traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county tax records.
- **Date range:** Tax records begin when counties were established in the territorial period.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds territorial and early county tax records. These are a critical census substitute for ca. 1800 when federal census coverage is absent.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary way to place a person in the Alabama region around 1800 before the 1810 federal census.

### Colonial records (Mobile area)
- **French period (1702–1763):** Colonial records including census returns and church registers are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **British period (1763–1780):** Records are at The National Archives (UK) and may be partially held at ADAH.
- **Spanish period (1780–1813):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Alabama Church Records 1803-1950; Alabama Compiled Census Substitutes 1810-1890; Alabama County Marriages 1809-1950; Alabama Probate Records 1809-1985; Mississippi Territorial Land Records 1798-1907; Mississippi County Court Records 1799-1920; Mississippi Compiled Census Substitutes 1792-1890; 2 browse-only digitized volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810 onward for Alabama) | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including War of 1812, pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents, territorial period onward | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical newspapers (Alabama papers post-1819) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Alabama for 1780–1820; these are the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The 4 Alabama-scope and 4 Mississippi-scope FamilySearch indexed collections are the complete returned set for each (4 each).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Mississippi Territory censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810; territorial and early county tax records; militia rolls; state and county records | In-person; some online finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| Alabama county courthouses | County deed books, probate records, marriage records from county formation dates | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives, Mobile, AL | Catholic sacramental registers from French colonial era onward | Contact directly |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias) | In-person; some digitized |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial and early state records | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial census, church registers, land grants for Mobile District | In-person or correspondence; some digitized at pares.mcu.es |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records 1702-1763 | In-person or correspondence |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (the 1810 census is partially online through compiled substitutes) — held physically at ADAH
- Most territorial-era county tax lists — held at ADAH and county courthouses
- Most Catholic sacramental registers for Mobile from the colonial era — held at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives and on microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District — at Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress; partially digitized separately
- French colonial records — at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- British colonial records — at The National Archives, UK
- Militia rolls and early territorial court records beyond the two digitized browse-only volumes at FamilySearch

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific record set for territorial Alabama was destroyed or lost. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890) being browse-only is a digitization/indexing gap, not a record loss. Coverage gaps in online collections (e.g., the Alabama collections starting in 1803 or 1809, missing the years 1798–1802) are gaps in digitization, not confirmed losses. Contact ADAH and individual county courthouses to determine what physical records survive for a specific county and period.

## Research tips
- **Search Mississippi collections for territorial Alabama records.** Around 1800, present-day Alabama was the Mississippi Territory. FamilySearch collections such as 'Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907' (collection 1919694) and 'Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890' (collection 1927171) are indexed under Mississippi but likely include records for the Alabama portion of the territory. ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))
- **Use territorial censuses and tax lists as the primary locating tools for ca. 1800.** No federal census covered the Alabama region in 1800. The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 are the main enumerations; they are at ADAH in Montgomery. County tax lists from the earliest Alabama counties (Washington County formed 1800, Madison County formed 1808, etc.) are a critical supplement.
- **Identify which county existed at the time of the event.** Alabama was carved into counties as the territorial period progressed. Washington County (1800) was one of the first. Knowing the county of residence determines which courthouse and which series to search.
- **For Mobile area ancestors, the colonial records chain runs through three foreign archives.** Spanish records (1780–1813) are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. French records (1702–1763) are at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence. Microfilm of the French records is at the Mobile Municipal Archives. ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Two browse-only FamilySearch volumes exist for territorial Alabama.** DGS 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images) and DGS 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803–1820, 96 images) must be examined image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search.
- **Alabama is a federal-land state.** Land passed from the U.S. government to individuals via patents, not state grants. Search the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents from the territorial period onward.
- **FamilySearch Alabama-specific wiki pages returned only generic content.** The pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Census, and Probate did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey. Go directly to the Alabama Department of Archives and History website (archives.alabama.gov) for authoritative guides to Alabama record types and start dates.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here is what the research shows:

---

The Arkansas region before 1800 was never a separate jurisdiction — it was part of **Spanish Louisiana (1763–1800)** and French Louisiana before that, administered from New Orleans. Key points:

**The Only Settlement of Note**
The only European settlement of any size was **Arkansas Post**, where French Catholic missionaries kept sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) that served as the entire vital records system for this period. There was no civil registration at all.

**Available Records & Where to Find Them**

| Record Type | What It Contains | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Catholic sacramental registers (1763–1800) | Baptisms, marriages, burials | FamilySearch (64 images, digitized but **not name-indexed** — must be browsed page by page); in Spanish |
| Spanish household censuses (*padrones*) | Household members, ages | Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm at Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) & Library of Congress |
| Land concessions | Land grants, settler names | Same as above |
| Military rosters | Soldiers at the Post | Same as above |
| Civil proceedings | Civil and legal matters | Louisiana State Archives; New Orleans Notarial Archives |

**Critical Warning: Don't Stop at Arkansas Repositories**
Because Arkansas Post was governed from New Orleans, **civil, notarial, and court records for Arkansas Post residents are in Louisiana archives**. Omitting Louisiana leaves a significant gap in your research.

**Next Steps**
A research plan targeting your specific ancestor would draw on the FamilySearch image browse for the Catholic registers, the Arkansas History Commission microfilms for Spanish padrones and land records, and Louisiana archives for civil and notarial records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, French and Spanish Colonial Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas did not exist as a jurisdiction before 1836. The territory comprised part of French Louisiana from 1682 and Spanish Louisiana from 1763. Arkansas Post (Poste des Arkansas), established in 1686 by Henri de Tonti, was the sole significant European settlement throughout this period.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post served as the administrative center under both French and Spanish colonial authority. Under Spain, a commandant at the Post held civil, military, and judicial authority locally, subject to the Governor of Louisiana in New Orleans.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana (1763-1800), administered from New Orleans; French Louisiana (1686-1763).
- **Population during period:** The European and mixed-race population at Arkansas Post was small throughout the colonial period — likely fewer than several hundred persons at any one time. The place_population tool returned no data for this pre-statehood period.
- **Economy:** Fur trade (primarily beaver and deerskins), subsistence agriculture, and garrison support. Arkansas Post functioned as a trade nexus between French/Spanish colonists and the Quapaw nation.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers and voyageurs; Spanish colonial administrators, soldiers, and settlers; Quapaw and other Native American nations; enslaved African and African-descended persons.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic only. French Franciscan missionaries initially served Arkansas Post; Capuchins later served under Spanish rule. No Protestant worship was legally permitted in Spanish Louisiana.
- **Key historical events:** 1686 founding of Arkansas Post; 1729 destruction and rebuilding of the Post after conflict with the Natchez; 1763 Treaty of Paris transferred Louisiana from France to Spain; 1783 British assault on Arkansas Post during the American Revolutionary War; 1800 Treaty of San Ildefonso returned Louisiana to France; 1803 Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: The Arkansas region was part of French Louisiana, administered from New Orleans.
- 1763: By the Treaty of Paris ending the Seven Years' War, France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi River (and the city of New Orleans) to Spain. The Arkansas territory became part of Spanish Louisiana.
- 1800: The secret Treaty of San Ildefonso returned Spanish Louisiana to France, though Spanish administration continued in practice until 1803.
- 1803: United States acquired the territory through the Louisiana Purchase. The Arkansas region passed through: District of Louisiana (1804), Territory of Louisiana (1805), Territory of Missouri (1812), Territory of Arkansas (1819), and State of Arkansas (1836).
- Records generated before 1800 follow the colonial jurisdiction, not modern Arkansas county boundaries. There were no counties in this period — the Post commandant's authority covered a loosely defined district.

## Available record types

All record types below are at the colonial post level (Arkansas Post) or the provincial level (New Orleans), not at any county level — counties did not exist before statehood.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- Spanish civil and court records from the Arkansas Post commandant — Louisiana State Archives / Archivo General de Indias
- Catholic sacramental registers from the French colonial period (pre-1763) — Diocese of Little Rock / Arkansas History Commission (the FamilySearch digitized volume covers only 1763-1800)
- Early colonial church records (1686-ca. 1763) — extent of survival unknown; contact Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey identified a verified record loss for a specific record set at Arkansas Post. The wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) notes that surviving registers are held at the Diocese and History Commission, which implies losses or non-survival of some registers, but does not name specific destroyed sets or years. The researcher should contact the Arkansas History Commission and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock directly to determine which years of registers survive before concluding that a gap reflects a record loss.

## Research tips
- **Start at the Arkansas History Commission.** The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) identifies the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock as holding transcriptions and microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records including padrones, sacramental registers, and land concessions — accessible without a trip to Spain.
- **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402.** This single digitized volume (64 images of sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763-1800) is free at FamilySearch but must be browsed page-by-page — it has no name index and is not full-text searchable. Plan to read colonial Spanish or work with a collaborator who can.
- **Use PARES to search the Archivo General de Indias.** The Spanish government portal (https://pares.mcu.es) provides online access to finding aids and some digitized documents. The 'Papeles de Cuba' series within the Archivo General de Indias is the main series for Spanish Louisiana colonial records and should be searched for Arkansas Post.
- **Bridge to American records through BLM land grant confirmations.** After 1803, the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners confirmed valid Spanish and French grants. The confirmed patents at the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov) name original colonial grantees with grant dates — these can be used to work backward into pre-1800 Spanish land records held at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Search Louisiana repositories — not only Arkansas ones.** Arkansas Post was governed from New Orleans throughout the colonial period. Civil disputes, estate proceedings, notarial acts, and Governor's correspondence were generated in New Orleans and remain in Louisiana archives. Limiting research to Arkansas repositories alone will miss a significant body of records.
- **Language and paleography.** Colonial-era records are in Latin (sacramental register formulas), French (French colonial-period notations), and Spanish (1763-1800). Engaging a professional genealogist or paleographer familiar with colonial Spanish and Latin ecclesiastical records is strongly advisable.
- **The Quapaw connection.** Sacramental registers include baptisms of Quapaw tribal members. If research involves Native American ancestry in this region, the church registers and Indian affairs records in the Archivo General de Indias (Papeles de Cuba) are directly relevant.
- **Neighboring jurisdictions.** The nearest neighboring colonial jurisdictions were the Illinois Country to the north (also French/Spanish) and the Red River settlements to the south/west. Families near these routes may have generated records in both districts. The Arkansas History Commission and Louisiana archives together cover the most probable neighboring-jurisdiction trail for Arkansas Post.

Here is the locality guide's findings for Ohio circa 1790:

---

**Ohio Before Statehood — Locality Guide (c. 1790)**

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working in a place that did not yet exist as a state. The territory was federally governed as the **Northwest Territory from 1787**; Ohio itself was not created until **1803**. Only two counties were organized by 1790:

- **Washington County** (est. 1788) — covered nearly all of future Ohio
- **Hamilton County** (est. 1790) — covered the southwest

Boundary lines shifted rapidly before statehood, so every record search must first pin down which county held authority at the exact date and place of the event.

---

**Records Available (Despite Early Documentation Gaps)**

| Record Type | Details | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Land grants & patents** | Three systems: federal rectangular survey (BLM/GLO), Virginia Military District metes-and-bounds warrants, and Connecticut Western Reserve grants | BLM GLO, Virginia State Library (Richmond), Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) |
| **County marriage records** | Starting from 1789 | FamilySearch (collection 1803785) |
| **Church records** | From 1787 onward — baptisms and burials serve as the *only* vital-event substitutes (no civil birth/death registration existed) | FamilySearch (collection 2246917) |
| **Territorial land records** | 1788–1799 (browse-only, no name index) | FamilySearch (collection 1542187) |
| **Washington County tax records** | 1799–1803 (12% indexed) | FamilySearch |
| **Territorial court records** | Physical holdings | Ohio History Connection, Columbus |

---

**Key Takeaways**

- **No civil vital registration** existed in 1790 — church baptism and burial registers are your only source for births and deaths.
- Sparse online coverage reflects a **digitization gap**, not confirmed record loss — do not assume records are gone.
- The Virginia Military District used a separate **metes-and-bounds** land system distinct from the federal rectangular survey; Virginia State Library holdings in Richmond are essential for that region.

**Next steps:** Search the FamilySearch collections listed above, and contact the **Ohio History Connection** directly to ask whether territorial court minutes survive for your county and date of interest.
