entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York. During the 1700s the city existed as a chartered municipality within New York County (Manhattan), part of the Province of New York under British Crown rule until 1783, then part of the State of New York. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City served as both the city and county seat of New York County (Manhattan). It was the capital of New York Province throughout the colonial era and briefly the first capital of the United States (1785-1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial) until 1783; State of New York thereafter.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction and time period.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading center; merchant activity, shipbuilding, and crafts trades were dominant. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, and African (enslaved and free) communities were present. Dutch cultural and linguistic influence persisted well into the 1700s despite the English takeover in 1664.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation, records from 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel). (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), French and Indian War (1754-1763), American Revolution (1775-1783) with British occupation of NYC 1776-1783, and post-Revolution reorganization as part of New York State.

## Boundary changes

In the 1700s, "New York City" comprised the city and county of New York (Manhattan island only). The five-borough consolidation did not occur until 1898. Records for what are now Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island (Richmond County) were created and are held under their respective counties — not under New York City. Researchers tracing families in those areas must search those county records separately.

The city itself was divided into wards for administrative purposes; some tax lists and militia rolls reference ward designations rather than street addresses.

The place_search_all tool returned no historical jurisdiction entries beyond the single city entry for "New York, New York, United States" (dateRange: +1624/), indicating no jurisdictional splits tracked at that granularity for this locality.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages specifically for New York Vital Records, New York Church Records, and New York Land and Property all returned only a generic "Genealogy Records" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) in this session rather than the New York-specific articles. No civil registration start date can be confirmed from the tools consulted. The generic page notes that "many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s."
- **What exists for the 1700s:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in colonial New York. Church registers are the only contemporary vital record series for the entire 1700s period.
- **Where held:** See Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700-1800 period precedes any civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptism, marriage, burial registers); probate records (wills and inventories naming family members); tax lists; newspaper notices.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records begin 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, and others. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers the full colonial period.
- **Digitized volume found:** One volume specifically for New York City Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 (imageGroupNumber: 007733180, 211 images) was identified by volume_search. This volume has **0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability. Digitization level: **browse-only images**.
- **Language warning:** Dutch Reformed registers through 1776 are written in Dutch. Researchers must be able to read Dutch (or obtain translation assistance) to use them.
- **Where held:** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial church record collections. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** No federal census was taken before 1790. The first enumeration that touches this jurisdiction is the 1790 US federal census — covering only the last decade of the target period. The first 80 years of the 1700s have no federal census coverage.
- **Colonial enumerations:** The wiki_search result notes that colonial-period tax lists and militia rolls can serve as population proxies. No specific colonial census enumeration appeared in any tool result for NYC.
- **State/provincial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Census returned only generic content; no specific state census dates for this period can be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Colonial jurisdiction:** Wills in colonial New York were proved before the Prerogative Court of the Province of New York, not at the county surrogate level. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Published index:** The New-York Historical Society published the *Abstracts of Wills* series, which indexes wills proved in the Prerogative Court. This is the primary finding aid for colonial-era probate.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) covers the colonial period.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When the ancestor left a will (testate), search the Prerogative Court wills and the NYHS Abstracts index. When no will was left (intestate), look for letters of administration in the same court.
- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil and criminal cases in the colonial period. Records of this court are cited in wiki_search as a key source. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts); New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch (digitized collection above).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. New York is a state-land state; the federal rectangular survey and Bureau of Land Management patent records do not apply.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial governor and the Provincial legislature issued land patents and grants. After independence, the State of New York took over this function. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Land and Property returned only generic content in this session; the determination that NY is a state-land state is drawn from the generic page's statement that "federal land states have patent records at the BLM GLO website" (implying non-federal-land states do not).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, conveyances.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) covers the colonial period.
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan — deed books); New York State Archives (colonial patents and grants); FamilySearch (digitized collection above).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War, King George's War, French and Indian War, American Revolution — all fall within the 1700s.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls are listed in wiki_search as naming men of military age and useful for identifying residents. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) Revolutionary War service records and pension files are held at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for Revolutionary War records; New York State Archives for colonial militia rolls; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church cemetery (Anglican/Episcopal, Manhattan) has been active since the colonial era. Dutch Reformed churches also maintained burial grounds throughout the 1700s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is listed in the external_links_search results and covers some historic cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual churches and by the NYGBS and the New-York Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *New York Gazette* (established 1725) is noted in the Wikipedia result as a colonial-era newspaper. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (runaway slave ads, estate sales), ship arrivals.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed in external_links_search. Historical newspaper archives are also held at the New-York Historical Society and the New York Public Library.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was one of the primary ports of entry for the colonial Atlantic world throughout the 1700s.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists and customs records; post-Revolution arrival manifests.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) is listed in external_links_search. Some colonial passenger records are also held at the New York State Archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Ward-level tax assessment lists.
- **From wiki_search:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial NYC and can substitute for the missing census years. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) covers the end of the target period.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the absence of census records before 1790 and for the gap years thereafter.

### Other record types

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds colonial manuscripts covering the Province of New York — a key source for provincial-level records. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Mayor's Court records:** Civil and criminal proceedings at the city level. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Published local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century histories of New York City often transcribed early records and listed founding families. The NYGBS and NYHS hold extensive collections of these.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (id: 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (id: 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id: 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id: 1678432); Dutch Reformed Registers 1700-1776 browse-only (imageGroupNumber 007733180) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 census covers end of period) | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | National Archives (immigration, military, naturalization) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New York City for 1700-1800 (totalResults: 1), which is the complete set for that query. The collections_search returned 5 collections at the New York state scope, of which 4 overlap the 1700s. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available as a tool in this session — microfilm and manuscript holdings for NYC colonial records in the FamilySearch Catalog are unassessed.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Colonial church records, local histories, published abstracts, finding aids | In-person / membership |
| New-York Historical Society | Colonial church records, Abstracts of Wills, Mayor's Court records, newspapers | In-person |
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, militia rolls, provincial records | In-person / online finding aids |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan Courthouse) | Deed books, court records | In-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican/Episcopal baptism, marriage, burial registers | Contact directly |
| Dutch Reformed Church Archives | Denominational registers | Contact directly |

## Records NOT online

- Dutch Reformed Church registers other than the 1700-1776 digitized volume (007733180) — additional volumes may exist only in physical form at church archives or NYGBS.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) 1700s registers — not found as a separate digitized volume in volume_search.
- Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed, and other denominational registers for the 1700s — not found as digitized volumes.
- Mayor's Court records — not found in volume_search or collections_search.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (NY State Archives) — cited by wiki_search but did not appear as a digitized volume or collection in the tools consulted.
- Colonial-era tax assessment lists (years before 1799) — not found as digitized collections.
- Colonial militia rolls — not found as a specific digitized collection.
- The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available in this session — microfilm holdings covering NYC colonial records are unknown from this survey.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this session states that a specific New York City record set from the 1700s was destroyed or lost. The absence of digitized volumes for many record types reflects a digitization gap, not a confirmed record loss. The physical repositories listed above should be consulted to confirm the existence and condition of undigitized series.

## Research tips

- **Church records are the essential starting point.** There was no civil registration in colonial NYC. Dutch Reformed baptism, marriage, and burial registers beginning in 1639 are the oldest continuous vital-record series. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The Dutch Reformed digitized volume is browse-only and in Dutch.** ImageGroupNumber 007733180 (211 images, 1700-1776) has 0% name-indexing. You must browse it page by page and must be able to read Dutch-language records.
- **Search the Prerogative Court — not the county surrogate — for colonial wills.** Wills were proved at the provincial level before 1783. The New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* series is the primary index. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Use tax lists and militia rolls as census substitutes.** No federal census existed before 1790. Ward-level tax lists survive for some years and can place a household in a specific ward; militia rolls list men of military age. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **NYC in the 1700s meant Manhattan (New York County) only.** Families in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, or the Bronx fall under separate counties — Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester respectively — each with their own record sets.
- **Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) creates a records gap.** During British occupation, regular record-keeping was disrupted. Some records from this period may be sparse or held in British archives.
- **The NYGBS is the specialist repository for colonial NYC research.** It holds church record transcriptions, published abstracts, and finding aids not widely available elsewhere. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The New York Genealogical and Biographical Record** (the NYGBS quarterly journal) published transcriptions of colonial records for over a century and is worth searching for published abstracts of the records you need.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York-specific topics** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all returned only generic content in this session. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy for up-to-date guidance.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established by the Dutch West India Company in 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York. During the 1700s the city existed as a chartered municipality within New York County (Manhattan), part of the Province of New York under British Crown rule until 1783, then part of the State of New York. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City served as both the city and county seat of New York County (Manhattan). It was the capital of New York Province throughout the colonial era and briefly the first capital of the United States (1785-1790).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial) until 1783; State of New York thereafter.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction and time period.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading center; merchant activity, shipbuilding, and crafts trades were dominant. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, and African (enslaved and free) communities were present. Dutch cultural and linguistic influence persisted well into the 1700s despite the English takeover in 1664.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous congregation, records from 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, Quaker, Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel). (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Key historical events:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), French and Indian War (1754-1763), American Revolution (1775-1783) with British occupation of NYC 1776-1783, and post-Revolution reorganization as part of New York State.

## Boundary changes

In the 1700s, "New York City" comprised the city and county of New York (Manhattan island only). The five-borough consolidation did not occur until 1898. Records for what are now Brooklyn (Kings County), Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island (Richmond County) were created and are held under their respective counties — not under New York City. Researchers tracing families in those areas must search those county records separately.

The city itself was divided into wards for administrative purposes; some tax lists and militia rolls reference ward designations rather than street addresses.

The place_search_all tool returned no historical jurisdiction entries beyond the single city entry for "New York, New York, United States" (dateRange: +1624/), indicating no jurisdictional splits tracked at that granularity for this locality.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages specifically for New York Vital Records, New York Church Records, and New York Land and Property all returned only a generic "Genealogy Records" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) in this session rather than the New York-specific articles. No civil registration start date can be confirmed from the tools consulted. The generic page notes that "many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s."
- **What exists for the 1700s:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in colonial New York. Church registers are the only contemporary vital record series for the entire 1700s period.
- **Where held:** See Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700-1800 period precedes any civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptism, marriage, burial registers); probate records (wills and inventories naming family members); tax lists; newspaper notices.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (records begin 1639), Anglican/Episcopal (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran, and others. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **FamilySearch digitized collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (id: 1469062, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) covers the full colonial period.
- **Digitized volume found:** One volume specifically for New York City Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700-1776 (imageGroupNumber: 007733180, 211 images) was identified by volume_search. This volume has **0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability. Digitization level: **browse-only images**.
- **Language warning:** Dutch Reformed registers through 1776 are written in Dutch. Researchers must be able to read Dutch (or obtain translation assistance) to use them.
- **Where held:** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial church record collections. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** No federal census was taken before 1790. The first enumeration that touches this jurisdiction is the 1790 US federal census — covering only the last decade of the target period. The first 80 years of the 1700s have no federal census coverage.
- **Colonial enumerations:** The wiki_search result notes that colonial-period tax lists and militia rolls can serve as population proxies. No specific colonial census enumeration appeared in any tool result for NYC.
- **State/provincial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Census returned only generic content; no specific state census dates for this period can be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Colonial jurisdiction:** Wills in colonial New York were proved before the Prerogative Court of the Province of New York, not at the county surrogate level. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Published index:** The New-York Historical Society published the *Abstracts of Wills* series, which indexes wills proved in the Prerogative Court. This is the primary finding aid for colonial-era probate.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) covers the colonial period.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When the ancestor left a will (testate), search the Prerogative Court wills and the NYHS Abstracts index. When no will was left (intestate), look for letters of administration in the same court.
- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil and criminal cases in the colonial period. Records of this court are cited in wiki_search as a key source. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts); New-York Historical Society; FamilySearch (digitized collection above).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. New York is a state-land state; the federal rectangular survey and Bureau of Land Management patent records do not apply.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial governor and the Provincial legislature issued land patents and grants. After independence, the State of New York took over this function. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New York Land and Property returned only generic content in this session; the determination that NY is a state-land state is drawn from the generic page's statement that "federal land states have patent records at the BLM GLO website" (implying non-federal-land states do not).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, conveyances.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) covers the colonial period.
- **Where held:** New York County Clerk (Manhattan — deed books); New York State Archives (colonial patents and grants); FamilySearch (digitized collection above).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War, King George's War, French and Indian War, American Revolution — all fall within the 1700s.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls are listed in wiki_search as naming men of military age and useful for identifying residents. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records) Revolutionary War service records and pension files are held at NARA.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for Revolutionary War records; New York State Archives for colonial militia rolls; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church cemetery (Anglican/Episcopal, Manhattan) has been active since the colonial era. Dutch Reformed churches also maintained burial grounds throughout the 1700s.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is listed in the external_links_search results and covers some historic cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual churches and by the NYGBS and the New-York Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *New York Gazette* (established 1725) is noted in the Wikipedia result as a colonial-era newspaper. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (runaway slave ads, estate sales), ship arrivals.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is listed in external_links_search. Historical newspaper archives are also held at the New-York Historical Society and the New York Public Library.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was one of the primary ports of entry for the colonial Atlantic world throughout the 1700s.
- **Record types:** Colonial-era ship passenger lists and customs records; post-Revolution arrival manifests.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) is listed in external_links_search. Some colonial passenger records are also held at the New York State Archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Ward-level tax assessment lists.
- **From wiki_search:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards of colonial NYC and can substitute for the missing census years. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) covers the end of the target period.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the absence of census records before 1790 and for the gap years thereafter.

### Other record types

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds colonial manuscripts covering the Province of New York — a key source for provincial-level records. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Mayor's Court records:** Civil and criminal proceedings at the city level. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Published local and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century histories of New York City often transcribed early records and listed founding families. The NYGBS and NYHS hold extensive collections of these.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (id: 1469062); Land Records 1630-1975 (id: 2078654); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id: 1542780); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id: 1678432); Dutch Reformed Registers 1700-1776 browse-only (imageGroupNumber 007733180) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 census covers end of period) | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | National Archives (immigration, military, naturalization) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching New York City for 1700-1800 (totalResults: 1), which is the complete set for that query. The collections_search returned 5 collections at the New York state scope, of which 4 overlap the 1700s. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available as a tool in this session — microfilm and manuscript holdings for NYC colonial records in the FamilySearch Catalog are unassessed.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Colonial church records, local histories, published abstracts, finding aids | In-person / membership |
| New-York Historical Society | Colonial church records, Abstracts of Wills, Mayor's Court records, newspapers | In-person |
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, militia rolls, provincial records | In-person / online finding aids |
| New York County Clerk (Manhattan Courthouse) | Deed books, court records | In-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican/Episcopal baptism, marriage, burial registers | Contact directly |
| Dutch Reformed Church Archives | Denominational registers | Contact directly |

## Records NOT online

- Dutch Reformed Church registers other than the 1700-1776 digitized volume (007733180) — additional volumes may exist only in physical form at church archives or NYGBS.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) 1700s registers — not found as a separate digitized volume in volume_search.
- Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed, and other denominational registers for the 1700s — not found as digitized volumes.
- Mayor's Court records — not found in volume_search or collections_search.
- New York Colonial Manuscripts (NY State Archives) — cited by wiki_search but did not appear as a digitized volume or collection in the tools consulted.
- Colonial-era tax assessment lists (years before 1799) — not found as digitized collections.
- Colonial militia rolls — not found as a specific digitized collection.
- The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not available in this session — microfilm holdings covering NYC colonial records are unknown from this survey.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this session states that a specific New York City record set from the 1700s was destroyed or lost. The absence of digitized volumes for many record types reflects a digitization gap, not a confirmed record loss. The physical repositories listed above should be consulted to confirm the existence and condition of undigitized series.

## Research tips

- **Church records are the essential starting point.** There was no civil registration in colonial NYC. Dutch Reformed baptism, marriage, and burial registers beginning in 1639 are the oldest continuous vital-record series. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The Dutch Reformed digitized volume is browse-only and in Dutch.** ImageGroupNumber 007733180 (211 images, 1700-1776) has 0% name-indexing. You must browse it page by page and must be able to read Dutch-language records.
- **Search the Prerogative Court — not the county surrogate — for colonial wills.** Wills were proved at the provincial level before 1783. The New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* series is the primary index. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Use tax lists and militia rolls as census substitutes.** No federal census existed before 1790. Ward-level tax lists survive for some years and can place a household in a specific ward; militia rolls list men of military age. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **NYC in the 1700s meant Manhattan (New York County) only.** Families in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, or the Bronx fall under separate counties — Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester respectively — each with their own record sets.
- **Revolutionary War occupation (1776-1783) creates a records gap.** During British occupation, regular record-keeping was disrupted. Some records from this period may be sparse or held in British archives.
- **The NYGBS is the specialist repository for colonial NYC research.** It holds church record transcriptions, published abstracts, and finding aids not widely available elsewhere. (wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **The New York Genealogical and Biographical Record** (the NYGBS quarterly journal) published transcriptions of colonial records for over a century and is worth searching for published abstracts of the records you need.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York-specific topics** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all returned only generic content in this session. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy for up-to-date guidance.

- **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** — Virginia state militia records, which document the large number of Virginians who served in local and state-level units rather than the Continental Army.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; it became the Commonwealth of Virginia at the start of the Revolution and ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital); each county maintained its own courthouse.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Virginia (British Crown) before 1776; thereafter an independent commonwealth.
- **Population during period:** No tool returned population figures for this specific window. Virginia was the most populous British colony and contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia).
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (tobacco), merchant trade, and some manufacturing; wartime disruption affected coastal commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English settlers; German and Scots-Irish communities in the western counties; a large enslaved African American population.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (the established colonial church), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Quaker congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence (1776); major campaigns including the Yorktown campaign (1781, fought on Virginia soil); British naval raids on the Chesapeake coast throughout the war.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's boundaries were stable during 1775–1783. No county-level splits are known to affect the state's outer boundaries during this period.
- Kentucky District was part of Virginia during the entire target period; Kentucky did not separate until 1792. If an ancestor was in western Virginia or the Kentucky District, records were created under Virginia county jurisdiction and are held in Virginia repositories.
- The FamilySearch `place_search_all` tool returned no historical representations beyond the standard Virginia entry, so no additional split is documented from tool results.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Vital Records returned Virginia-specific content in this survey (the constructed-URL fetch resolved to a generic page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). The FamilySearch Wiki does not confirm a statewide start date via this survey's tool results. No civil vital registration system at the statewide level is documented for the target period 1775–1783.
- **What exists:** No FamilySearch collection for Virginia vital records covers this period as civil registration.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for the target period.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration is effectively absent for 1775–1783.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (see Church records below); county marriage bonds and marriage registers held at county courthouses; family Bible records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (the established church whose parish registers were mandated by colonial law), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry records (Anglican/Episcopal), meeting minutes (Quaker).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection ID 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) — covers the target period.
- **Where else held:** Local parish archives, diocesan archives (Episcopal Diocese of Virginia, Richmond), and the Library of Virginia.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** No federal census was taken during 1775–1783. The first federal census (1790) was taken after the war, but **Virginia's 1790 census schedules were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814** (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The earliest surviving federal census for Virginia is 1800.
- **State/provincial census:** None known for this period from tool results.
- **Primary substitutes for census:** Virginia county tax lists beginning in 1782 are the recognized substitute for the missing 1790 census:
  - FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection ID 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) begins within the target period.
  - Digitized volume 005301449: "State enumerations / tax lists, 1782-1799" — 87 images, **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** (browse-only by name).
- **Access:** Tax list volume 005301449 must be searched via full-text search, not a name index.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, county court order books, civil and criminal proceedings.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection ID 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) — covers the target period.
- **Digitized volume:** 005301448 — Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795, 158 images, **61% name-indexed** (indexed + images). Augusta County in the western Shenandoah Valley was a major recruiting and supply county during the Revolution.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia holds many transcripts and microfilm copies.
- **Note on probate strategy:** A soldier who died during service (testate or intestate) would generate estate papers in his home county. Search the will books and administration bonds for the specific county of residence.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia granted its own land patents and military bounty lands. The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for Virginia returned only generic content in this survey; the Virginia State Land Office (Library of Virginia) holds original grants and patents.
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants, patents, bounty land warrants (Revolutionary War), mortgages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection ID 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) — covers the target period.
- **Digitized volume — bounty warrants:** 005301447 — "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779-1800," 341 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image.** This is a critical post-war record linking soldiers to land claims.
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio:** After the war Virginia issued bounty land warrants redeemable in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records are at the Virginia State Library (Library of Virginia). These records name the veteran and often the unit of service. Search them separately from Virginia deed books (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Where held (originals):** County courthouses (deed books); Library of Virginia (patents, grants, bounty warrant files).

### Military records — PRIMARY FOCUS
Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia). Multiple overlapping record series must be searched:

**FamilySearch collection — directly on target:**
- "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection ID 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678).

**At NARA (federal records):**
- **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — NARA Record Group 93. These document regular Continental Army service for Virginia Line soldiers. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) indexes much of this material.
- **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA Record Group 15. Pension files are among the richest genealogical sources; they often include a veteran's narrative of service, family relationships, and places of residence. Many are digitized on Fold3 and at Ancestry.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**At the Library of Virginia (state records):**
- **Virginia militia records** — The Library of Virginia in Richmond holds the original Virginia militia muster rolls, pay vouchers, and claims. These are **physical/microfilm records** not fully available online.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Published / transcribed sources:**
- Virginia State Navy records have been published and transcribed.
- The Virginia Genealogical Society and DAR have published pension abstracts and rosters.

**Digitization levels for military-adjacent volumes:**
- Volume 005301447 (bounty warrants): browse-only images (0% indexed, not full-text).
- Volume 005301449 (tax lists): full-text searchable, not name-indexed.
- Volume 005301448 (Augusta court order books): 61% name-indexed + images.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards affiliated with Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations; family burial grounds on plantations and farms.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Virginia burial grounds.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this period; church vestry books sometimes record burials. The Association for the Preservation of Virginia Antiquities and local historical societies have transcribed many early graveyards.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, published from 1736 through the Revolutionary era) is the principal wartime newspaper. Multiple competing editions existed.
- **Content value:** Wartime issues carried military appointments, muster notices, loyalty oaths, runaway and deserter notices, and death notices.
- **Where held:** Microfilm at the Library of Virginia; some digitized issues available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and through university libraries.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Immigration to Virginia largely predates or postdates the war. Wartime Loyalist departures (emigration) and arrival of French allies are the primary movement events.
- **Record types:** No passenger-list series covers wartime arrivals in any systematic way. Loyalist claims (British records) document those who left. Continental Army muster rolls record French officers who served in Virginia.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; Virginia county court order books may contain naturalization proceedings.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax and land tax — both instituted in Virginia in 1782, making them the earliest systematic post-colonial enumeration.
- **Date range:** 1782 onward (collection 1456723 begins 1782).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (originals and microfilm); FamilySearch collection 1456723 and volume 005301449 (full-text searchable).
- **Substitute value:** These lists name heads of household and taxable males, replacing the lost 1790 census. They also document property — horses, slaves, carriages — that can differentiate families of the same name.

### Other record types
- **County court minute books:** County courts transacted road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and local administrative business that names ordinary residents — not just litigants. Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books) is 61% indexed.
- **Vestry records:** Anglican vestry books recorded poor relief recipients and overseers of the poor — the wartime poor lists name families displaced or impoverished by the conflict.
- **Loyalist records:** If an ancestor sided with the Crown, British Loyalist Claims Commission records (held at the National Archives, UK, and on microfilm) document their losses and movements.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (ID 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (ID 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (ID 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (ID 2134567); plus 3 digitized volumes (see above) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — Continental Line service, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription; https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (online portal) | Finding aids for RG 93 and RG 15; some digitized pension files | Free to browse; https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census, military collections | Subscription; https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and burial transcriptions | Free; https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Virginia Gazette and other historical newspapers | Subscription; https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` for the target period returned 3 digitized volumes (totalResults: 3, no nextPageToken — this is the complete result set for the military, land, and tax record-type groups searched). A separate volume search across all record type groups also returned the same 3 volumes, confirming no additional unindexed volumes were missed. The 5 indexed FamilySearch collections above were returned by `collections_search` as the complete set (totalForPlace: 5).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, state military records, land patents, tax lists, court records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington D.C. | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person or written request; some digitized on Fold3 |
| County courthouses (each Virginia county) | Deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or mail |
| Virginia State Land Office (Library of Virginia) | Land patents, grants, bounty warrant surveys | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Virginia Historical Society / Virginia Museum of History & Culture, Richmond | Published rosters, local histories, family papers | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records held at the Library of Virginia — not fully digitized or indexed online (per FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- Virginia Military District of Ohio warrant and survey files at the Virginia State Library — physical access required for the full series.
- County-level deed books, marriage bonds, and court order books for most Virginia counties (only Augusta County court order books are confirmed in the FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period).
- Vestry records and poor relief books for most Anglican/Episcopal parishes.
- Virginia Loyalist records (held at the National Archives, UK).

## Known record losses
- **1790 Virginia federal census:** Destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from 1782 are the recognized substitute (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). No other census survives for the 1775–1800 window.
- No other record-class losses were stated by tool results in this survey. An empty search result should be treated as a coverage or digitization gap, not proof of destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files at NARA.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant applications (NARA RG 15) are among the most genealogically detailed records of the era — a veteran's narrative of service, affidavits by neighbors, and family data are frequently included. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry index much of this material (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Search both NARA and the Library of Virginia.** NARA holds the federal Continental Army records; the Library of Virginia holds separate Virginia state militia records. A man could appear in one system but not the other, or in both (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use the 1782 Virginia tax lists as your census.** Virginia's 1790 census is gone. Personal property and land tax lists (collection 1456723; volume 005301449) beginning in 1782 name heads of household across the state — they are the first systematic post-war enumeration available. Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable but not name-indexed, so use full-text search rather than the standard name-search interface (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Check the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Post-war bounty land warrants were redeemable in Ohio, not Virginia. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect a veteran's name to his unit and land claim — a separate search trail from Virginia deed books (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Browse Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume 005301447.** This 341-image volume (1779-1800) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image. Plan for manual browsing if you pursue the bounty warrant trail.
- **Augusta County court order books (volume 005301448) are 61% indexed.** Augusta County in the western Shenandoah Valley was a major recruitment and supply region during the Revolution; its court records name many wartime residents. Search directly on FamilySearch for this volume.
- **Church records substitute for missing vital records.** No statewide civil registration existed in Virginia during 1775–1783. Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and Baptist and Presbyterian registers are the primary sources for births, marriages, and deaths. Collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929) covers the period.
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned generic content.** All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) resolved to a generic guide rather than Virginia-specific pages in this survey. Consult the Virginia Military Records article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records for authoritative, jurisdiction-specific guidance.

- **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA Record Group 15. Pension files are among the richest genealogical sources; they often include a veteran's narrative of service, family relationships, and places of residence. Many are digitized on Fold3 and at Ancestry.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Revolutionary War section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**At the Library of Virginia (state records):**
- **Virginia militia records** — The Library of Virginia in Richmond holds the original Virginia militia muster rolls, pay vouchers, and claims. These are **physical/microfilm records** not fully available online.
(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)

**Published / transcribed sources:**
- Virginia State Navy records have been published and transcribed.
- The Virginia Genealogical Society and DAR have published pension abstracts and rosters.

**Digitization levels for military-adjacent volumes:**
- Volume 005301447 (bounty warrants): browse-only images (0% indexed, not full-text).
- Volume 005301449 (tax lists): full-text searchable, not name-indexed.
- Volume 005301448 (Augusta court order books): 61% name-indexed + images.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards affiliated with Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations; family burial grounds on plantations and farms.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Virginia burial grounds.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this period; church vestry books sometimes record burials. The Association for the Preservation of Virginia Antiquities and local historical societies have transcribed many early graveyards.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg, published from 1736 through the Revolutionary era) is the principal wartime newspaper. Multiple competing editions existed.
- **Content value:** Wartime issues carried military appointments, muster notices, loyalty oaths, runaway and deserter notices, and death notices.
- **Where held:** Microfilm at the Library of Virginia; some digitized issues available via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and through university libraries.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Immigration to Virginia largely predates or postdates the war. Wartime Loyalist departures (emigration) and arrival of French allies are the primary movement events.
- **Record types:** No passenger-list series covers wartime arrivals in any systematic way. Loyalist claims (British records) document those who left. Continental Army muster rolls record French officers who served in Virginia.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; Virginia county court order books may contain naturalization proceedings.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax and land tax — both instituted in Virginia in 1782, making them the earliest systematic post-colonial enumeration.
- **Date range:** 1782 onward (collection 1456723 begins 1782).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (originals and microfilm); FamilySearch collection 1456723 and volume 005301449 (full-text searchable).
- **Substitute value:** These lists name heads of household and taxable males, replacing the lost 1790 census. They also document property — horses, slaves, carriages — that can differentiate families of the same name.

### Other record types
- **County court minute books:** County courts transacted road maintenance assignments, poor relief, and local administrative business that names ordinary residents — not just litigants. Volume 005301448 (Augusta County court order books) is 61% indexed.
- **Vestry records:** Anglican vestry books recorded poor relief recipients and overseers of the poor — the wartime poor lists name families displaced or impoverished by the conflict.
- **Loyalist records:** If an ancestor sided with the Crown, British Loyalist Claims Commission records (held at the National Archives, UK, and on microfilm) document their losses and movements.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (ID 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (ID 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (ID 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (ID 2134567); plus 3 digitized volumes (see above) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — Continental Line service, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription; https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (online portal) | Finding aids for RG 93 and RG 15; some digitized pension files | Free to browse; https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census, military collections | Subscription; https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and burial transcriptions | Free; https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Virginia Gazette and other historical newspapers | Subscription; https://www.newspapers.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` for the target period returned 3 digitized volumes (totalResults: 3, no nextPageToken — this is the complete result set for the military, land, and tax record-type groups searched). A separate volume search across all record type groups also returned the same 3 volumes, confirming no additional unindexed volumes were missed. The 5 indexed FamilySearch collections above were returned by `collections_search` as the complete set (totalForPlace: 5).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, state military records, land patents, tax lists, court records | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington D.C. | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person or written request; some digitized on Fold3 |
| County courthouses (each Virginia county) | Deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds | In-person or mail |
| Virginia State Land Office (Library of Virginia) | Land patents, grants, bounty warrant surveys | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Virginia Historical Society / Virginia Museum of History & Culture, Richmond | Published rosters, local histories, family papers | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records held at the Library of Virginia — not fully digitized or indexed online (per FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- Virginia Military District of Ohio warrant and survey files at the Virginia State Library — physical access required for the full series.
- County-level deed books, marriage bonds, and court order books for most Virginia counties (only Augusta County court order books are confirmed in the FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period).
- Vestry records and poor relief books for most Anglican/Episcopal parishes.
- Virginia Loyalist records (held at the National Archives, UK).

## Known record losses
- **1790 Virginia federal census:** Destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists from 1782 are the recognized substitute (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). No other census survives for the 1775–1800 window.
- No other record-class losses were stated by tool results in this survey. An empty search result should be treated as a coverage or digitization gap, not proof of destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files at NARA.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant applications (NARA RG 15) are among the most genealogically detailed records of the era — a veteran's narrative of service, affidavits by neighbors, and family data are frequently included. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and Ancestry index much of this material (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Search both NARA and the Library of Virginia.** NARA holds the federal Continental Army records; the Library of Virginia holds separate Virginia state militia records. A man could appear in one system but not the other, or in both (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use the 1782 Virginia tax lists as your census.** Virginia's 1790 census is gone. Personal property and land tax lists (collection 1456723; volume 005301449) beginning in 1782 name heads of household across the state — they are the first systematic post-war enumeration available. Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable but not name-indexed, so use full-text search rather than the standard name-search interface (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Check the Virginia Military District of Ohio.** Post-war bounty land warrants were redeemable in Ohio, not Virginia. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect a veteran's name to his unit and land claim — a separate search trail from Virginia deed books (FamilySearch Wiki, Virginia Military Records, Post-War Bounty Lands: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Browse Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume 005301447.** This 341-image volume (1779-1800) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image. Plan for manual browsing if you pursue the bounty warrant trail.
- **Augusta County court order books (volume 005301448) are 61% indexed.** Augusta County in the western Shenandoah Valley was a major recruitment and supply region during the Revolution; its court records name many wartime residents. Search directly on FamilySearch for this volume.
- **Church records substitute for missing vital records.** No statewide civil registration existed in Virginia during 1775–1783. Anglican/Episcopal vestry books and Baptist and Presbyterian registers are the primary sources for births, marriages, and deaths. Collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929) covers the period.
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned generic content.** All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) resolved to a generic guide rather than Virginia-specific pages in this survey. Consult the Virginia Military Records article directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records for authoritative, jurisdiction-specific guidance.

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

New Orleans in the early 1800s is a complicated research environment precisely because of disaster history. The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records, and subsequent yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further archival damage. What the locality guide explains about survival and substitutes comes down to three things: what made it through, where copies are held, and what fills the gaps.

**Records that survived**

The records that made it through are primarily the **notarial archives** and **Catholic sacramental registers**. Notarial acts — covering property transfers, marriage contracts, successions (the Louisiana civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships, emancipations, and slave transactions — survived because individual notaries kept their own copies and duplicates were maintained separately. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** now holds over 30 million pages of these acts dating to 1734, covering the whole of your early-1800s window. *Critical warning:* these records are organized by notary name and date, not by the parties' names — you cannot search by your ancestor's name; you need to know approximately when an act was executed and which notary handled it.

Colonial-era notarial records from the French period (1718–1769) and Spanish period (1769–1803) sit separately at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building.

**Catholic sacramental registers** at the **Archdiocese of New Orleans** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 at St. Louis Cathedral, with gaps — are the primary substitute for vital records before civil registration began. Many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch and are searchable through the **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** collection (~987,000 indexed records with images). Records before 1803 will be in French or Spanish, not English.

**Where to look for copies and substitutes**

- **FamilySearch** — one digitized volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts covering 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images) exists, but it is entirely unindexed and must be browsed page by page.
- **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) — territorial and early state records.
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — the Louisiana pages (vital records, church records, notarial archives) provide the most current details on what survives and where civil registration begins; worth visiting directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/.

**Key takeaway on empty results**

An empty result in an online database for this period almost always means the record has not been digitized or the index has gaps — *not* that the record was destroyed. The notarial archives in particular are enormous and largely unindexed online, so original visits or a local researcher are often necessary for the early 1800s.

Notarial records are organized by notary name and date, NOT by the names of the parties involved. A researcher must know an approximate date and the acting notary's name to locate a record — searching by ancestor name will not work in notarial indexes.

Colonial-era notarial records from the French period (1718-1769) and Spanish period (1769-1803) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — not at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, which holds records from 1733 onward including post-colonial records.

Fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further archival damage. Empty search results may reflect destruction, not absence of record creation.

Catholic sacramental registers (St. Louis Cathedral, 1731-present) are the primary vital records substitute for the pre-civil-registration period. These exist in French (1718-1769), Spanish (1769-1803), and English (after 1803) — researchers must be able to read the relevant language.

The FamilySearch collections for this area are indexed at the Louisiana state level, not at the Orleans Parish or New Orleans city level. Always search the Louisiana-level collection, not a city-specific one.

The one digitized FamilySearch volume for Orleans, Louisiana 1803-1820 (Notarial Acts, image group 004990115, 167 images) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image-by-image in French and English.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718. It passed to Spanish control in 1763 and briefly reverted to France before the Louisiana Purchase brought it under US authority in 1803. Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)
- **Parish seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana, United States. Louisiana uses parishes rather than counties.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** A major port city. Trade, shipping, cotton, sugar, and enslaved-labor plantations drove the economy. New Orleans was one of the largest cities in the antebellum United States.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American (post-1803), free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African and Afro-Caribbean populations, Irish and German immigrants (by the 1840s-50s), and others.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic, reflecting the French and Spanish colonial heritage. Protestant congregations grew after 1803 with Anglo-American in-migration.
- **Key historical events:** Great Fires of 1788 and 1794 (destroyed much of the French Quarter and many records); Louisiana Purchase 1803; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics; hurricanes and floods throughout the period. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)

## Boundary changes
- The territory that became Orleans Parish was administered successively under French colonial authority (1718-1769), Spanish colonial authority (1769-1803), a brief French interval, then the Territory of Orleans (1803-1812), and finally the State of Louisiana (1812-present).
- Records for events before 1803 are colonial records, not US records, and fall under either French or Spanish administrative systems.
- No further boundary changes affecting New Orleans itself within the 1800-1860 period were identified in tool results.

## Disaster history and record survival

This is the most critical section for early-1800s New Orleans research.

**Known losses:** The great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Subsequent yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods caused further damage to archival holdings. (Sources: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)

**What survived:** Despite these disasters, significant sources survive for the early 1800s:
1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, though with gaps caused by the fires. - **Parish seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana, United States. Louisiana uses parishes rather than counties.

### Land records
