# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States (Late 1700s, ca. 1750–1800) — Quaker Communities

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was chartered in 1681 by William Penn as a proprietary colony; it became a U.S. state in 1787 (FamilySearch standardPlace date range +1787/). The late 1700s thus spans both the colonial and early statehood periods.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and the largest Quaker center in North America)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Pennsylvania (to 1776); Commonwealth of Pennsylvania / United States (1787–)
- **Population during period:** No FamilySearch population data was returned for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, trade, commerce, and milling dominated rural counties; Philadelphia was the leading mercantile city of the colonies.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers predominated in early settlement; Welsh Quakers, German (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite, Brethren), and Scots-Irish (Presbyterian) communities were also significant by the late 1700s.
- **Religious denominations:** Friends (Quakers) — the founding and dominant denomination; German Reformed; Lutheran; Presbyterian; Anglican/Episcopal; Mennonite; Baptist.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783) — Quakers held a pacifist position and many members were disowned for bearing arms or paying war taxes; Constitutional Convention (Philadelphia, 1787).

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's southern boundary with Maryland was settled by the Mason-Dixon Line survey (1763–1767).
- Internal county boundaries changed frequently during the late 1700s as settlement expanded westward. Chester County, for example, gave rise to Delaware County in 1789; records before 1789 for that territory are in Chester County files; records after 1789 may be in either county depending on the precise location of the event within old Chester County — search both.
- For any family research event, identify which county existed at that date, since deeds, probates, tax lists, and court records follow the county of creation, not modern boundaries.

## Available record types

Records in Pennsylvania during this period are held primarily at the county level (deeds, probate, court minutes) or the meeting level (Quaker registers). No statewide civil registration existed before 1906.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records and Pennsylvania Church Records were not returned as distinct Pennsylvania-specific pages in this survey (a generic overview page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records was returned instead); no Pennsylvania-specific registration start date can be cited from a page fetched in this run.
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No statewide civil birth, marriage, or death registration. Quaker meeting registers are the closest functional equivalent — see Church Records below.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker meeting records, other church registers, county deed books, probate records, tax lists, and newspapers.

### Church records (PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD)

**Quaker (Society of Friends) — the central record class for late-1700s Pennsylvania Quaker families**

Quaker monthly meetings kept meticulous records. According to the FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), monthly meetings recorded:
- **Births and deaths** — registered in the meeting's birth and death registers
- **Marriages** — performed "in the manner of Friends," witnessed by the full meeting; marriage certificates bore the signatures of all attendees (typically 30–100 or more names), making these an exceptionally rich source of community and family connections
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when a member moved from one monthly meeting to another; both the sending and receiving meeting recorded the transfer; essential for tracing family migration between counties and states
- **Disownments (disciplinary proceedings)** — recorded when a member violated Friends' discipline (bearing arms, marrying outside the meeting, paying war taxes, etc.); these name the individual and often family members, and for the Revolutionary War period they are a proxy source for identifying Quaker men caught up in the conflict

**Meeting hierarchy (religious jurisdiction):** Local monthly meetings reported to quarterly meetings, which reported to Philadelphia Yearly Meeting. Philadelphia Yearly Meeting governed Friends across Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia — so a certificate of removal could move a family from Chester County, PA into another state entirely; always search the receiving meeting's records, not only Pennsylvania ones.

**Key Quaker counties for this period:** Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia, and Delaware County had particularly dense Quaker populations (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).

**Language:** English.

**Digitization status:** FamilySearch volume_search returned one digitized volume: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only images.** FamilySearch has microfilmed many additional monthly meeting minutes and registers beyond this one volume (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), but only one volume appeared in the first page of volume_search results (see Coverage note in Repository Guide below).

**Other denominations present in this period:**
- German Reformed and Lutheran — kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers, usually in German
- Presbyterian — session records and baptismal rolls
- Anglican/Episcopal — vestry records and registers
- Mennonite / German Baptist (Brethren) — congregational records, often in German

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first U.S. federal census was 1790 (heads of household only; no individual ages; women named only as heads of household). Pennsylvania's 1790 census is indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Pre-1790:** No federal census exists. Pennsylvania tax assessments (see Tax Records) are the primary substitute.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct its own state census during this period.

### Probate and court records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 1999196, Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994, covers the target period and contains 3,200,560 images. The collection has 0 indexed records and is not full-text searchable — **browse-only.** Access at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196.
- **Holding level:** County (the county that existed at the date of death).
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Research value:** Quaker wills often identify a Friends' burial ground as the intended place of interment, confirming meeting affiliation. Inventories describe household goods and can help date a family's economic situation.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was granted under the Penn proprietary system (metes and bounds descriptions), not the federal rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Originally the Penn family proprietorship; after the Revolution, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds warrants, surveys, and patents. The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Land and Property page was not returned as a distinct Pennsylvania-specific page in this survey.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deed books (county level), and tax lists.
- **Research value:** Quaker families often appear in clusters in county deed books — neighbors and grantees were frequently fellow meeting members, and identifying them can extend a family network.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783).
- **Quaker note:** Friends were pacifists; many were disowned by their meeting for military service or for paying war taxes or fines in lieu of service. Disownment records in meeting minutes are thus a source for identifying Quaker men whose relationship to the Revolution would not otherwise appear in military service records.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and militia rolls at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/). Published Pennsylvania Archives volumes contain many militia and muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal service and pension records; Pennsylvania State Archives and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for state records.

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Friends' meetinghouses maintained their own burial grounds; in the 18th century, Quaker graves were often marked with small plain stones or none at all. Sexton records and burial lists are typically part of the meeting register.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has memorial pages for many Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds, though 18th-century stones may be unreadable, unmarked, or not yet recorded in the database.
- **Physical records:** The meeting register and any separate burial list held by the meeting or at the Friends Historical Library.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) and Pennsylvania Packet (1771–) published death notices and some community news. Quaker marriages were not typically advertised in newspapers (Quaker marriage was a meeting proceeding, not a civil or church ceremony), but death notices occasionally appeared.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; digitized issues available at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Accessible Archives.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Quaker context:** By the late 1700s, most Pennsylvania Quaker families were third- or fourth-generation residents. Certificates of removal are the primary mobility document within the Quaker network; they function as the Quaker equivalent of a transfer letter and are held in meeting records.
- **Earlier colonial arrivals:** Ship passenger lists for earlier Quaker immigrants (pre-1750) are indexed in William P. Filby's Passenger and Immigration Lists Index and at Ancestry.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. Pennsylvania county court records hold declarations and final papers; these are generally not indexed online for this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania tax lists survive from the colonial period onward. County-level property and personal property assessments are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and county courthouses.
- **Research value:** Pennsylvania tax assessments from 1779 and 1782 are particularly important: they place a head of household in a specific township for the pre-1790 period before any federal census exists. Tax lists substitute for census records for the entire 1750–1790 window.
- **Access:** Pennsylvania State Archives; many have been abstracted and published by county genealogical societies.

- **Meeting minutes (narrative):** Beyond the registers of births/marriages/deaths, the narrative minutes of monthly meeting business often name ordinary members in the context of appointing oversight committees, managing relief for the poor, and handling disciplinary cases. These are part of the same meeting archive.
- **Meeting poor relief records:** Friends' meetings supported their own members in need; relief accounts and lists name recipients and can document people who surface nowhere else.
- **William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy** (6 volumes): Abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records. This published finding aid is the standard starting point for Pennsylvania Quaker research before consulting original registers (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).

Here is the locality guide the research agent produced:

---

## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry Research Guide

**Coverage period surveyed:** 1870–1910 (heart of Pittsburgh's steel boom)

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**City Directories**
The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds annual city directories from the 1810s onward, listing **name, occupation, and address** — an essential tool for tracking steel workers year by year between censuses.

**Federal Census Records**
The 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses each include an occupation column useful for identifying steel and mill workers. Note: the 1890 census was largely destroyed and is unavailable.

**Catholic Ethnic Parish Registers**
For many Pittsburgh steel-worker families (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), Catholic parish registers are the **primary source for births, marriages, and deaths** before Pennsylvania's statewide registration began in 1906. Registers are held at individual parishes or the Diocese of Pittsburgh archives. A critical tip: Pittsburgh Catholic parishes were organized by **ethnicity, not geography** — identify the national-origin community first to find the right parish.

**County Marriage Records**
Indexed at FamilySearch from 1885; the Allegheny County courthouse holds earlier records.

**Naturalization Records**
Pre-1906 naturalization petitions are held at the **Allegheny County courthouse** and the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region). These often reveal origin village and arrival date for immigrant steel workers.

**Probate Records**
FamilySearch holds approximately 3.2 million browse-only images of Allegheny County probate records — digitized but **not name-indexed**, so browsing by date is required.

**Company Employment & Union Records**
Fragmentary employment rolls and union membership records are held physically at:
- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh)
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives**

These are among the most valuable industrial-occupational sources and are **not available online**.

**Newspaper Obituaries**
Because Pennsylvania statewide death certificates don't begin until 1906, newspaper obituaries are a primary death source for the entire 19th century. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh and the Heinz History Center hold Pittsburgh newspaper runs.

**Church Burial Registers**
Also a key death source for pre-1906 deaths, especially for immigrants whose deaths predate civil registration.

---

### Critical Research Tips

1. **Don't rely only on online databases.** The most important occupational and industrial records for Pittsburgh are physical-only collections at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives.

2. **Identify national origin first.** Catholic parishes were organized by ethnicity — knowing whether an ancestor was Polish, Slovak, Croatian, or Italian points you to the right parish register.

3. **Watch the Allegheny City boundary.** Allegheny City was an independent municipality until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in **1907**. Records for families living there are filed separately from Pittsburgh proper.

---

A targeted research plan for specific individuals in the Pittsburgh steel workforce can be built from this guide as a next step.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1870–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh chartered as a city in 1816; Allegheny County formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; consult U.S. decennial census published totals directly (1870: ~86,000 city; 1900: ~322,000 city; county significantly larger).
- **Economy:** Dominant industry was iron and steel manufacturing, anchored by Carnegie Steel and dozens of subsidiary mills along the Monongahela, Allegheny, and Ohio rivers. Glass manufacturing, coal and coke, railroads, and river trade were also major employers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive in-migration from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, and Italy from the 1870s onward. Earlier settler stock was predominantly Scots-Irish, English, and German. By 1900 the majority of mill workers were recent immigrants from Central and Southern Europe.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, and various Eastern Orthodox bodies serving Slavic communities.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike (1892) — a pivotal labor event generating newspaper coverage and court records naming workers; rapid industrialization 1870–1900; massive annexations of surrounding boroughs into Pittsburgh (1907 consolidation absorbed Allegheny City).

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County's boundaries have been stable since 1800. No mid-period splits affect this survey.
- **Important:** The independent city of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was merged into Pittsburgh in 1907. Records for people living in Allegheny City before 1907 are filed under Allegheny City, not Pittsburgh. Search both city directories and church registers under both names.
- Pennsylvania is a state-land (not federal-land) state; land records originate with the state land office and the county recorder of deeds, not the Bureau of Land Management.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (FamilySearch collection 1921317) begins in 1906, which is consistent with statewide death registration beginning that year. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; a specific statewide birth-registration start date was not confirmed by any tool result — do not assume one. For marriages, the FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (id: 1921317) begins in 1885 at the county level.
- **What exists:**
  - Marriages from 1885: county-level records, indexed and imaged at FamilySearch (collection 1921317, 524,189 records).
  - Civil marriages 1677–1950: FamilySearch collection 1571957 (312,045 records, indexed + images).
  - Compiled marriages 1700–1900: FamilySearch collection 1502909 (198,765 records, name-indexed, no images).
  - Death certificates: the Pennsylvania statewide series begins 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records fully indexed + images) — this is just outside the core 1870–1900 window but covers deaths in the decade after.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online); Allegheny County courthouse for originals; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for state copies.
- **Gaps:** Births in the late 1800s are not covered by any indexed Pennsylvania statewide collection identified in this survey. Deaths before 1906 are likewise not in the statewide series.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers (see Church records below); Pittsburgh city directories for address and occupation; mortality schedules in the federal census (available 1850–1885, listing deaths in the preceding year).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (many ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Serbian Orthodox, and others.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic parish registers are the primary source for vital events among Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian steel workers.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes retain their own registers; diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh for Roman Catholic records) hold some consolidated series. FamilySearch has microfilmed selected Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch wiki_search results note that Catholic parish registers are often the best source for immigrant family data in this period.
- **Key access point:** The FamilySearch wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records states that Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and that their registers are often the best source for family data.
- **Language:** Many early Catholic registers for Polish, Slovak, and Croatian parishes are in Latin (sacramental entries) with vernacular marginalia. German Lutheran registers may be in German. The researcher must be able to read the original language or use a translator.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 enumerations all cover Allegheny County. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed; only a fragment survives nationally. The 1870–1900 schedules list each person's occupation — a critical source for identifying steel and mill workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1870 and 1880, listing deaths in the year preceding the census with cause of death and occupation.
- **Access:** 1870–1910 federal censuses are indexed and searchable at Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a systematic statewide census between federal enumerations during this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate records run from county formation (1788) through the present.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (Pittsburgh). FamilySearch holds 3,200,560 browse-only probate images in collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When the ancestor left a will, search the will books; when no will is found, search the administration bonds and letters of administration.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania's colonial and post-colonial land system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania's land grants originate with the state land office (Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg). County-level deed transfers are recorded with the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records (annual county assessment rolls), and state warrants/patents.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1788; state land office warrants from colonial period.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (Pittsburgh) for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for original warrants and patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) immediately precedes the target window; Spanish-American War (1898); World War I (1917–1918) falls just after.
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA; pension files often contain family information including wife's and children's names. Draft registration cards (World War I) capture men born approximately 1872–1900.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and National Archives at Philadelphia for regional records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, nonsectarian, 1844); St. Mary's Cemetery and other Catholic parish cemeteries; numerous ethnic community cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries with headstone photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemetery offices; some transferred to the Heinz History Center.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily newspapers throughout the late 1800s. Historical Newspapers — Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized Pittsburgh-area papers.
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription online).
- **Content value:** Obituaries (often the only death record for this period), marriage announcements, strike and labor coverage naming workers, legal notices (estate advertisements, naturalization notices), and neighborhood news columns that identify residents by name.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** The massive immigration to Pittsburgh's steel mills in the late 1800s is documented in naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records.
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New York (Ellis Island, pre-1892 Castle Garden) and Port of Baltimore were the primary entry points for Central and Southern European immigrants bound for Pittsburgh.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization (filed in any Pennsylvania court of record before 1906 — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas is the primary venue). FamilySearch holds a partially indexed naturalization volume (image group 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, covering 1790–1915, with English and German).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.
- **Post-1906 naturalizations:** After 27 September 1906, naturalizations were handled exclusively by federal courts and the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization; NARA holds these records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county assessment rolls (real and personal property); per-capita (poll) tax.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County assessment rolls from the late 18th century.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds assessment rolls for many counties; some are at Allegheny County offices. These records name all taxable residents annually and are valuable substitutes for census years.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists fill gaps between census years (especially 1880–1900) and are the primary tool when the 1890 census for a household is missing.

### Occupational and industrial records (primary focus)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary. The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) states that some survive at the **Heinz History Center** and the **Rivers of Steel archives**. Contact both repositories before concluding records do not exist for a specific company.
- **Union membership records:** Labor union records for steelworkers are held by the United Steelworkers (USW) archives at the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (now part of the Heinz History Center) and at the Walter P. Reuther Library, Wayne State University.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward. Directories list name, occupation, and street address for each year — essential for tracking workers between censuses.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania published annual reports of the Bureau of Factory Inspection from 1889 onward, listing factories by location and workforce size. These do not name individual workers but establish which plants operated in which mill towns and years.
- **Federal census occupation columns:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses each include an occupation column for every individual. The 1880 census also records relationship to head of household, which is valuable for identifying boarders (common among steel workers) and extended family.

### Other record types
- **Ethnic newspapers:** The Pittsburgh area had Slovak, Polish, and Croatian-language newspapers serving the immigrant community. These published birth, marriage, and death notices in the heritage language and survive on microfilm at the Carnegie Library and at ethnic fraternal organization archives.
- **Fraternal and beneficial society records:** Organizations such as the National Slovak Society, Polish National Alliance, and Croatian fraternal unions kept membership rolls and death benefit claims. These records often survive at national headquarters and may include birth and death dates, beneficiary names, and place of origin in Europe.
- **Coroner's records:** Allegheny County Coroner's inquest files document deaths by accident, violence, and sudden illness — disproportionately covering industrial accidents, which were common in the steel mills. Held at the Allegheny County offices; some are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Homestead and mill town records:** Many steel workers lived in company-controlled mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport) rather than Pittsburgh proper. These boroughs kept their own civic records — voter registrations, school enrollment, local court minutes — at the borough office or county courthouse.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1870–1910 for Allegheny County) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records and headstone photographs for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Pittsburgh-area newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records (Civil War service and pension files; WWI draft cards) | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger arrival manifests; post-1906 naturalization records; federal court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search and collections_search tools resolved to the Pennsylvania state level (not Allegheny County specifically) and returned 3 digitized volumes and 6 indexed collections total. These represent the available indexed material at the state scope; Allegheny County-specific unindexed volumes may exist at FamilySearch beyond what appeared in this page of results. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not separately queried in this run — consult it directly for Allegheny County microfilm holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial and immigration records; some surviving company employment records; union archives; local history collections | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Rivers of Steel archives | Steel-industry company records (fragmentary) | Contact for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from the 1810s; local newspaper microfilm; local history books | In-person; some digitized |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Pittsburgh) | County marriages (1885–); deeds; naturalization petitions (pre-1906); probate; coroner records | In-person; some records at state archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State land warrants; county assessment rolls; state vital records; factory inspector reports | In-person; some online |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers and sacramental records | Contact archives; appointment required |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania / Heinz History Center | USW labor union archives; ethnic fraternal records; manuscript collections | In-person |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | Naturalization records; federal court records for Pennsylvania | In-person / mail request |

## Records NOT online
- **Company employment records** for specific steel mills — fragmentary survival; physical only at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives.
- **Union membership rolls** — physical at Heinz History Center / USW archives and Reuther Library.
- **State factory inspector reports** (post-1889) — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives; not yet digitized or indexed.
- **Allegheny County coroner's inquest files** — physical at Allegheny County or Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Borough civic records** (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport, Allegheny City pre-1907) — physical at borough offices or county courthouse.
- **Ethnic fraternal society membership and death benefit records** — physical at national headquarters of each organization.
- **Pre-1906 birth registrations** — no statewide Pennsylvania series exists for this period; rely on church baptismal registers, which are held physically at individual parishes or diocesan archives.
- **County property tax assessment rolls** — largely physical at Pennsylvania State Archives.

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire at the Commerce Department — only fragments survive nationally. No tool result in this survey named specific Allegheny County losses beyond that. An empty search result in any online database is a coverage gap (records not yet digitized), not confirmation of destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with city directories.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s, as reported by the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records. A directory entry gives occupation and address for each year, letting you track a worker through the 1880–1900 window when the 1890 census is missing.
- **Identify the ethnic community before the parish.** Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by ethnicity (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), not geography. Identify the ancestor's national origin from the census or naturalization record first, then find the corresponding ethnic parish to locate baptismal and marriage registers. The FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records makes this the recommended first step.
- **Naturalization records document immigration origin.** Petitions for naturalization (filed in Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas before 1906) and declarations of intention name the country and often the village of origin in Europe. These are indexed only at 15% in the FamilySearch volume; search the Allegheny County courthouse records directly for the pre-1906 period.
- **Use the 1880 census relationship column.** The 1880 federal census records each person's relationship to the head of household. Many steel workers boarded with a family from the same village or ethnic group — the boarders and their hosts may be relatives.
- **Allegheny City records are separate from Pittsburgh records before 1907.** If an ancestor lived in what is now the North Shore or adjacent neighborhoods, check records under Allegheny City (an independent city until 1907) in addition to Pittsburgh.
- **Check fraternal and beneficial societies.** Organizations such as the National Slovak Society, Polish National Alliance, and Croatian fraternal unions held death benefit insurance policies. Claims files often survive with birth and death dates and the beneficiary's (spouse's or child's) identity.
- **Factory inspector reports establish employment context.** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Factory Inspection published annual reports from 1889 listing factories by location. These do not name workers but identify which mill was operating in which year — useful for dating an ancestor's employment period at a specific facility.
- **The Homestead Strike of 1892** generated extensive newspaper coverage and court records. If an ancestor worked at the Homestead works, Pittsburgh newspaper archives (Newspapers.com) for July–August 1892 may name workers directly.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1870–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh chartered as a city in 1816; Allegheny County formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; consult U.S. decennial census published totals directly (1870: ~86,000 city; 1900: ~322,000 city; county significantly larger).
- **Economy:** Dominant industry was iron and steel manufacturing, anchored by Carnegie Steel and dozens of subsidiary mills along the Monongahela, Allegheny, and Ohio rivers. Glass manufacturing, coal and coke, railroads, and river trade were also major employers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive in-migration from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, and Italy from the 1870s onward. Earlier settler stock was predominantly Scots-Irish, English, and German. By 1900 the majority of mill workers were recent immigrants from Central and Southern Europe.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (numerous ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, and various Eastern Orthodox bodies serving Slavic communities.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike (1892) — a pivotal labor event generating newspaper coverage and court records naming workers; rapid industrialization 1870–1900; massive annexations of surrounding boroughs into Pittsburgh (1907 consolidation absorbed Allegheny City).

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County's boundaries have been stable since 1800. No mid-period splits affect this survey.
- **Important:** The independent city of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was merged into Pittsburgh in 1907. Records for people living in Allegheny City before 1907 are filed under Allegheny City, not Pittsburgh. Search both city directories and church registers under both names.
- Pennsylvania is a state-land (not federal-land) state; land records originate with the state land office and the county recorder of deeds, not the Bureau of Land Management.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (FamilySearch collection 1921317) begins in 1906, which is consistent with statewide death registration beginning that year. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey; a specific statewide birth-registration start date was not confirmed by any tool result — do not assume one. For marriages, the FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (id: 1921317) begins in 1885 at the county level.
- **What exists:**
  - Marriages from 1885: county-level records, indexed and imaged at FamilySearch (collection 1921317, 524,189 records).
  - Civil marriages 1677–1950: FamilySearch collection 1571957 (312,045 records, indexed + images).
  - Compiled marriages 1700–1900: FamilySearch collection 1502909 (198,765 records, name-indexed, no images).
  - Death certificates: the Pennsylvania statewide series begins 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 records fully indexed + images) — this is just outside the core 1870–1900 window but covers deaths in the decade after.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online); Allegheny County courthouse for originals; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for state copies.
- **Gaps:** Births in the late 1800s are not covered by any indexed Pennsylvania statewide collection identified in this survey. Deaths before 1906 are likewise not in the statewide series.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers (see Church records below); Pittsburgh city directories for address and occupation; mortality schedules in the federal census (available 1850–1885, listing deaths in the preceding year).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (many ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Serbian Orthodox, and others.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic parish registers are the primary source for vital events among Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian steel workers.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes retain their own registers; diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh for Roman Catholic records) hold some consolidated series. FamilySearch has microfilmed selected Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch wiki_search results note that Catholic parish registers are often the best source for immigrant family data in this period.
- **Key access point:** The FamilySearch wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records states that Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and that their registers are often the best source for family data.
- **Language:** Many early Catholic registers for Polish, Slovak, and Croatian parishes are in Latin (sacramental entries) with vernacular marginalia. German Lutheran registers may be in German. The researcher must be able to read the original language or use a translator.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 enumerations all cover Allegheny County. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed; only a fragment survives nationally. The 1870–1900 schedules list each person's occupation — a critical source for identifying steel and mill workers.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1870 and 1880, listing deaths in the year preceding the census with cause of death and occupation.
- **Access:** 1870–1910 federal censuses are indexed and searchable at Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a systematic statewide census between federal enumerations during this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate records run from county formation (1788) through the present.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (Pittsburgh). FamilySearch holds 3,200,560 browse-only probate images in collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** When the ancestor left a will, search the will books; when no will is found, search the administration bonds and letters of administration.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania's colonial and post-colonial land system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania's land grants originate with the state land office (Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg). County-level deed transfers are recorded with the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records (annual county assessment rolls), and state warrants/patents.
- **Date range:** County deed records from 1788; state land office warrants from colonial period.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (Pittsburgh) for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for original warrants and patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) immediately precedes the target window; Spanish-American War (1898); World War I (1917–1918) falls just after.
- **Record types:** Civil War service and pension records at NARA; pension files often contain family information including wife's and children's names. Draft registration cards (World War I) capture men born approximately 1872–1900.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and National Archives at Philadelphia for regional records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, nonsectarian, 1844); St. Mary's Cemetery and other Catholic parish cemeteries; numerous ethnic community cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries with headstone photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual cemetery offices; some transferred to the Heinz History Center.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily newspapers throughout the late 1800s. Historical Newspapers — Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds digitized Pittsburgh-area papers.
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription online).
- **Content value:** Obituaries (often the only death record for this period), marriage announcements, strike and labor coverage naming workers, legal notices (estate advertisements, naturalization notices), and neighborhood news columns that identify residents by name.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** The massive immigration to Pittsburgh's steel mills in the late 1800s is documented in naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia, per the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records.
- **Relevant ports:** The Port of New York (Ellis Island, pre-1892 Castle Garden) and Port of Baltimore were the primary entry points for Central and Southern European immigrants bound for Pittsburgh.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA); declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization (filed in any Pennsylvania court of record before 1906 — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas is the primary venue). FamilySearch holds a partially indexed naturalization volume (image group 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, covering 1790–1915, with English and German).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.
- **Post-1906 naturalizations:** After 27 September 1906, naturalizations were handled exclusively by federal courts and the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization; NARA holds these records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county assessment rolls (real and personal property); per-capita (poll) tax.
- **Date range:** Allegheny County assessment rolls from the late 18th century.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds assessment rolls for many counties; some are at Allegheny County offices. These records name all taxable residents annually and are valuable substitutes for census years.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists fill gaps between census years (especially 1880–1900) and are the primary tool when the 1890 census for a household is missing.

### Occupational and industrial records (primary focus)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary. The FamilySearch wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records) states that some survive at the **Heinz History Center** and the **Rivers of Steel archives**. Contact both repositories before concluding records do not exist for a specific company.
- **Union membership records:** Labor union records for steelworkers are held by the United Steelworkers (USW) archives at the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania (now part of the Heinz History Center) and at the Walter P. Reuther Library, Wayne State University.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s onward. Directories list name, occupation, and street address for each year — essential for tracking workers between censuses.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania published annual reports of the Bureau of Factory Inspection from 1889 onward, listing factories by location and workforce size. These do not name individual workers but establish which plants operated in which mill towns and years.
- **Federal census occupation columns:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses each include an occupation column for every individual. The 1880 census also records relationship to head of household, which is valuable for identifying boarders (common among steel workers) and extended family.

### Other record types
- **Ethnic newspapers:** The Pittsburgh area had Slovak, Polish, and Croatian-language newspapers serving the immigrant community. These published birth, marriage, and death notices in the heritage language and survive on microfilm at the Carnegie Library and at ethnic fraternal organization archives.
- **Fraternal and beneficial society records:** Organizations such as the National Slovak Society, Polish National Alliance, and Croatian fraternal unions kept membership rolls and death benefit claims. These records often survive at national headquarters and may include birth and death dates, beneficiary names, and place of origin in Europe.
- **Coroner's records:** Allegheny County Coroner's inquest files document deaths by accident, violence, and sudden illness — disproportionately covering industrial accidents, which were common in the steel mills. Held at the Allegheny County offices; some are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Homestead and mill town records:** Many steel workers lived in company-controlled mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport) rather than Pittsburgh proper. These boroughs kept their own civic records — voter registrations, school enrollment, local court minutes — at the borough office or county courthouse.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (vol. 008120443, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1870–1910 for Allegheny County) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records and headstone photographs for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Pittsburgh-area newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records (Civil War service and pension files; WWI draft cards) | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger arrival manifests; post-1906 naturalization records; federal court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search and collections_search tools resolved to the Pennsylvania state level (not Allegheny County specifically) and returned 3 digitized volumes and 6 indexed collections total. These represent the available indexed material at the state scope; Allegheny County-specific unindexed volumes may exist at FamilySearch beyond what appeared in this page of results. The FamilySearch Catalog (catalog_search) was not separately queried in this run — consult it directly for Allegheny County microfilm holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial and immigration records; some surviving company employment records; union archives; local history collections | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| Rivers of Steel archives | Steel-industry company records (fragmentary) | Contact for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from the 1810s; local newspaper microfilm; local history books | In-person; some digitized |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Pittsburgh) | County marriages (1885–); deeds; naturalization petitions (pre-1906); probate; coroner records | In-person; some records at state archives |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State land warrants; county assessment rolls; state vital records; factory inspector reports | In-person; some online |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers and sacramental records | Contact archives; appointment required |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania / Heinz History Center | USW labor union archives; ethnic fraternal records; manuscript collections | In-person |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | Naturalization records; federal court records for Pennsylvania | In-person / mail request |

## Records NOT online
- **Company employment records** for specific steel mills — fragmentary survival; physical only at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives.
- **Union membership rolls** — physical at Heinz History Center / USW archives and Reuther Library.
- **State factory inspector reports** (post-1889) — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives; not yet digitized or indexed.
- **Allegheny County coroner's inquest files** — physical at Allegheny County or Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Borough civic records** (Homestead, Braddock, Duquesne, McKeesport, Allegheny City pre-1907) — physical at borough offices or county courthouse.
- **Ethnic fraternal society membership and death benefit records** — physical at national headquarters of each organization.
- **Pre-1906 birth registrations** — no statewide Pennsylvania series exists for this period; rely on church baptismal registers, which are held physically at individual parishes or diocesan archives.
- **County property tax assessment rolls** — largely physical at Pennsylvania State Archives.

## Known record losses
- The 1890 U.S. federal census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire at the Commerce Department — only fragments survive nationally. No tool result in this survey named specific Allegheny County losses beyond that. An empty search result in any online database is a coverage gap (records not yet digitized), not confirmation of destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start with city directories.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s, as reported by the FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records. A directory entry gives occupation and address for each year, letting you track a worker through the 1880–1900 window when the 1890 census is missing.
- **Identify the ethnic community before the parish.** Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by ethnicity (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), not geography. Identify the ancestor's national origin from the census or naturalization record first, then find the corresponding ethnic parish to locate baptismal and marriage registers. The FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records makes this the recommended first step.
- **Naturalization records document immigration origin.** Petitions for naturalization (filed in Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas before 1906) and declarations of intention name the country and often the village of origin in Europe. These are indexed only at 15% in the FamilySearch volume; search the Allegheny County courthouse records directly for the pre-1906 period.
- **Use the 1880 census relationship column.** The 1880 federal census records each person's relationship to the head of household. Many steel workers boarded with a family from the same village or ethnic group — the boarders and their hosts may be relatives.
- **Allegheny City records are separate from Pittsburgh records before 1907.** If an ancestor lived in what is now the North Shore or adjacent neighborhoods, check records under Allegheny City (an independent city until 1907) in addition to Pittsburgh.
- **Check fraternal and beneficial societies.** Organizations such as the National Slovak Society, Polish National Alliance, and Croatian fraternal unions held death benefit insurance policies. Claims files often survive with birth and death dates and the beneficiary's (spouse's or child's) identity.
- **Factory inspector reports establish employment context.** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Factory Inspection published annual reports from 1889 listing factories by location. These do not name workers but identify which mill was operating in which year — useful for dating an ancestor's employment period at a specific facility.
- **The Homestead Strike of 1892** generated extensive newspaper coverage and court records. If an ancestor worked at the Homestead works, Pittsburgh newspaper archives (Newspapers.com) for July–August 1892 may name workers directly.
- **Consult the Allegheny County Genealogy wiki page directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy — the FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool returned only generic content for all four sections in this survey, so local research detail must be retrieved from that page directly.

**Philadelphia County/City, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic**
*(Locality Guide: loc_001)*

## Key Finding Up Front

No civil vital registration existed in Pennsylvania in 1793. **Church burial records are the only primary documentation of deaths.** The most genealogically valuable epidemic-specific sources are physical-only collections — not yet digitized or indexed online.

---

These are the highest-priority records for tracing families directly affected by the 1793 outbreak:

- **Mathew Carey's published list of the dead** — names victims; held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**
- **Committee of Citizens minutes** — the emergency relief committee organized during the epidemic; at **HSP**
- **Bush Hill Hospital records** — the makeshift hospital that treated epidemic patients; also at **HSP** and/or the **Philadelphia City Archives**

None of these have been indexed or digitized in the FamilySearch/Ancestry ecosystem as of this survey. On-site or mail research at HSP or the Philadelphia City Archives is required.

---

## Church Burial Records

Because civil death registration didn't exist, church sexton records and burial registers are critical. Look especially for:

- **African Methodist Episcopal (Mother Bethel) Church** — African American community was hit hard and organized much of the relief effort (Richard Allen/Absalom Jones)
- **Christ Church**, **St. Peter's**, **St. Mary's** (Episcopal/Catholic)
- **Society of Friends (Quaker)** Monthly Meeting registers — the **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800** are digitized on FamilySearch but *unindexed* (browse image-by-image only)
- **German Lutheran and Reformed** congregations

**Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has published transcriptions of many Philadelphia church registers; check their holdings and the **Pennsylvania Vital Records** collection.

---

## Bracketing Census Records

| Record | Coverage | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1790 U.S. Federal Census | Pre-epidemic household snapshot | Indexed on FamilySearch & Ancestry |
| 1800 U.S. Federal Census | Post-epidemic household snapshot | Indexed on FamilySearch & Ancestry |

Comparing the two censuses for the same household can reveal epidemic losses (missing adults, household size changes, changed head of household).

---

## Probate Records

A **surge of probate filings from late 1793 through early 1794** is one of the most practical places to search for epidemic casualties. Wills and administrations filed in that window frequently name surviving family members.

- FamilySearch holds Philadelphia probate records (~3.2 million images) but they require **image-by-image browsing** — no name index for this period.
- Originals: **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (City Hall)

---

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** — Philadelphia | Carey's list of the dead, Committee of Citizens records, Bush Hill materials, manuscript collections |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records, some hospital/institutional records |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** | Transcribed church registers, compiled indexes |
| **FamilySearch** | Quaker minutes (unindexed), probate images (browse-only), some indexed marriage records, federal censuses |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses, Philadelphia death certificates (begin 1803), some church transcriptions |
