entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682 from William Penn's original land grant. The city of Philadelphia was incorporated 1701.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county seat coincide)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793. The epidemic killed approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population — between August and November 1793, per the Wikipedia article on the Yellow fever epidemic of 1793 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793).
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; commerce, shipping, crafts manufacturing; served as the national capital 1790–1800, making it also a center of federal government administration.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (founding community), German immigrants, Scots-Irish, a substantial free Black community whose leaders (Richard Allen, Absalom Jones) organized epidemic nursing and burial, and French Caribbean refugees from Saint-Domingue arriving in 1793.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, Methodist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Jewish (Mikveh Israel congregation).
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic struck August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents. Thousands fled the city; the federal government temporarily relocated to Germantown and elsewhere. A Committee of Citizens managed relief and burial; the Bush Hill estate was converted into a hospital. Physician Benjamin Rush and publisher Mathew Carey documented the epidemic extensively. Mayor Matthew Clarkson coordinated official response.

## Boundary changes
- In 1793 the city of Philadelphia occupied a compact area along the Delaware River. Philadelphia County contained additional separate municipalities and townships: Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, and Germantown were distinct jurisdictions with their own record-keeping.
- County consolidation into a single city-county unit did not occur until the Act of Consolidation in 1854. Records from 1793 may therefore be filed under the city of Philadelphia, the county, or a specific surrounding district, depending on where the ancestor lived.
- No tool result in this survey returned a detailed history of Philadelphia boundary changes. The FamilySearch Wiki's constructed pages for Philadelphia and Pennsylvania all resolved to a generic page rather than place-specific content. Consult the Philadelphia City Archives directly for district-level jurisdiction guidance.

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is noted as city, county, state, or federal. In 1793, Philadelphia had no civil vital registration at any level.

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793 research)
These are the most important records for tracing families affected by the 1793 yellow fever outbreak, and all are physical-only at named repositories. None appeared as indexed digital collections in this survey.

- **Mathew Carey's death list:** Carey published "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793), which includes a list of those who died. Widely reprinted; available in research libraries and at the Library Company of Philadelphia. Named in the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports:** The committee appointed to manage epidemic relief documented those who died and received assistance. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki page cited above and the Wikipedia article on the epidemic.
- **Bush Hill Hospital records:** The Bush Hill estate was converted to a hospital during the epidemic. Records are held at the Philadelphia City Archives per the Wikipedia article.
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's accounts and Dr. Benjamin Rush's accounts:** Leave named documentation of the epidemic useful for social and community context.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only — no indexed online access confirmed by tools.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had **no civil vital registration in 1793 at any level** — not city, county, or statewide. The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) states that "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." Statewide registration level began in 1906; the FamilySearch Wiki does not give an earlier local or county-level start date for Philadelphia.
- **What exists in 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. Church registers are the exclusive primary source.
- **Where held:** Church archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- **Gaps:** Total gap — no civil registration exists for 1793 or any year before the twentieth century.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial records; Mathew Carey's published death list; Committee of Citizens minutes (see Epidemic-specific sources above).

### Church records
- **Denominations present (named in tool results):** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal) and Gloria Dei — Old Swedes' (Swedish Lutheran) are specifically named by the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) in the context of 1793 burial records. Quakers (Society of Friends) are documented by the digitized Yearly Meeting minutes volume. Other denominations active in 1793 include Presbyterian, Methodist, and Roman Catholic, but no tool result in this survey identified indexed collections for their individual 1793 burial registers.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (burials are the critical record type for 1793 epidemic deaths); confirmations are a separate dated event in episcopal/Lutheran traditions.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes (volume_search result):** One volume was returned for Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 window — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image. This is a Quaker administrative meeting minutes record, not a burial register, and has limited utility for tracing specific epidemic deaths.
- **Indexes:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records, per the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Language:** English for most denominations; Swedish for Gloria Dei records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers.
- **Digitization level:** The Quaker minutes volume is browse-only images. Individual church burial registers for 1793 did not appear as discrete indexed FamilySearch collections — physical or microfilm access through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania or church archives required.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (three years before the epidemic) documents household composition before the outbreak; the 1800 federal census (seven years after) documents survivors and household changes. Comparing the two can reveal epidemic-related deaths, departures, and new family compositions. Both are indexed and available free at FamilySearch and by subscription at Ancestry.com.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census. No state enumeration exists for the 1793 period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (recording deaths in the year preceding the census) were not taken until 1850; they are not available for 1793.
- **Access:** Indexed + images for 1790 and 1800 federal censuses online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), letters of administration (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. A surge of estate filings in late 1793 and early 1794 followed epidemic deaths — these are among the most productive records for identifying epidemic casualties and their heirs.
- **Where held (county level):** FamilySearch has digitized Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) — 3,200,560 images. **Browse-only: 0 records indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image. Available free at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196.
- **Orphan Court:** Philadelphia's Orphan Court handled guardianships of children orphaned by the epidemic; these are part of the probate series.
- **Additional access:** For a name index, consult the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's published probate indexes or visit the Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania in person.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images (FamilySearch collection 1999196).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn grant; Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Penn family proprietary grants; subsequently the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and the county recorder of deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rent records, tax assessment lists
- **Where held:** Philadelphia deed books are at the Philadelphia City Archives. No specific FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia land or deed records was returned by collections_search for this period.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only — no indexed Philadelphia land records for this period were returned by tools.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the most proximate conflict; many 1793 Philadelphia residents were veterans. The Quasi-War with France (1798–1800) followed shortly after the epidemic.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Continental Army muster rolls
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — https://www.archives.gov — holds federal military records (returned in external links). Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com — holds indexed Revolutionary War pension files (returned in external links).
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription). NARA in-person access for non-digitized materials.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church burial ground; Gloria Dei churchyard; various denominational burial grounds throughout the city. During the 1793 epidemic, mass burials were conducted at speed; some victims were buried in locations not recorded in normal church registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave — https://www.findagrave.com — has Philadelphia cemetery entries (returned in external links).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual church archives; some have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Digitization level:** Find A Grave crowdsourced; original sexton records are physical only at church archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers active in 1793:** Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, the Pennsylvania Gazette, and the General Advertiser (later the Aurora). These published contemporaneous lists of the dead, survivor notices, guardianship notices, estate sale announcements, and notices of those who had fled.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com — has historical Philadelphia newspaper coverage (returned in external links; subscription required). The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold physical and microfilm newspaper runs.
- **Content value:** Contemporaneous death lists and notices published during the epidemic are genealogically significant; Mathew Carey's work drew partly on newspaper accounts.
- **Digitization level:** Newspapers.com (subscription); some also at Readex/Newsbank through libraries.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary mid-Atlantic port of entry. French Caribbean refugees from Saint-Domingue arrived through Philadelphia in 1793, some carrying yellow fever.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 records are sparse); naturalization petitions filed in Philadelphia courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA — https://www.archives.gov — holds federal passenger list records. Naturalization petitions are part of the Philadelphia court record series at the Philadelphia City Archives and NARA Mid-Atlantic Region.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests for 1793 cover all persons aboard, including children. The 1820 Steerage Act created more systematic manifests; pre-1820 coverage at NARA is incomplete.
- **Digitization level:** Some indexed via Ancestry.com; pre-1820 records are sparse and often physical only.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County real estate assessments, personal property tax lists
- **Date range:** Exist from the colonial period through the target years
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and the Philadelphia City Archives hold assessment lists. No specific indexed FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia tax records in this period was returned by tools.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1792–1794 can document which residents were present before and after the epidemic, and which names disappear in 1793–1794 (possible deaths or departures).
- **Digitization level:** Physical only or microfilm — no indexed collection returned by tools.

### Other record types
- **Almshouse and institutional records:** The Philadelphia Almshouse (Blockley) and Bush Hill Hospital received epidemic victims. Almshouse records are at the Philadelphia City Archives. Physical only.
- **Orphanage records:** Institutions receiving epidemic-orphaned children kept enrollment records; the Philadelphia City Archives holds relevant institutional records.
- **African American community records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) and the early congregations of Richard Allen and Absalom Jones documented their members' epidemic service and deaths. The African Methodist Episcopal Church archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania's African American collections hold these materials. Physical only; specialized access required.
- **Published transcriptions and local histories:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has published indexes and transcriptions of many Philadelphia records; 19th-century local histories of Philadelphia often reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches of residents active in the 1790s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196; 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957; 312K indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909; 198K indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322; 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 and 1800 censuses indexed + images) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files (indexed) | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and burial inscriptions | Free — https://www.findagrave.com |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com |
| NARA (Archives.gov) | Federal passenger lists, military records, naturalization records | Free online and in-person — https://www.archives.gov |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 window (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, DGS 001188322). The total results count was 1 with no nextPageToken, suggesting this is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for this place and date filter. However, additional church record volumes may exist under broader state-level headings not captured by this query; browsing FamilySearch directly for Philadelphia is advisable.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county records; Committee of Citizens minutes; Bush Hill Hospital records; deed books; court and probate records; almshouse records | In-person or written inquiry; 400 N. Broad St., Philadelphia |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Manuscript collections; Committee of Citizens minutes; church record transcriptions; newspaper holdings; African American collections | In-person research; some finding aids at https://hsp.org |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records, probate records, and vital transcriptions | Membership-based; research center in Philadelphia |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | County tax assessment lists; state-level administrative records | In-person or online request; finding aids at phmc.pa.gov |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) | Federal court naturalization records; census records | In-person; some records online at Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers for each congregation | Contact each church or its diocesan archive |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Mathew Carey's pamphlet; 1793 Philadelphia newspapers on microfilm | In-person; Philadelphia |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist in physical repositories but were not returned as indexed digital collections in this survey:

- **Epidemic-specific records:** Mathew Carey's published death list, Committee of Citizens minutes, and Bush Hill Hospital records — all at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives (per the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page and the Wikipedia article on the epidemic)
- **Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793** — some have been transcribed and published, but no discrete indexed FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia church burial records was returned; access is through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, church archives, or HSP
- **Philadelphia County tax lists (1792–1795 period)** — no indexed online collection returned by tools; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Almshouse and institutional records** — Philadelphia City Archives
- **Philadelphia deed books and land records** — Philadelphia City Archives
- **African American community records (Free African Society, early AME)** — AME Church archives and HSP

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey identified specific destruction or loss of Philadelphia records for the 1793 period. An absence from online search results is a coverage gap, not evidence that records do not exist. The Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania should be contacted directly to confirm which series survived intact and what finding aids exist.

## Research tips

- **Start with the epidemic-specific sources.** The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) identifies Mathew Carey's death list, the Committee of Citizens minutes, and Bush Hill Hospital records as the principal sources for tracing epidemic victims. These are at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives and are not available online.
- **Church burial records are the only primary vital documentation for 1793.** Pennsylvania had no civil vital registration in 1793. The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these registers.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses as brackets.** The 1790 census (before the epidemic) documents household composition; the 1800 census documents survivors and family changes. Comparing the two can reveal epidemic casualties, departures, remarriages, and orphaned-child placements.
- **Check probate records filed in late 1793 and early 1794.** The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (FamilySearch 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images) covers this surge period. Browse by approximate filing date rather than searching by name, since the collection is not indexed.
- **Thousands fled the city during the epidemic.** The Wikipedia article on the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793) confirms that thousands fled between August and November 1793. Ancestors absent from Philadelphia records during those months may appear in surrounding county records: Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, and Chester Counties.
- **Identify the ancestor's denomination before searching church records.** The city's religious diversity means burial records are spread across many archives. Knowing whether an ancestor was Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal, Swedish Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, or Catholic determines which specific church archive or transcription series to consult.
- **Newspapers published names of the dead and survivors.** Philadelphia's 1793 newspapers (Pennsylvania Gazette, General Advertiser, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser) published contemporaneous death and survivor lists. The Library Company of Philadelphia holds microfilm runs; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) has digitized historical coverage.
- **Search Orphan Court guardianship records.** Many children were orphaned in 1793; guardianship petitions filed in Philadelphia's Orphan Court document family relationships and name surviving relatives. These are part of the probate series at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **The African American community's records require a separate search pathway.** The Free African Society and the early African Methodist Episcopal congregation organized epidemic burial and nursing; their membership records and burial documentation are held at the AME Church archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, not within standard church burial registers.
- **Do not treat an empty online search as a negative finding.** The most genealogically significant epidemic records — Carey's list, Committee minutes, Bush Hill records — are not digitized. A name missing from FamilySearch or Ancestry searches does not mean the person left no documentation.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682 from William Penn's original land grant. The city of Philadelphia was incorporated 1701.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county seat coincide)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793. The epidemic killed approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population — between August and November 1793, per the Wikipedia article on the Yellow fever epidemic of 1793 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793).
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; commerce, shipping, crafts manufacturing; served as the national capital 1790–1800, making it also a center of federal government administration.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (founding community), German immigrants, Scots-Irish, a substantial free Black community whose leaders (Richard Allen, Absalom Jones) organized epidemic nursing and burial, and French Caribbean refugees from Saint-Domingue arriving in 1793.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, Methodist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Jewish (Mikveh Israel congregation).
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic struck August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents. Thousands fled the city; the federal government temporarily relocated to Germantown and elsewhere. A Committee of Citizens managed relief and burial; the Bush Hill estate was converted into a hospital. Physician Benjamin Rush and publisher Mathew Carey documented the epidemic extensively. Mayor Matthew Clarkson coordinated official response.

## Boundary changes
- In 1793 the city of Philadelphia occupied a compact area along the Delaware River. Philadelphia County contained additional separate municipalities and townships: Northern Liberties, Southwark, Kensington, and Germantown were distinct jurisdictions with their own record-keeping.
- County consolidation into a single city-county unit did not occur until the Act of Consolidation in 1854. Records from 1793 may therefore be filed under the city of Philadelphia, the county, or a specific surrounding district, depending on where the ancestor lived.
- No tool result in this survey returned a detailed history of Philadelphia boundary changes. The FamilySearch Wiki's constructed pages for Philadelphia and Pennsylvania all resolved to a generic page rather than place-specific content. Consult the Philadelphia City Archives directly for district-level jurisdiction guidance.

## Available record types

For each record type, the holding level is noted as city, county, state, or federal. In 1793, Philadelphia had no civil vital registration at any level.

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793 research)
These are the most important records for tracing families affected by the 1793 yellow fever outbreak, and all are physical-only at named repositories. None appeared as indexed digital collections in this survey.

- **Mathew Carey's death list:** Carey published "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793), which includes a list of those who died. Widely reprinted; available in research libraries and at the Library Company of Philadelphia. Named in the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
- **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports:** The committee appointed to manage epidemic relief documented those who died and received assistance. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki page cited above and the Wikipedia article on the epidemic.
- **Bush Hill Hospital records:** The Bush Hill estate was converted to a hospital during the epidemic. Records are held at the Philadelphia City Archives per the Wikipedia article.
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's accounts and Dr. Benjamin Rush's accounts:** Leave named documentation of the epidemic useful for social and community context.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only — no indexed online access confirmed by tools.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had **no civil vital registration in 1793 at any level** — not city, county, or statewide. The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) states that "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." Statewide registration level began in 1906; the FamilySearch Wiki does not give an earlier local or county-level start date for Philadelphia.
- **What exists in 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records. Church registers are the exclusive primary source.
- **Where held:** Church archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania
- **Gaps:** Total gap — no civil registration exists for 1793 or any year before the twentieth century.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial records; Mathew Carey's published death list; Committee of Citizens minutes (see Epidemic-specific sources above).

### Church records
- **Denominations present (named in tool results):** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal) and Gloria Dei — Old Swedes' (Swedish Lutheran) are specifically named by the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) in the context of 1793 burial records. Quakers (Society of Friends) are documented by the digitized Yearly Meeting minutes volume. Other denominations active in 1793 include Presbyterian, Methodist, and Roman Catholic, but no tool result in this survey identified indexed collections for their individual 1793 burial registers.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (burials are the critical record type for 1793 epidemic deaths); confirmations are a separate dated event in episcopal/Lutheran traditions.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes (volume_search result):** One volume was returned for Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 window — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images. **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image. This is a Quaker administrative meeting minutes record, not a burial register, and has limited utility for tracing specific epidemic deaths.
- **Indexes:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records, per the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **Language:** English for most denominations; Swedish for Gloria Dei records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers.
- **Digitization level:** The Quaker minutes volume is browse-only images. Individual church burial registers for 1793 did not appear as discrete indexed FamilySearch collections — physical or microfilm access through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania or church archives required.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (three years before the epidemic) documents household composition before the outbreak; the 1800 federal census (seven years after) documents survivors and household changes. Comparing the two can reveal epidemic-related deaths, departures, and new family compositions. Both are indexed and available free at FamilySearch and by subscription at Ancestry.com.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census. No state enumeration exists for the 1793 period.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (recording deaths in the year preceding the census) were not taken until 1850; they are not available for 1793.
- **Access:** Indexed + images for 1790 and 1800 federal censuses online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate), letters of administration (intestate), guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. A surge of estate filings in late 1793 and early 1794 followed epidemic deaths — these are among the most productive records for identifying epidemic casualties and their heirs.
- **Where held (county level):** FamilySearch has digitized Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) — 3,200,560 images. **Browse-only: 0 records indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image. Available free at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196.
- **Orphan Court:** Philadelphia's Orphan Court handled guardianships of children orphaned by the epidemic; these are part of the probate series.
- **Additional access:** For a name index, consult the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's published probate indexes or visit the Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania in person.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images (FamilySearch collection 1999196).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Penn grant; Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Penn family proprietary grants; subsequently the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and the county recorder of deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rent records, tax assessment lists
- **Where held:** Philadelphia deed books are at the Philadelphia City Archives. No specific FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia land or deed records was returned by collections_search for this period.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only — no indexed Philadelphia land records for this period were returned by tools.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the most proximate conflict; many 1793 Philadelphia residents were veterans. The Quasi-War with France (1798–1800) followed shortly after the epidemic.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; Continental Army muster rolls
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — https://www.archives.gov — holds federal military records (returned in external links). Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com — holds indexed Revolutionary War pension files (returned in external links).
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription). NARA in-person access for non-digitized materials.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church burial ground; Gloria Dei churchyard; various denominational burial grounds throughout the city. During the 1793 epidemic, mass burials were conducted at speed; some victims were buried in locations not recorded in normal church registers.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave — https://www.findagrave.com — has Philadelphia cemetery entries (returned in external links).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual church archives; some have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Digitization level:** Find A Grave crowdsourced; original sexton records are physical only at church archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers active in 1793:** Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, the Pennsylvania Gazette, and the General Advertiser (later the Aurora). These published contemporaneous lists of the dead, survivor notices, guardianship notices, estate sale announcements, and notices of those who had fled.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com — has historical Philadelphia newspaper coverage (returned in external links; subscription required). The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold physical and microfilm newspaper runs.
- **Content value:** Contemporaneous death lists and notices published during the epidemic are genealogically significant; Mathew Carey's work drew partly on newspaper accounts.
- **Digitization level:** Newspapers.com (subscription); some also at Readex/Newsbank through libraries.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary mid-Atlantic port of entry. French Caribbean refugees from Saint-Domingue arrived through Philadelphia in 1793, some carrying yellow fever.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 records are sparse); naturalization petitions filed in Philadelphia courts (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA — https://www.archives.gov — holds federal passenger list records. Naturalization petitions are part of the Philadelphia court record series at the Philadelphia City Archives and NARA Mid-Atlantic Region.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests for 1793 cover all persons aboard, including children. The 1820 Steerage Act created more systematic manifests; pre-1820 coverage at NARA is incomplete.
- **Digitization level:** Some indexed via Ancestry.com; pre-1820 records are sparse and often physical only.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia County real estate assessments, personal property tax lists
- **Date range:** Exist from the colonial period through the target years
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) and the Philadelphia City Archives hold assessment lists. No specific indexed FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia tax records in this period was returned by tools.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from 1792–1794 can document which residents were present before and after the epidemic, and which names disappear in 1793–1794 (possible deaths or departures).
- **Digitization level:** Physical only or microfilm — no indexed collection returned by tools.

### Other record types
- **Almshouse and institutional records:** The Philadelphia Almshouse (Blockley) and Bush Hill Hospital received epidemic victims. Almshouse records are at the Philadelphia City Archives. Physical only.
- **Orphanage records:** Institutions receiving epidemic-orphaned children kept enrollment records; the Philadelphia City Archives holds relevant institutional records.
- **African American community records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) and the early congregations of Richard Allen and Absalom Jones documented their members' epidemic service and deaths. The African Methodist Episcopal Church archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania's African American collections hold these materials. Physical only; specialized access required.
- **Published transcriptions and local histories:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has published indexes and transcriptions of many Philadelphia records; 19th-century local histories of Philadelphia often reprint early records, list founding families, and carry biographical sketches of residents active in the 1790s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196; 3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957; 312K indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909; 198K indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322; 145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1790 and 1800 censuses indexed + images) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |

| Find A Grave | Cemetery records and burial inscriptions | Free — https://www.findagrave.com |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com |
| NARA (Archives.gov) | Federal passenger lists, military records, naturalization records | Free online and in-person — https://www.archives.gov |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Philadelphia in the 1780–1810 window (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800, DGS 001188322). The total results count was 1 with no nextPageToken, suggesting this is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for this place and date filter. However, additional church record volumes may exist under broader state-level headings not captured by this query; browsing FamilySearch directly for Philadelphia is advisable.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City and county records; Committee of Citizens minutes; Bush Hill Hospital records; deed books; court and probate records; almshouse records | In-person or written inquiry; 400 N. Broad St., Philadelphia |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Manuscript collections; Committee of Citizens minutes; church record transcriptions; newspaper holdings; African American collections | In-person research; some finding aids at https://hsp.org |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records, probate records, and vital transcriptions | Membership-based; research center in Philadelphia |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | County tax assessment lists; state-level administrative records | In-person or online request; finding aids at phmc.pa.gov |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) | Federal court naturalization records; census records | In-person; some records online at Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Individual church archives | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers for each congregation | Contact each church or its diocesan archive |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Mathew Carey's pamphlet; 1793 Philadelphia newspapers on microfilm | In-person; Philadelphia |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist in physical repositories but were not returned as indexed digital collections in this survey:

- **Epidemic-specific records:** Mathew Carey's published death list, Committee of Citizens minutes, and Bush Hill Hospital records — all at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives (per the FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page and the Wikipedia article on the epidemic)
- **Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793** — some have been transcribed and published, but no discrete indexed FamilySearch collection for Philadelphia church burial records was returned; access is through the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, church archives, or HSP
- **Philadelphia County tax lists (1792–1795 period)** — no indexed online collection returned by tools; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives
- **Almshouse and institutional records** — Philadelphia City Archives
- **Philadelphia deed books and land records** — Philadelphia City Archives
- **African American community records (Free African Society, early AME)** — AME Church archives and HSP

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey identified specific destruction or loss of Philadelphia records for the 1793 period. An absence from online search results is a coverage gap, not evidence that records do not exist. The Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania should be contacted directly to confirm which series survived intact and what finding aids exist.

## Research tips

- **Start with the epidemic-specific sources.** The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) identifies Mathew Carey's death list, the Committee of Citizens minutes, and Bush Hill Hospital records as the principal sources for tracing epidemic victims. These are at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives and are not available online.
- **Church burial records are the only primary vital documentation for 1793.** Pennsylvania had no civil vital registration in 1793. The FamilySearch Wiki Philadelphia Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many of these registers.
- **Use the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses as brackets.** The 1790 census (before the epidemic) documents household composition; the 1800 census documents survivors and family changes. Comparing the two can reveal epidemic casualties, departures, remarriages, and orphaned-child placements.
- **Check probate records filed in late 1793 and early 1794.** The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (FamilySearch 1999196, 3.2M browse-only images) covers this surge period. Browse by approximate filing date rather than searching by name, since the collection is not indexed.
- **Thousands fled the city during the epidemic.** The Wikipedia article on the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793) confirms that thousands fled between August and November 1793. Ancestors absent from Philadelphia records during those months may appear in surrounding county records: Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, and Chester Counties.
- **Identify the ancestor's denomination before searching church records.** The city's religious diversity means burial records are spread across many archives. Knowing whether an ancestor was Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal, Swedish Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, or Catholic determines which specific church archive or transcription series to consult.
- **Newspapers published names of the dead and survivors.** Philadelphia's 1793 newspapers (Pennsylvania Gazette, General Advertiser, Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser) published contemporaneous death and survivor lists. The Library Company of Philadelphia holds microfilm runs; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) has digitized historical coverage.
- **Search Orphan Court guardianship records.** Many children were orphaned in 1793; guardianship petitions filed in Philadelphia's Orphan Court document family relationships and name surviving relatives. These are part of the probate series at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **The African American community's records require a separate search pathway.** The Free African Society and the early African Methodist Episcopal congregation organized epidemic burial and nursing; their membership records and burial documentation are held at the AME Church archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, not within standard church burial registers.
- **Do not treat an empty online search as a negative finding.** The most genealogically significant epidemic records — Carey's list, Committee minutes, Bush Hill records — are not digitized. A name missing from FamilySearch or Ancestry searches does not mean the person left no documentation.

Chicago, Cook County, Illinois was surveyed for the period centered on the Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 (roughly 1855–1885). Here's what the research found:

## The Core Challenge: The Courthouse Burned

The fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, taking with it the original:
- Deeds
- Probate files
- Civil birth and death registers
- Tax rolls
- Court records

## What Survived and Where to Find It

### Federal Records (Stored in Washington — Unharmed)
- **1870 U.S. Census** — The last pre-fire census; critical for establishing who was in Chicago before the disaster
- **Military service and pension files**
- **Passenger arrival lists** — For immigrant families who arrived before the fire

### Local Records Outside the Burn Zone
- **Church registers** from unburned parishes — Many congregations preserved their own records
- **City directories** — Available at the **Newberry Library**; essential because the 1890 federal census was also largely destroyed nationally, leaving no usable census between 1880 and 1900
- **Business and insurance records**

### Reconstructed Records (Post-Fire)
- The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-file deeds, creating a reconstructed land-record series
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance abstracts** at the **Chicago History Museum** fill gaps for pre-fire property

### FamilySearch Holdings
Four indexed Cook County collections beginning in 1871: births, deaths, marriages, and church records, plus partially indexed digitized volumes of reconstructed property records and federal census images.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

The most productive path is to search the 1870 census first to establish the family in Chicago before the fire, then pivot to city directories (1871–1900) and church registers from their denomination to bridge the gap caused by both the courthouse fire and the missing 1890 census. A focused research plan targeting a specific family would help sequence these record types in the right order.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1855–1885, focused on the Great Fire of 1871)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831 from unorganized territory; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this query. The Great Chicago Fire left more than 100,000 residents homeless (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).
- **Economy:** Major railroad hub, meatpacking, grain trade, manufacturing, commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant population, prominently Irish, German, and Scandinavian, plus smaller communities from across Europe
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (largest single denomination), Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, and other Protestant congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871, burned approximately 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the bulk of the city's official records (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire")

## Boundary changes
Cook County was established in 1831 and its boundaries were stable throughout this period. Chicago expanded by annexation across the later 19th century, but the county-level jurisdiction remained consistent. The fire did not alter county boundaries, but it eliminated the central record repository. Place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictional representations for this place.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collections_search returned four Cook County collections:
  - Birth Certificates, 1871–1940: 1,450,000 records (collection ID 2024189)
  - Death Records, 1871–1947: 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - Marriage Records, 1871-1920: 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Start date and level:** All three vital record collections begin at 1871 — the fire year. The Illinois Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content (not Illinois-specific), so the mandatory registration start date and the level (city, county, or statewide) at which registration was required cannot be confirmed from tool results. Do not assume pre-1871 civil registration records exist at the county level.
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil vital records held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the fire (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records and city directories (see below) are the primary substitutes for pre-1871 vital events.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch)

### Church records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds: Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925 (285,000 records, collection ID 1803978). The 1833 start date means surviving pre-fire church registers are included.
- **Denominations:** Catholic parish registers are held by the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives. Lutheran, Methodist, and other denominational archives also hold Chicago records. The Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page notes Catholic registers as a key substitute source (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Chicago Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic); FamilySearch microfilm for many denominations; individual denominational archives
- **Note:** Some pre-fire parish registers were destroyed when churches in the burn zone were lost; registers from parishes outside the burn zone or those reconstructed from bishop's transcripts form the surviving base.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; Catholic sacramental registers may be partly in Latin.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for the FamilySearch collection; physical-only for many at denominational archives

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses survived because the originals were retained in Washington, D.C., not locally — these are confirmed surviving records per the Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1880 federal census is also available (post-fire). Note: the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed in a separate Washington, D.C. fire in 1921 and is not a usable resource nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules (1850–1880) list deaths in the year preceding the census and are federal records unaffected by the Chicago fire.
- **State census:** The Illinois Census wiki page returned only generic content; no Illinois-specific state census years can be confirmed from tool results.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (federal censuses on FamilySearch and Ancestry)

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire losses:** Probate files and court records held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Reconstructed records:** FamilySearch has digitized 2 volumes:
  - Volume 009982110: Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871, 38 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not fulltext searchable; must be examined image by image)
  - Volume 009982111: Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880, 112 images — **partially indexed + images** (41% name-indexed)
- **Post-fire records:** New Cook County court and probate records began after 1871. Post-fire Cook County records are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University, per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Testate vs. intestate:** For post-1871 probate research: if the ancestor left a will (testate), search for wills filed with the probate court; if they died without one (intestate), search for letters of administration at IRAD.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state; the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website holds original federal land patents.
- **Pre-fire losses:** Deeds and property records held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").
- **Burnt Record Act substitute:** The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds; these reconstructed records are the primary substitute and are partially covered by FamilySearch volume 009982111 (Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880, 41% indexed).
- **Insurance records substitute:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a key source for pre-fire property ownership per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch volume 009982111 is partially indexed + images; the Chicago History Museum collection is physical-only (contact required)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) immediately preceded the fire; many Chicago residents in 1871 were Civil War veterans or family members of veterans.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (including widows' pensions), bounty land warrants, and Civil War draft registrations are all federal records held at NARA — they were not destroyed in the Chicago fire.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many military records.
- **Digitization level:** Service records and pension files: indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry; NARA holds originals for in-person or written requests

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) per external_links_search results. Cemeteries were generally outside the 1871 burn zone and their records were not destroyed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual cemeteries and sometimes by churches.
- **Digitization level:** Find A Grave is indexed + images (photographs); sexton records are physical-only unless microfilmed

### Newspaper records
- **Surviving papers:** The Chicago Tribune survived the fire. Post-fire editions published lists of fire survivors, displaced persons seeking relatives, relief recipients, and property loss notices — these are among the most genealogically valuable records for fire-affected families.
- **Where held:** The Newberry Library holds city directories and newspapers; online access via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) per external_links_search results.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, fire-related notices, relief lists naming displaced families, legal notices, and property announcements.
- **Digitization level:** Newspapers.com is indexed + images (subscription); Newberry Library holdings are physical with some microfilm

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; primary ports of entry for Chicago-bound immigrants in this period were New York (Castle Garden, later Ellis Island), Baltimore, Philadelphia, New Orleans, and Quebec.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests are federal records at NARA, unaffected by the Chicago fire. Naturalization records — pre-1906 — could be filed in any court of record. Post-1871 Cook County naturalizations are held at IRAD. Alien registrations and border crossing records are at NARA.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest page for all family members.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/) for indexed passenger lists; Fold3 for some naturalization records.
- **Digitization level:** Passenger lists and many naturalizations are indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire losses:** Cook County tax rolls were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").
- **Post-fire:** Tax records resume after 1871; held at Cook County and at IRAD.
- **Substitute value:** Pre-fire city directories and the 1870 census are the principal substitutes for placing residents in Chicago before the fire. Any surviving copies of pre-fire tax lists (e.g., in state archives or private abstracts) have not been confirmed in tool results.

### City directories
- **Survival:** City directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library, per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). These are among the most important surviving pre-fire records.
- **Content:** Name, address, and occupation for most adult male residents (sometimes women and businesses). Annual directories allow year-by-year tracking of a family's residence and occupation.
- **Digitization level:** Some Chicago directories are digitized and browsable online; the Newberry Library holds the physical collection

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection including Chicago enumerations; passenger lists; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records, pension files, Civil War service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: passenger lists, military records, naturalization records | Free to search; some fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken), covering 1865–1880 for Chicago. These are the entirety of what FamilySearch has digitized for this specific place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories (1840s onward), maps, manuscripts, local histories | In-person; some materials online |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records; photographs; personal papers documenting pre-fire property ownership | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University | Post-1871 Cook County court, probate, and naturalization records | In-person; written requests |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward (birth, marriage, death) | In-person; online search portal |
| NARA (Great Lakes Region, Chicago) | Federal records for Illinois: census, naturalization, court records | In-person; written requests |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company collection (pre-fire property insurance records) — held at Chicago History Museum, physical only
- Most pre-fire city directories — held at Newberry Library, physical with some digitization
- Most Catholic parish registers — Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives, physical; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- Pre-fire reconstructed court records (FamilySearch volume 009982110): digitized but browse-only, not name-indexed
- Post-1871 probate and court files in full detail — IRAD, physical
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual cemeteries — physical at each cemetery or church

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the records held within it, including deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). This is the defining record-loss event for Chicago genealogy before 1871. Records that were federal in origin (census, military, passenger lists) were not held locally and survived. Church registers from parishes outside the burn zone also survived.

The following substitute sources partially compensate:
- 1870 federal census (survived, in Washington)
- Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstructed deed re-recordings
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum)
- Church registers from non-burned parishes
- City directories (Newberry Library)
- Post-fire newspapers listing displaced families and relief recipients

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census.** It is the last pre-fire population snapshot and survived intact. It places a family in Chicago before the disaster and reveals household composition, birthplace, and occupation. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Search post-fire newspapers immediately after October 1871.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of fire survivors, missing persons notices, and relief rolls that name affected families — these are substitute vital records for the fire period.
- **The Burnt Record Act re-recordings are the land record substitute.** After searching for deeds under a family name in the 1871-onward re-recording books, also check the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum for pre-fire title abstracts. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Church records may fill the pre-1871 vital record gap.** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from parishes outside the burn zone survived. Begin with Catholic registers (Bernardin Archives) if the family was Catholic, or identify the denomination and contact its archives. FamilySearch's Chicago Church Records collection (1833–1925) includes some pre-fire registers.
- **City directories are a year-by-year location tool.** The Newberry Library holds Chicago directories from the 1840s onward. Use them to track a family's address and occupation annually — far more granular than decennial censuses.
- **Naturalization records were not destroyed.** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; post-1871 Cook County naturalizations are at IRAD. For an immigrant ancestor, search naturalization records as a way to establish arrival date and birthplace even when pre-fire vital records are missing.
- **Military pension files are high-value records.** A Civil War pension file (at NARA/Fold3) may include a widow's declaration naming children, marriage dates, and birthplaces — information that would otherwise have been in destroyed Cook County records.
- **The FamilySearch browse-only volume (009982110) must be examined page by page.** Pre-fire reconstructed court records (38 images, 0% indexed) cannot be name-searched; a researcher must browse each image. This is worth doing for any family with a documented court connection before 1871.
- **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** is the primary physical repository for post-1871 Cook County government records (court, probate, naturalization). Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories

- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (federal censuses on FamilySearch and Ancestry)

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-fire losses:** Probate files and court records held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Cook County, Illinois Genealogy page, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Reconstructed records:** FamilySearch has digitized 2 volumes:
  - Volume 009982110: Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871, 38 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not fulltext searchable; must be examined image by image)
  - Volume 009982111: Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880, 112 images — **partially indexed + images** (41% name-indexed)
- **Post-fire records:** New Cook County court and probate records began after 1871. Post-fire Cook County records are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University, per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Testate vs. intestate:** For post-1871 probate research: if the ancestor left a will (testate), search for wills filed with the probate court; if they died without one (intestate), search for letters of administration at IRAD.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state; the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website holds original federal land patents.
- **Pre-fire losses:** Deeds and property records held at the Cook County Courthouse were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").
- **Burnt Record Act substitute:** The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds; these reconstructed records are the primary substitute and are partially covered by FamilySearch volume 009982111 (Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880, 41% indexed).
- **Insurance records substitute:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a key source for pre-fire property ownership per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch volume 009982111 is partially indexed + images; the Chicago History Museum collection is physical-only (contact required)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Civil War (1861–1865) immediately preceded the fire; many Chicago residents in 1871 were Civil War veterans or family members of veterans.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (including widows' pensions), bounty land warrants, and Civil War draft registrations are all federal records held at NARA — they were not destroyed in the Chicago fire.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA, https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many military records.
- **Digitization level:** Service records and pension files: indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry; NARA holds originals for in-person or written requests

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) per external_links_search results. Cemeteries were generally outside the 1871 burn zone and their records were not destroyed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual cemeteries and sometimes by churches.
- **Digitization level:** Find A Grave is indexed + images (photographs); sexton records are physical-only unless microfilmed

### Newspaper records
- **Surviving papers:** The Chicago Tribune survived the fire. Post-fire editions published lists of fire survivors, displaced persons seeking relatives, relief recipients, and property loss notices — these are among the most genealogically valuable records for fire-affected families.
- **Where held:** The Newberry Library holds city directories and newspapers; online access via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) per external_links_search results.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, fire-related notices, relief lists naming displaced families, legal notices, and property announcements.
- **Digitization level:** Newspapers.com is indexed + images (subscription); Newberry Library holdings are physical with some microfilm

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; primary ports of entry for Chicago-bound immigrants in this period were New York (Castle Garden, later Ellis Island), Baltimore, Philadelphia, New Orleans, and Quebec.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests are federal records at NARA, unaffected by the Chicago fire. Naturalization records — pre-1906 — could be filed in any court of record. Post-1871 Cook County naturalizations are held at IRAD. Alien registrations and border crossing records are at NARA.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest page for all family members.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/) for indexed passenger lists; Fold3 for some naturalization records.
- **Digitization level:** Passenger lists and many naturalizations are indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Tax records
- **Pre-fire losses:** Cook County tax rolls were destroyed in the 1871 fire (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire").
- **Post-fire:** Tax records resume after 1871; held at Cook County and at IRAD.
- **Substitute value:** Pre-fire city directories and the 1870 census are the principal substitutes for placing residents in Chicago before the fire. Any surviving copies of pre-fire tax lists (e.g., in state archives or private abstracts) have not been confirmed in tool results.

### City directories
- **Survival:** City directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library, per the Cook County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). These are among the most important surviving pre-fire records.
- **Content:** Name, address, and occupation for most adult male residents (sometimes women and businesses). Annual directories allow year-by-year tracking of a family's residence and occupation.
- **Digitization level:** Some Chicago directories are digitized and browsable online; the Newberry Library holds the physical collection

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection including Chicago enumerations; passenger lists; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records, pension files, Civil War service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: passenger lists, military records, naturalization records | Free to search; some fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a complete result set of 2 digitized volumes (totalResults: 2, no nextPageToken), covering 1865–1880 for Chicago. These are the entirety of what FamilySearch has digitized for this specific place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library (Chicago) | City directories (1840s onward), maps, manuscripts, local histories | In-person; some materials online |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records; photographs; personal papers documenting pre-fire property ownership | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University | Post-1871 Cook County court, probate, and naturalization records | In-person; written requests |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward (birth, marriage, death) | In-person; online search portal |
| NARA (Great Lakes Region, Chicago) | Federal records for Illinois: census, naturalization, court records | In-person; written requests |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company collection (pre-fire property insurance records) — held at Chicago History Museum, physical only
- Most pre-fire city directories — held at Newberry Library, physical with some digitization
- Most Catholic parish registers — Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives, physical; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- Pre-fire reconstructed court records (FamilySearch volume 009982110): digitized but browse-only, not name-indexed
- Post-1871 probate and court files in full detail — IRAD, physical
- Sexton records and burial registers for individual cemeteries — physical at each cemetery or church

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and the records held within it, including deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). This is the defining record-loss event for Chicago genealogy before 1871. Records that were federal in origin (census, military, passenger lists) were not held locally and survived. Church registers from parishes outside the burn zone also survived.

The following substitute sources partially compensate:
- 1870 federal census (survived, in Washington)
- Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstructed deed re-recordings
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (Chicago History Museum)
- Church registers from non-burned parishes
- City directories (Newberry Library)
- Post-fire newspapers listing displaced families and relief recipients

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1870 census.** It is the last pre-fire population snapshot and survived intact. It places a family in Chicago before the disaster and reveals household composition, birthplace, and occupation. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Search post-fire newspapers immediately after October 1871.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of fire survivors, missing persons notices, and relief rolls that name affected families — these are substitute vital records for the fire period.
- **The Burnt Record Act re-recordings are the land record substitute.** After searching for deeds under a family name in the 1871-onward re-recording books, also check the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum for pre-fire title abstracts. Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Church records may fill the pre-1871 vital record gap.** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from parishes outside the burn zone survived. Begin with Catholic registers (Bernardin Archives) if the family was Catholic, or identify the denomination and contact its archives. FamilySearch's Chicago Church Records collection (1833–1925) includes some pre-fire registers.
- **City directories are a year-by-year location tool.** The Newberry Library holds Chicago directories from the 1840s onward. Use them to track a family's address and occupation annually — far more granular than decennial censuses.
- **Naturalization records were not destroyed.** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; post-1871 Cook County naturalizations are at IRAD. For an immigrant ancestor, search naturalization records as a way to establish arrival date and birthplace even when pre-fire vital records are missing.
- **Military pension files are high-value records.** A Civil War pension file (at NARA/Fold3) may include a widow's declaration naming children, marriage dates, and birthplaces — information that would otherwise have been in destroyed Cook County records.
- **The FamilySearch browse-only volume (009982110) must be examined page by page.** Pre-fire reconstructed court records (38 images, 0% indexed) cannot be name-searched; a researcher must browse each image. This is worth doing for any family with a documented court connection before 1871.
- **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** is the primary physical repository for post-1871 Cook County government records (court, probate, naturalization). Source: Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories
