# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States — Land Run Era (1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory organized May 2, 1890, from the Unassigned Lands under the Organic Act; Oklahoma admitted to statehood November 16, 1907
- **Capital / administrative center:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890–1907); Oklahoma City (state capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal Indian Territory / Unassigned Lands (pre-May 2, 1890); U.S. federal jurisdiction throughout the territorial period
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 settlers participated in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 alone (Wikipedia, Land Run of 1889); no population figure was returned by the place_population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Agriculture (homesteading, farming), cattle ranching, nascent oil industry; the Land Run created an overnight settler economy from scratch in 1889
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers came primarily from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts); a significant Native American population was present throughout Indian Territory, subject to the Dawes Commission enrollment process (1898–1906)
- **Religious denominations:** Christian denominations established congregations sporadically beginning in 1889 as new towns formed; mission records begin as early as 1820 (FamilySearch collection 1654321)
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889; subsequent land runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895; Oklahoma Territory organized May 2, 1890; Dawes Commission enrollment of Five Civilized Tribes 1898–1906; Oklahoma statehood November 16, 1907

## Boundary changes
- **Before April 22, 1889:** The area was Indian Territory under federal jurisdiction; the Unassigned Lands had no civil settler government.
- **May 2, 1890:** Oklahoma Territory organized from the Unassigned Lands (Organic Act); counties formed and county-level record-keeping began.
- **1898–1906:** The Dawes Commission enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory (the eastern portion, separate from Oklahoma Territory).
- **November 16, 1907:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into the State of Oklahoma. Records created before this date under either territorial jurisdiction are now split between county courthouses, the Oklahoma State Archives, NARA at Fort Worth, and the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Important:** The Land Run itself (April 22, 1889) predates Oklahoma Territory by over a year. For events dated April–May 1889, no county-level territorial government yet existed. Records for this exact moment are federal in nature (General Land Office homestead filings) or absent.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma-specific vital records page did not return usable content in this survey — all requested pages redirected to a generic guide. Statehood was November 16, 1907. No FamilySearch Wiki source in this survey states the year statewide civil registration began in Oklahoma. The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection 2134789) shows county-level marriage registration began in 1890.
- **What exists for the territorial period (1890–1907):** County marriages at the county level from 1890 onward. No indexed FamilySearch birth or death collections for the territorial period were returned by this survey.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriages; also any county-registered births/deaths); Oklahoma State Archives
- **Gaps:** Civil registration was county-level for most of the territorial period. Statewide registration did not begin until after statehood — exact date not confirmed by any tool result in this survey. Before county organization (pre-May 1890), no civil vital registration existed in the territory.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (below); homestead final proof files; territorial census (1890 special census at Oklahoma Historical Society)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Mission and church records documented from 1820 onward per FamilySearch collection 1654321; Christian denominations began establishing congregations in 1889 as towns formed (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; mission records for Native American communities from 1820
- **Where held:** FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321); denominational archives; local congregations
- **Language:** English for most Protestant denominations; some mission records may be in other languages

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Oklahoma Territory did not exist in 1880. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide, but **a surviving Oklahoma Territory special census from 1890** is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society — one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are fully available.
- **Indian censuses:** FamilySearch "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records, 283,945 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) — covers the Five Civilized Tribes and others in Indian Territory
- **Territorial/county enumerations:** County tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts); held at Oklahoma State Archives and county level
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed online. The 1890 Oklahoma special census is at the Oklahoma Historical Society — contact them for remote access options.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Territorial district court civil and criminal cases, probate, guardianship, and naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record)
- **Date range:** From May 2, 1890 (territorial organization) through statehood 1907 for territorial records
- **Where held:** NARA at Fort Worth, Texas (Southwest Region), and the Oklahoma State Archives (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Digitization level:** Not returned as a digitized or indexed collection in this survey — physical or microfilm access required

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range) — Oklahoma is a federal-land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office, administered at the Guthrie and Kingfisher land offices for the 1889 Land Run (Wikipedia, Land Run of 1889)
- **Types:** Homestead applications, homestead final proofs (including witness statements naming neighbors), rejected applications, land patents; county deed records after May 2, 1890
- **Date range:** Homestead filings begin April 22, 1889; county deed records begin after territorial organization
- **Where held:**
  - NARA, Washington D.C. — Record Group 49 (General Land Office), homestead case files (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
  - BLM General Land Office Records: glorecords.blm.gov — land patents searchable online
  - FamilySearch — collection 1541872 (234,567 records, 117,283 images; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872); volume 005221388 (402 images, 74% name-indexed, 1889–1907, land-entry case files / homestead final proofs — **indexed + images**)
  - County courthouses — deed books from 1890 onward
- **Digitization level:** Volume 005221388 is 74% name-indexed (**indexed + images**).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (veterans who participated in the Land Run); Spanish-American War 1898; WWI draft registrations 1917–1918
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files; bounty land warrants; Spanish-American War service records; WWI Selective Service draft cards
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pensions); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/ — online)

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** Territorial cemeteries established from 1889 onward
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records held by individual cemeteries and county repositories

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** New towns established in April 1889 (Guthrie, Oklahoma City, Kingfisher) began publishing newspapers almost immediately after the Land Run
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Oklahoma Historical Society holds microfilmed territorial newspapers
- **Content value:** Homestead legal notices, obituaries, community news — especially valuable for 1889–1907 when other records are sparse

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** The Land Run was an internal migration event. Many settlers were first- or second-generation immigrants whose arrival records predate Oklahoma.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (for European-born ancestors who arrived before coming to Oklahoma); naturalization records in Oklahoma territorial courts (1890–1906)
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists and pre-1906 naturalization records); territorial court records at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all family members aboard, including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest when tracing families that arrived in America before the Land Run.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property tax rolls
- **Date range:** County tax rolls from the 1890s
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives; county level
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls bridge the critical gap between the 1890 special census and the 1900 federal census — a 10-year window for which federal census coverage is destroyed (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

### Other record types
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (1898–1910):** FamilySearch volume 005221389 (176 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse-only images**, must be searched image by image). For families with Native American heritage or those living in Indian Territory, enrollment in the Dawes rolls was required to establish citizenship in the Five Civilized Tribes. These files often include detailed family information.
- **Oklahoma Historical Society territorial records:** Holds territorial-era records not fully digitized online, including the surviving 1890 special census (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **County and town histories:** Early local histories (published 1900–1920) often list founding settlers and reprint early records; consult the Oklahoma Historical Society and local libraries

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Free |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) — RG 49 GLO, territorial court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma for 1880–1910; both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete set returned for this place and period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth, TX | Territorial court records (1890–1907): civil, criminal, probate, naturalization | In-person / NARA online request |
| National Archives, Washington D.C. | Record Group 49 (General Land Office) — homestead case files | In-person / written request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; territorial newspapers; early county records | In-person; contact OHS for remote access |
| Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City | Territorial court records; county tax rolls from 1890s; state records from 1907 | In-person / online catalog |
| County courthouses | County deed books (from 1890); county marriage registers; probate files | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online

- **Territorial court probate and civil records (1890–1907):** At NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives — not returned as a digitized or indexed collection in this survey
- **Pre-statehood birth and death records:** No FamilySearch collections or volumes for territorial-era birth or death registration were returned by this survey
- **County tax rolls from the 1890s:** At Oklahoma State Archives and county level — not returned as an online digitized collection
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census:** At the Oklahoma Historical Society — not returned as an online FamilySearch or Ancestry collection in this survey
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume 005221389):** Present on FamilySearch as 176 browse-only images — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey specifically stated that a particular Oklahoma territorial record set was destroyed or lost. The nationwide destruction of the 1890 federal census is confirmed by the wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run), which also notes the Oklahoma Territory special census as a surviving exception. The fate of any specific county or territorial records not returned by this survey is not settled by the tools consulted here; contact the Oklahoma Historical Society or Oklahoma State Archives directly.

## Research tips

- **Start with homestead land records.** For any family that participated in the Land Run, the homestead case file is the single most information-rich document available. Files typically include the original application, proof of settlement with witness statements naming neighbors, and the final patent (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and the BLM GLO website first.
- **Do not overlook rejected applications.** Rejected homestead applications survive at NARA RG 49 and can contain detailed family information — a family that lost its claim still left a paper trail (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Trace settlers back to their origin states.** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Research those states' records for the years before 1889 is essential to establish origins, prior vital events, and family connections.
- **Use the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census.** One of the few surviving 1890 census records anywhere in the nation. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society for access (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **County tax rolls bridge the 1890–1900 gap.** With the 1890 federal census largely destroyed, county tax rolls from the 1890s at the Oklahoma State Archives help establish a family's presence between the 1890 special census and the 1900 federal census (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **For Native American ancestry or Indian Territory residence, check both series.** The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 records) is name-indexed. The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume 005221389) are browse-only; browse systematically by family.
- **Naturalization records are in territorial court files.** Oklahoma territorial district court records at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives are the primary place to search for naturalizations of immigrant Land Run settlers (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Newspapers are a key substitute source.** New towns printed newspapers almost immediately after the Land Run. Territorial newspapers at the Oklahoma Historical Society and partially available at Newspapers.com carry homestead legal notices, early community news, and obituaries that predate formal vital registration.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma-specific research pages did not return usable content in this survey** (all four wiki_place_page sections returned only a generic guide). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy for additional guidance.

---

## Alabama ca. 1800 — Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Background

The Alabama region around 1800 sits in a layered jurisdictional puzzle:

- **The interior** (present-day northern and central Alabama) was part of the **eastern half of the Mississippi Territory**, organized in 1798.
- **The Mobile Bay coast** remained under **Spanish colonial rule** until the United States seized it in 1813.

Each side has its own distinct record base, so determining where your ancestor lived is the critical first step.

---

### Available Genealogical Records

#### FamilySearch — Indexed Collections
FamilySearch has four indexed collections touching this era:
- **Church Records** from 1803
- **County Marriages and Probate** from 1809 onward
- **Census Substitutes Index** (covering the 1810 period)

#### Territorial-Era Records (Physical Holdings)
The most important records for ca. 1800 are physical and held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery:
- **Mississippi Territory Censuses** of 1801, 1805, and 1808 — the closest thing to a census before statehood
- County **tax lists**
- **Militia rolls**
- **Court minutes**

#### Spanish Colonial Records (Mobile Area)
If your ancestor was in the Mobile Bay region, the relevant records are in:
- **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain**
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France**
- Microfilm copies are available in **Mobile, Alabama** and **Washington D.C.**
  
These include Catholic church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and colonial civil records.

---

Unfortunately, the volume search returned **zero digitized, browsable image volumes** on FamilySearch specifically for the pre-statehood Alabama period (~1800). There is nothing to browse page-by-page for that era — the earliest digitized material appears after 1803–1809.

---

1. **Alabama Department of Archives and History** — Visit their online finding aids at [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov) to request or plan access to the territorial censuses and county-level records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region — Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The territory now comprising Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory, established April 7, 1798, from lands ceded by Georgia and Spain. The eastern half was reorganized as the Alabama Territory on March 3, 1817; Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative centers:** Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); St. Stephens (Alabama Territory capital, 1817–1819).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government / Mississippi Territory (1798–1817); Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for Alabama in 1790–1820. The 1810 federal census (the first to enumerate the Alabama region) recorded approximately 9,046 free white persons and 17,088 enslaved persons in the area. Population grew sharply after the Creek War of 1813–1814 opened interior lands to settlement.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation, river trade along the Mobile-Tensaw delta, and land speculation. The Mobile area supported a small mercantile economy under Spanish and then U.S. administration.
- **Ethnic composition:** American settler families from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, and Tennessee; French Creoles and Spanish colonists in the Mobile area; Creek and Cherokee nations in the interior; African Americans (largely enslaved, a major share of the population); a small number of British and French traders.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, established ca. 1703); Baptist (frontier congregations from ca. 1808, north Alabama); Methodist (circuit riders active ca. 1800+); Presbyterian (early missions and congregations).
- **Key historical events:** Spain ceded the Mobile District to the U.S. in 1813; Creek War of 1813–1814 cleared interior lands for American settlement; massive migration from the Southeast followed 1815–1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1763:** Mobile area was French colonial territory (French Louisiana / Mobile District, 1702–1763).
- **1763–1780:** Mobile area under British West Florida administration.
- **1780–1813:** Mobile District under Spanish West Florida. Spanish census returns, church registers, and land grants were created for this area and are not held in U.S. repositories.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory established; initially a narrow strip, expanded in 1804 and 1812 to include all of present-day Alabama.
- **1813:** U.S. annexation of the Mobile District ended Spanish authority.
- **1817:** Western half of Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; eastern half organized as Alabama Territory. Records created before 1817 carry "Mississippi Territory" as the jurisdiction of record.
- **County formation:** Washington County (1800) was the first county organized in present-day Alabama. Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Clarke (1812), Monroe (1815), and others followed rapidly. Records are filed at the county level once a county was organized.

## Available record types

Note: For the ca. 1800 period, the jurisdictional level for most records is the **individual county** (once formed) or the **Mississippi Territory** (before county formation), not a state.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of vital events existed in the Mississippi Territory or Alabama Territory period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey, so a statewide civil registration start date cannot be stated from tool results.
- **What exists for the territorial period:** Marriage bonds and licenses survive at the county level beginning with each county's organization. FamilySearch has **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images; **indexed + images**), which overlaps the final decade of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; individual county probate offices for originals.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records exist for ca. 1800. Marriage records before individual counties were formed do not exist in civil form.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); territorial and county court minutes recording marriages by justices; tombstone inscriptions.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, established ca. 1703); Baptist (frontier ca. 1808+); Methodist (circuit riders ca. 1800+); Presbyterian (early missions).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Mobile's Catholic registers are the richest pre-1815 church records in the region.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images; **indexed + images**), beginning in 1803 (the territorial period). For Mobile-area Catholic records predating U.S. control, original registers are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile; microfilm copies of French and Spanish colonial-era Mobile records are at the Mobile Municipal Archives and the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French colonial period are in French; Spanish colonial records are in Spanish. Early American-settler church records are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census capturing the Alabama region was 1810. No federal census was taken for the Mississippi Territory in 1800 (the territory was newly organized and sparsely settled). FamilySearch has **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756; 287,634 records; **index only, no images**). Images of the 1810 census are on Ancestry.com and at NARA.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, and 1808 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). These are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery. The FamilySearch volume_search tool returned 0 digitized volumes for Alabama in 1780–1819, confirming these censuses are **not digitized or browsable on FamilySearch**.
- **Access:** Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808: physical-only at ADAH. 1810 federal census: name-indexed on FamilySearch (no images there); images on Ancestry.com.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Territorial and county court minutes (civil suits, road assignments, jury rolls, poor relief) are also important sources.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images; **indexed + images**), beginning at the earliest county formations. Pre-1809 territorial court records may exist at ADAH.
- **Testate or intestate:** Both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) are included in collection 1537764; determine which applies to the individual before searching.
- **Where held:** ADAH; individual county probate courts for originals.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (public land survey system). Alabama is a federal land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued federal land patents beginning with the earliest land sales, ca. 1809–1820 in most areas. Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile District predate U.S. control and were separately adjudicated; they are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal patents, Spanish land grants, British colonial grants, deeds, county tax records.
- **Date range:** Federal patents from ca. 1809+; Spanish colonial grants from 1780–1813 for the Mobile District.
- **Where held:** BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov, free online) for federal patents; Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress for Spanish grants; ADAH and county courthouses for deeds and tax records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (1812–1815); Creek War (1813–1814); territorial militia actions ca. 1800–1817.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Creek War), territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for service records and pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for digitized military records; ADAH for state and territorial militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries in Mobile (including the colonial-era Church Street Graveyard). Frontier burial grounds throughout the territory — many were family plots with no surviving documentation.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some Alabama cemetery transcriptions; coverage for burials ca. 1800 is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for Mobile's Catholic cemeteries, held by the Archdiocese of Mobile, are the best-documented early burial records in the region.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Alabama region at ca. 1800. The first newspaper was the Mobile Centinel (1811), followed by the Alabama Republican (Huntsville, 1816).
- **Where held:** ADAH; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free).
- **Content value:** Newspapers from 1811–1819 may carry legal notices, land sales, and early obituaries but cannot cover events before ca. 1811.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (adjacent).
- **Record types:** Most settlers arrived overland from the east and south — passenger manifests are not the primary research tool for the interior. Naturalization records: no organized territorial naturalization system existed for ordinary settlers ca. 1800. Spanish subjects in Mobile could take oaths of allegiance.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for New Orleans port records; Library of Congress for Spanish colonial records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine full manifests for any Mobile-bound sea arrivals. Most Alabama-region migrants of ca. 1800 were American-born settlers moving overland; genealogical passenger-list research applies primarily to the Mobile area for European (French, Spanish) arrivals.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax; poll tax. In a federal land state, tax records often predate the federal patent and are the earliest evidence of residence.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax records from ca. 1800; other counties from their formation dates.
- **Where held:** ADAH (primary repository); some county courthouses retain originals. Noted as territorial records at ADAH (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1800 federal census does not cover the Alabama territory and the 1810 census has no images on FamilySearch, tax lists and territorial censuses are among the best substitutes for placing families in the territory around 1800.

### Other record types
- **Territorial and county court minutes:** Record ordinary county business — road assignments, poor relief, justice-of-the-peace marriages, petit jury rolls — naming settlers who appear in no other record type.
- **Militia rolls:** Territorial militia muster rolls name free adult males. Listed as territorial records at ADAH (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Spanish colonial records (Mobile District):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants from 1780–1813, held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence), with copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century local histories (e.g., Albert J. Pickett's *History of Alabama*, 1851) reprint early records and list founding families, and are sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (collection 1598408; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756; index only, no images) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1810 U.S. Federal Census images; U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 / Creek War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files, federal land records | Free finding aids; some digitized |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Alabama newspapers (1811+) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey (digitized volumes):** The volume_search tool returned 0 digitized volumes on FamilySearch for Alabama in 1780–1819. This is a genuine digitization gap for the pre-statehood era: no browse-only image volumes for ca. 1800 are available on FamilySearch. The 4 collections listed above are name-indexed and include images, but their coverage begins at 1803 (Church Records) and 1809 (Marriages, Probate) at the earliest; the Census Substitutes Index starts at 1810 and has no images.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808), tax records, militia rolls, county court minutes, early deeds | In-person; finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| NARA, Washington DC / Southeast Region, Atlanta | Military service records, pension files, Creek War records, federal land records (RG 49, RG 15, RG 94) | In-person; NARA.gov request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile, colonial era onward) | Contact archives office |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias); some French colonial material | In-person; some digitized at loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records: Mobile District census, church registers, land grants, 1780–1813 | Contact or use microfilm copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | Original French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763 | Contact archives; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| County probate courts (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Clarke, etc.) | Original deed books, court minutes, marriage bonds | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 — physical only at ADAH, not digitized on FamilySearch
- County tax lists for ca. 1800–1817 — physical or microfilm at ADAH and county courthouses
- Territorial and county court minutes — physical at county courthouses and ADAH
- Militia rolls — physical at ADAH
- Spanish colonial land grants and civil records for the Mobile District (1780–1813) — originals in Seville; microfilm copies in Mobile and Washington
- French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763) — originals in Aix-en-Provence; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Early Baptist and Methodist church registers (ca. 1808–1819) — scattered, many congregations hold their own records

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for the Alabama territorial period were returned by the tools used in this survey. The Alabama Department of Archives and History holds the primary repository of territorial-era records. Researchers should contact ADAH directly to confirm the survival and availability of any specific series before concluding records are missing.

## Research tips
- **Pre-1817 records are labeled 'Mississippi Territory,' not Alabama.** Any record created before March 3, 1817 carries "Mississippi Territory" as its jurisdiction. Searching indexes by modern state name "Alabama" alone will miss all pre-1817 material (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Start with territorial censuses and tax lists, not the 1810 federal census.** The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (at ADAH) may be the earliest documentary evidence of a family in present-day Alabama. Tax lists from the county's formation date also predate the 1810 census (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Treat Mobile separately from the interior.** The Mobile District had an entirely different colonial history and record base. Spanish-era Catholic church registers, census returns, and land grants exist for Mobile residents ca. 1800 and are held in European archives. Interior Alabama settler research follows American territorial-era record patterns (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Alabama is a federal land state — use the BLM GLO website.** Land was distributed by the U.S. General Land Office. Federal patent records for the earliest land sales (ca. 1809+) are free and searchable at glorecords.blm.gov. Prior Spanish and British grants in the Mobile area were adjudicated under U.S. law and may be in NARA land claim records.
- **Church records are the only vital records for this period.** FamilySearch collection 1986396 (Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950) is indexed and includes images, beginning in 1803. Mobile's Catholic registers are the oldest surviving vital records in the region.
- **Militia rolls and court minutes at ADAH** are among the richest sources for free adult males ca. 1800 who appear in no other surviving record type. County court minute books record road assignments, jury lists, and poor relief.
- **Bounty land warrant records for War of 1812 and Creek War veterans** can establish a settler's former state of residence and military service history. These are at NARA and on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Check adjoining jurisdictions.** The Mississippi Territory (western half, now Mississippi state) borders Alabama to the west; Georgia borders to the east; Tennessee to the north. Families near these borders generated records on multiple sides. Many families who appear in Alabama after 1815 migrated directly from Georgia and have prior records there.
- **Read the 1810 census images, not just the index.** FamilySearch has only an index (collection 2016756, no images) for the 1810 census. Full images are on Ancestry.com and at NARA; the images reveal household composition and neighbors that the index does not.

- **1780–1813:** Mobile District under Spanish West Florida. Spanish census returns, church registers, and land grants were created for this area and are not held in U.S. repositories.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory established; initially a narrow strip, expanded in 1804 and 1812 to include all of present-day Alabama.
- **1813:** U.S. annexation of the Mobile District ended Spanish authority.
- **1817:** Western half of Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; eastern half organized as Alabama Territory. Records created before 1817 carry "Mississippi Territory" as the jurisdiction of record.
- **County formation:** Washington County (1800) was the first county organized in present-day Alabama. Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), Clarke (1812), Monroe (1815), and others followed rapidly. Records are filed at the county level once a county was organized.

## Available record types

Note: For the ca. 1800 period, the jurisdictional level for most records is the **individual county** (once formed) or the **Mississippi Territory** (before county formation), not a state.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of vital events existed in the Mississippi Territory or Alabama Territory period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records did not return Alabama-specific content in this survey, so a statewide civil registration start date cannot be stated from tool results.
- **What exists for the territorial period:** Marriage bonds and licenses survive at the county level beginning with each county's organization. FamilySearch has **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images; **indexed + images**), which overlaps the final decade of the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; individual county probate offices for originals.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records exist for ca. 1800. Marriage records before individual counties were formed do not exist in civil form.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); territorial and county court minutes recording marriages by justices; tombstone inscriptions.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, established ca. 1703); Baptist (frontier ca. 1808+); Methodist (circuit riders ca. 1800+); Presbyterian (early missions).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Mobile's Catholic registers are the richest pre-1815 church records in the region.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images; **indexed + images**), beginning in 1803 (the territorial period). For Mobile-area Catholic records predating U.S. control, original registers are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile; microfilm copies of French and Spanish colonial-era Mobile records are at the Mobile Municipal Archives and the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French colonial period are in French; Spanish colonial records are in Spanish. Early American-settler church records are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census capturing the Alabama region was 1810. No federal census was taken for the Mississippi Territory in 1800 (the territory was newly organized and sparsely settled). FamilySearch has **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756; 287,634 records; **index only, no images**). Images of the 1810 census are on Ancestry.com and at NARA.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, and 1808 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). These are held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery. The FamilySearch volume_search tool returned 0 digitized volumes for Alabama in 1780–1819, confirming these censuses are **not digitized or browsable on FamilySearch**.
- **Access:** Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808: physical-only at ADAH. 1810 federal census: name-indexed on FamilySearch (no images there); images on Ancestry.com.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Territorial and county court minutes (civil suits, road assignments, jury rolls, poor relief) are also important sources.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch has **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images; **indexed + images**), beginning at the earliest county formations. Pre-1809 territorial court records may exist at ADAH.
- **Testate or intestate:** Both wills (testate) and administrations (intestate) are included in collection 1537764; determine which applies to the individual before searching.
- **Where held:** ADAH; individual county probate courts for originals.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (public land survey system). Alabama is a federal land state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued federal land patents beginning with the earliest land sales, ca. 1809–1820 in most areas. Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile District predate U.S. control and were separately adjudicated; they are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Types:** Federal patents, Spanish land grants, British colonial grants, deeds, county tax records.
- **Date range:** Federal patents from ca. 1809+; Spanish colonial grants from 1780–1813 for the Mobile District.
- **Where held:** BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov, free online) for federal patents; Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress for Spanish grants; ADAH and county courthouses for deeds and tax records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (1812–1815); Creek War (1813–1814); territorial militia actions ca. 1800–1817.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Creek War), territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for service records and pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) for digitized military records; ADAH for state and territorial militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries in Mobile (including the colonial-era Church Street Graveyard). Frontier burial grounds throughout the territory — many were family plots with no surviving documentation.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some Alabama cemetery transcriptions; coverage for burials ca. 1800 is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for Mobile's Catholic cemeteries, held by the Archdiocese of Mobile, are the best-documented early burial records in the region.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Alabama region at ca. 1800. The first newspaper was the Mobile Centinel (1811), followed by the Alabama Republican (Huntsville, 1816).
- **Where held:** ADAH; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription); Library of Congress Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free).
- **Content value:** Newspapers from 1811–1819 may carry legal notices, land sales, and early obituaries but cannot cover events before ca. 1811.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile Bay (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (adjacent).
- **Record types:** Most settlers arrived overland from the east and south — passenger manifests are not the primary research tool for the interior. Naturalization records: no organized territorial naturalization system existed for ordinary settlers ca. 1800. Spanish subjects in Mobile could take oaths of allegiance.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for New Orleans port records; Library of Congress for Spanish colonial records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine full manifests for any Mobile-bound sea arrivals. Most Alabama-region migrants of ca. 1800 were American-born settlers moving overland; genealogical passenger-list research applies primarily to the Mobile area for European (French, Spanish) arrivals.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax; poll tax. In a federal land state, tax records often predate the federal patent and are the earliest evidence of residence.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax records from ca. 1800; other counties from their formation dates.
- **Where held:** ADAH (primary repository); some county courthouses retain originals. Noted as territorial records at ADAH (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1800 federal census does not cover the Alabama territory and the 1810 census has no images on FamilySearch, tax lists and territorial censuses are among the best substitutes for placing families in the territory around 1800.

### Other record types
- **Territorial and county court minutes:** Record ordinary county business — road assignments, poor relief, justice-of-the-peace marriages, petit jury rolls — naming settlers who appear in no other record type.
- **Militia rolls:** Territorial militia muster rolls name free adult males. Listed as territorial records at ADAH (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Spanish colonial records (Mobile District):** Census returns, church registers, and land grants from 1780–1813, held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence), with copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century local histories (e.g., Albert J. Pickett's *History of Alabama*, 1851) reprint early records and list founding families, and are sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (collection 1986396; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (collection 1598408; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (collection 1537764; indexed + images) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (collection 2016756; index only, no images) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1810 U.S. Federal Census images; U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 / Creek War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files, federal land records | Free finding aids; some digitized |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Alabama newspapers (1811+) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey (digitized volumes):** The volume_search tool returned 0 digitized volumes on FamilySearch for Alabama in 1780–1819. This is a genuine digitization gap for the pre-statehood era: no browse-only image volumes for ca. 1800 are available on FamilySearch. The 4 collections listed above are name-indexed and include images, but their coverage begins at 1803 (Church Records) and 1809 (Marriages, Probate) at the earliest; the Census Substitutes Index starts at 1810 and has no images.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808), tax records, militia rolls, county court minutes, early deeds | In-person; finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| NARA, Washington DC / Southeast Region, Atlanta | Military service records, pension files, Creek War records, federal land records (RG 49, RG 15, RG 94) | In-person; NARA.gov request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile, colonial era onward) | Contact archives office |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records | In-person |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias); some French colonial material | In-person; some digitized at loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records: Mobile District census, church registers, land grants, 1780–1813 | Contact or use microfilm copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | Original French colonial records for Mobile, 1702–1763 | Contact archives; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| County probate courts (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Clarke, etc.) | Original deed books, court minutes, marriage bonds | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 — physical only at ADAH, not digitized on FamilySearch
- County tax lists for ca. 1800–1817 — physical or microfilm at ADAH and county courthouses
- Territorial and county court minutes — physical at county courthouses and ADAH
- Militia rolls — physical at ADAH
- Spanish colonial land grants and civil records for the Mobile District (1780–1813) — originals in Seville; microfilm copies in Mobile and Washington
- French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763) — originals in Aix-en-Provence; some microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Early Baptist and Methodist church registers (ca. 1808–1819) — scattered, many congregations hold their own records

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for the Alabama territorial period were returned by the tools used in this survey. The Alabama Department of Archives and History holds the primary repository of territorial-era records. Researchers should contact ADAH directly to confirm the survival and availability of any specific series before concluding records are missing.

## Research tips
- **Pre-1817 records are labeled 'Mississippi Territory,' not Alabama.** Any record created before March 3, 1817 carries "Mississippi Territory" as its jurisdiction. Searching indexes by modern state name "Alabama" alone will miss all pre-1817 material (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Start with territorial censuses and tax lists, not the 1810 federal census.** The Mississippi Territory censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (at ADAH) may be the earliest documentary evidence of a family in present-day Alabama. Tax lists from the county's formation date also predate the 1810 census (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Treat Mobile separately from the interior.** The Mobile District had an entirely different colonial history and record base. Spanish-era Catholic church registers, census returns, and land grants exist for Mobile residents ca. 1800 and are held in European archives. Interior Alabama settler research follows American territorial-era record patterns (source: FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Alabama is a federal land state — use the BLM GLO website.** Land was distributed by the U.S. General Land Office. Federal patent records for the earliest land sales (ca. 1809+) are free and searchable at glorecords.blm.gov. Prior Spanish and British grants in the Mobile area were adjudicated under U.S. law and may be in NARA land claim records.
- **Church records are the only vital records for this period.** FamilySearch collection 1986396 (Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950) is indexed and includes images, beginning in 1803. Mobile's Catholic registers are the oldest surviving vital records in the region.
- **Militia rolls and court minutes at ADAH** are among the richest sources for free adult males ca. 1800 who appear in no other surviving record type. County court minute books record road assignments, jury lists, and poor relief.
- **Bounty land warrant records for War of 1812 and Creek War veterans** can establish a settler's former state of residence and military service history. These are at NARA and on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Check adjoining jurisdictions.** The Mississippi Territory (western half, now Mississippi state) borders Alabama to the west; Georgia borders to the east; Tennessee to the north. Families near these borders generated records on multiple sides. Many families who appear in Alabama after 1815 migrated directly from Georgia and have prior records there.
- **Read the 1810 census images, not just the index.** FamilySearch has only an index (collection 2016756, no images) for the 1810 census. Full images are on Ancestry.com and at NARA; the images reveal household composition and neighbors that the index does not.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) — U.S. Census data
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining, dominated by collieries in the Southern Coal Field. Mine operators included the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and other large concerns. Breakerboys, loaders, contract miners, mule drivers, and mine bosses were the primary occupational roles recorded in payroll and census records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish Catholic immigration from the 1840s famine era onward, with Welsh, English, and German miners arriving earlier. By the 1870s–1880s Eastern European (Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian) immigration was beginning. The Irish concentrated in towns such as Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Girardville, and Minersville.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Welsh Congregationalist, Anglican/Episcopal, German Lutheran and Reformed, and later Eastern-rite Catholic congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires conflict and trials (mid-1870s) generated significant court and newspaper records. The Long Strike of 1875 appears in corporate records and local newspapers. Mine-accident records begin in earnest after the Pennsylvania Mine Safety Acts of the 1870s.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties.
- Records predating 1811 must be sought in those two parent counties.
- The five anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) are the geographic scope of the coal region; **this guide surveys Schuylkill County only.** Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland each require their own locality surveys.
- Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878; records for what is now Lackawanna before 1878 are held under Luzerne County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Vital Records page returned only generic content and did not state a specific registration date or level for Pennsylvania; the researcher should consult that page directly. The generic guidance notes that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s.
- **What exists (digitized):** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Marriage Records for Schuylkill County, 1870–1910 (DGS 007936753, 94 images), accessible as browse-only images with 0% name indexing — must be examined image by image with no name search.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse, Pottsville. FamilySearch browse-only images available for the marriage volume.
- **Gaps:** Birth and death registration digitization is not represented in the five FamilySearch volumes returned by the survey. The researcher should check the Pennsylvania State Archives for civil registration records and county clerk holdings.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers (see Church Records below) and triennial state tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) are the primary substitutes for missing civil vital records in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish and later Eastern European parishes established 1840–1870+); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; German Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal. The coal region had dense Catholic parish formation to serve immigrant communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations (dated separately from baptisms).
- **Diocesan jurisdiction — critical quirk:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties fell under the Catholic Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna moved to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg. Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Route Catholic record requests to the Diocese of Allentown (for Schuylkill County events after 1961's diocesan formation) or the Diocese of Philadelphia (for events before that). Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Church Records for Schuylkill County, 1842–1895 (DGS 007936751, 187 images). **This volume is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and contains both English and German-language entries.** The researcher must browse image by image and be prepared to read German script.
- A collection titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, dates 1708–1985) appeared in FamilySearch collections results but is labeled in its title as a synthetic test fixture — confirm whether it represents a real public collection on FamilySearch before relying on it.
- **Language:** English and German within the DGS 007936751 volume. Irish-immigrant Catholic registers are in English (Latin formula entries with vernacular names).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 within the target period. The 1880 census is fully indexed. The 1870 and 1860 censuses are indexed. Mortality schedules (1860–1880) list deaths in the year preceding the census — particularly valuable for mining communities with high accident rates.
- **State/other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853. These triennial assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — use them as substitutes in off-census years and to track mobility between collieries. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Triennial assessment ledgers are a physical/microfilm source — consult the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Probate Records for Schuylkill County, 1851–1930 (DGS 007936749, 412 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
- Additionally, FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) contains 3,200,560 images with 0 indexed records — browse-only at scale.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (Register of Wills office), Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Court records note:** Naturalization records (see Immigration below) are held within the court system and may appear in Common Pleas minute books alongside other county business.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses the metes-and-bounds system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Land and Property page returned only generic content. The researcher should consult that page directly for Pennsylvania-specific grants and patent information.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, grants. Deed records are the most consistently available land record for this period.
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Deed Records for Schuylkill County, 1815–1900 (DGS 007936752, 543 images). This is the **only partially name-indexed volume in the survey: 22% of records are name-indexed** and images are available. The remaining 78% must be browsed.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania infantry regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files are at NARA (National Archives, Washington, D.C. and Philadelphia regional branch). Pennsylvania adjutant general records for Civil War service may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Draft registration records (Civil War-era) are at NARA.
- **Bounty land:** Bounty land warrant applications (for earlier service) and pension files can document family relationships and birthplaces not found in vital records.
- **Access:** Pension files at NARA are physical; many are indexed on Ancestry and FoldedSoldiers (fold3.com). Pennsylvania Civil War service indices are online at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Multiple Catholic cemeteries (Saint Patrick's, Saint Clair's, and others in mining towns), as well as Protestant and non-sectarian cemeteries in Pottsville and surrounding patches.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have indexed many Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage is uneven for small patch-town cemeteries. Check both.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual parishes or cemetery associations. Contact the relevant Catholic diocese archive (Diocese of Allentown) for parish burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville), founded 1825, is the dominant regional paper of record for the coal region in this period. It published obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, court proceedings, and labor news.
- **Content value:** Extremely high for Irish coal-mining families — mine accident notices, Molly Maguires trial coverage, labor-union meeting notices, and immigration-community news. Obituaries often name country of origin, surviving family, and church affiliation.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archives are held in various repositories including the Schuylkill County Historical Society and on microfilm. Some issues have been digitized; consult the Chronicling America portal (Library of Congress) and the Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive for available digital runs.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Irish immigrants arriving in the 1840s–1860s most commonly entered through New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island predecessor) and Philadelphia. Some came through Boston, Baltimore, or Quebec.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (Castle Garden records from 1855; pre-1855 records are thinner and often indexed only by ship), naturalization declarations, affidavits.
- **Naturalization — critical:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of Naturalization Records for Schuylkill County, 1849–1915 (DGS 007936750, 298 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Pre-1906 declarations of intention could be filed in any court of record — check Common Pleas, Orphans Court, and federal district courts, not just one series. The naturalization form often recorded birthplace, year of emigration, and port of arrival.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Access:** NARA holds passenger lists; Castle Garden (pre-1892) records are at CastleGarden.org; Ellis Island records are at ElliIsland.org. Naturalization browse-only images are on FamilySearch.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state assessment ledgers (from 1853); county property and poll tax records.
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments from 1853 cover the full 1860–1890 target period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; some county-level holdings at Schuylkill County courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments are the primary census substitute for off-years (1861, 1864, 1867, etc.) and can trace year-to-year mobility between collieries. They record occupation and sometimes nativity. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).

### Other record types

#### Colliery employment records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field (primarily Luzerne/Lackawanna counties), drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names are inconsistently recorded in census records. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Note:** This index covers the *lower* anthracite field. A comparable index for the southern (Schuylkill County) field was not identified in tool results; the researcher should inquire with the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Pennsylvania State Archives about payroll-derived indexes for Schuylkill County collieries.
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less direct as a genealogical finding aid, but valuable once a colliery is identified.

#### Organizational records
- The Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH) had active divisions in the Schuylkill coal region. AOH membership records (held locally and at divisional archives) can document Irish identity, community ties, and family connections.
- Labor union records (Workingmen's Benevolent Association; later the United Mine Workers) may document membership.

#### School records
- Public school enrollment records are held by individual school districts (Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, etc.); most are physical-only holdings at the district or local historical society.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 digitized volumes (Probate 1851–1930, Naturalization 1849–1915, Church Records 1842–1895, Deed Records 1815–1900, Marriage Records 1870–1910); Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1683–1994 (3.2M images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 U.S. Federal Census — Schuylkill County (pre-period); Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (pre-period) | Subscription |
| Castle Garden | Pre-1892 passenger arrivals for Irish immigrant research | Free |
| NARA (online via Ancestry/Fold3) | Civil War service and pension records; passenger lists | Mixed |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County in the 1860–1890 period; all 5 were returned (no additional pages). FamilySearch curated external links for this place and time window returned only 2 results, both predating 1860 — FamilySearch has no curated external links for Schuylkill County specifically within the 1860–1890 window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed records, court minutes, naturalization dockets, marriage licenses | In-person or written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, state-level vital records, colonial and state land records, military records | In-person; some holdings online at PA State Archives portal |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, Miners' Journal microfilm runs, cemetery transcriptions, genealogical files | In-person; contact for hours |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill and Carbon counties) | Written request; check diocesan archive access policy |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers predating Allentown's 1961 erection | Written request |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Branch | Federal court naturalization records, Civil War pension files | In-person or NARA request |

## Records NOT online
- Triennial Pennsylvania state assessment ledgers (primary census substitute) — physical, Pennsylvania State Archives
- Mine-inspection and accident reports — organized by colliery, not indexed by name; physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- AOH and labor union membership records — physical at local/divisional archives
- Catholic parish baptismal and burial registers beyond the single digitized Church Records volume — contact Diocese of Allentown or Diocese of Philadelphia
- Public school enrollment records — physical at individual school districts
- County court minute books (which record ordinary county business, road maintenance assignments, poor relief payments) — physical at Schuylkill County courthouse

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified a specific record loss for Schuylkill County. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction. The FamilySearch Wiki's Schuylkill County Genealogy page and Pennsylvania-specific wiki pages returned only generic content and did not address record losses. The researcher should consult the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Pennsylvania State Archives directly regarding any known courthouse fires or losses for this county.

## Research tips
- **Distinguish the colliery employment indexes by field.** The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898) covers the lower anthracite field — primarily Luzerne and Lackawanna counties. For Schuylkill County specifically, payroll-derived indexes were not confirmed in tool results; inquire with the Schuylkill County Historical Society about surviving company records for specific collieries. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Use the triennial assessments as your census substitute.** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated residents every three years from 1853, listing occupation and sometimes nativity. These ledgers fill the gaps between federal censuses (1861, 1864, 1867, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1881, 1884, 1887) and can trace a miner's movement between patch towns. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Route Catholic records by diocese carefully.** Schuylkill County Catholic records from the 1860s–1890s fall under Philadelphia (pre-1961). The Diocese of Allentown holds records from 1961 onward. Direct requests to the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives for registers created before Allentown's erection. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations require a broad court search.** Because declarations of intention could be filed in any court of record before 1906, check the FamilySearch browse-only naturalization volume (DGS 007936750) but also search Common Pleas minute books and NARA federal district court records. The naturalization form often recorded birthplace, year of emigration, and port of arrival — critical for tracing Irish origin.
- **The Miners' Journal is the first newspaper to check.** Its continuous run from 1825 through the target period covers mine accidents, Molly Maguires trials, labor actions, and community vital notices for Irish families in the Schuylkill region. Check the Schuylkill County Historical Society and Chronicling America for available runs.
- **Deed Records are the most searchable land source.** With 22% of DGS 007936752 name-indexed, deed records are the only partially name-searchable volume for Schuylkill County in this survey. Start here for property transactions; the remaining 78% requires browsing.
- **Search adjoining coal counties.** Irish miners moved frequently between patch towns across county lines. The wiki home page for Schuylkill County returned generic content and did not supply a Neighboring Counties table; the researcher should search Carbon, Luzerne, Northumberland, Columbia, Dauphin, Lebanon, and Berks counties for records of the same families. Lackawanna County (formed 1878 from Luzerne) also needs its own locality survey.
- **Records before 1811 are under Berks and Northampton counties.** If tracing family lines before Schuylkill County's formation, search those two parent counties for deeds, court records, and church records.
