- **What exists (digitized):** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Marriage Records for Schuylkill County, 1870–1910 (DGS 007936753, 94 images), accessible as browse-only images with 0% name indexing — must be examined image by image with no name search.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse, Pottsville. FamilySearch browse-only images available for the marriage volume.
- **Gaps:** Birth and death registration digitization is not represented in the five FamilySearch volumes returned by the survey. The researcher should check the Pennsylvania State Archives for civil registration records and county clerk holdings.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers (see Church Records below) and triennial state tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) are the primary substitutes for missing civil vital records in this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish and later Eastern European parishes established 1840–1870+); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; German Lutheran; German Reformed; Episcopal. The coal region had dense Catholic parish formation to serve immigrant communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations (dated separately from baptisms).
- **Diocesan jurisdiction — critical quirk:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties fell under the Catholic Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna moved to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg. Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Route Catholic record requests to the Diocese of Allentown (for Schuylkill County events after 1961's diocesan formation) or the Diocese of Philadelphia (for events before that). Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Church Records for Schuylkill County, 1842–1895 (DGS 007936751, 187 images). **This volume is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and contains both English and German-language entries.** The researcher must browse image by image and be prepared to read German script.
- A collection titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, dates 1708–1985) appeared in FamilySearch collections results but is labeled in its title as a synthetic test fixture — confirm whether it represents a real public collection on FamilySearch before relying on it.
- **Language:** English and German within the DGS 007936751 volume. Irish-immigrant Catholic registers are in English (Latin formula entries with vernacular names).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 within the target period. The 1880 census is fully indexed. The 1870 and 1860 censuses are indexed. Mortality schedules (1860–1880) list deaths in the year preceding the census — particularly valuable for mining communities with high accident rates.
- **State/other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853. These triennial assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — use them as substitutes in off-census years and to track mobility between collieries. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Triennial assessment ledgers are a physical/microfilm source — consult the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Probate Records for Schuylkill County, 1851–1930 (DGS 007936749, 412 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed image by image.
- Additionally, FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) contains 3,200,560 images with 0 indexed records — browse-only at scale.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (Register of Wills office), Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Court records note:** Naturalization records (see Immigration below) are held within the court system and may appear in Common Pleas minute books alongside other county business.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses the metes-and-bounds system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Land and Property page returned only generic content. The researcher should consult that page directly for Pennsylvania-specific grants and patent information.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, grants. Deed records are the most consistently available land record for this period.
- **Digitized holdings:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Deed Records for Schuylkill County, 1815–1900 (DGS 007936752, 543 images). This is the **only partially name-indexed volume in the survey: 22% of records are name-indexed** and images are available. The remaining 78% must be browsed.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania infantry regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files are at NARA (National Archives, Washington, D.C. and Philadelphia regional branch). Pennsylvania adjutant general records for Civil War service may be at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Draft registration records (Civil War-era) are at NARA.
- **Bounty land:** Bounty land warrant applications (for earlier service) and pension files can document family relationships and birthplaces not found in vital records.
- **Access:** Pension files at NARA are physical; many are indexed on Ancestry and FoldedSoldiers (fold3.com). Pennsylvania Civil War service indices are online at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Multiple Catholic cemeteries (Saint Patrick's, Saint Clair's, and others in mining towns), as well as Protestant and non-sectarian cemeteries in Pottsville and surrounding patches.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have indexed many Schuylkill County cemeteries; coverage is uneven for small patch-town cemeteries. Check both.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual parishes or cemetery associations. Contact the relevant Catholic diocese archive (Diocese of Allentown) for parish burial registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville), founded 1825, is the dominant regional paper of record for the coal region in this period. It published obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, court proceedings, and labor news.
- **Content value:** Extremely high for Irish coal-mining families — mine accident notices, Molly Maguires trial coverage, labor-union meeting notices, and immigration-community news. Obituaries often name country of origin, surviving family, and church affiliation.
- **Where held:** The Miners' Journal archives are held in various repositories including the Schuylkill County Historical Society and on microfilm. Some issues have been digitized; consult the Chronicling America portal (Library of Congress) and the Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive for available digital runs.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Irish immigrants arriving in the 1840s–1860s most commonly entered through New York (Castle Garden / Ellis Island predecessor) and Philadelphia. Some came through Boston, Baltimore, or Quebec.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (Castle Garden records from 1855; pre-1855 records are thinner and often indexed only by ship), naturalization declarations, affidavits.
- **Naturalization — critical:** FamilySearch holds a digitized volume of Naturalization Records for Schuylkill County, 1849–1915 (DGS 007936750, 298 images). **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Pre-1906 declarations of intention could be filed in any court of record — check Common Pleas, Orphans Court, and federal district courts, not just one series. The naturalization form often recorded birthplace, year of emigration, and port of arrival.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Access:** NARA holds passenger lists; Castle Garden (pre-1892) records are at CastleGarden.org; Ellis Island records are at ElliIsland.org. Naturalization browse-only images are on FamilySearch.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state assessment ledgers (from 1853); county property and poll tax records.
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments from 1853 cover the full 1860–1890 target period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; some county-level holdings at Schuylkill County courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments are the primary census substitute for off-years (1861, 1864, 1867, etc.) and can trace year-to-year mobility between collieries. They record occupation and sometimes nativity. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).

### Other record types

#### Colliery employment records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field (primarily Luzerne/Lackawanna counties), drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names are inconsistently recorded in census records. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Note:** This index covers the *lower* anthracite field. A comparable index for the southern (Schuylkill County) field was not identified in tool results; the researcher should inquire with the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Pennsylvania State Archives about payroll-derived indexes for Schuylkill County collieries.
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less direct as a genealogical finding aid, but valuable once a colliery is identified.

#### Organizational records
- The Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH) had active divisions in the Schuylkill coal region. AOH membership records (held locally and at divisional archives) can document Irish identity, community ties, and family connections.
- Labor union records (Workingmen's Benevolent Association; later the United Mine Workers) may document membership.

#### School records
- Public school enrollment records are held by individual school districts (Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, etc.); most are physical-only holdings at the district or local historical society.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 5 digitized volumes (Probate 1851–1930, Naturalization 1849–1915, Church Records 1842–1895, Deed Records 1815–1900, Marriage Records 1870–1910); Pennsylvania Probate Records collection 1683–1994 (3.2M images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 U.S. Federal Census — Schuylkill County (pre-period); Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (pre-period) | Subscription |
| Castle Garden | Pre-1892 passenger arrivals for Irish immigrant research | Free |
| NARA (online via Ancestry/Fold3) | Civil War service and pension records; passenger lists | Mixed |

**Coverage of this survey:** 5 digitized volumes match Schuylkill County in the 1860–1890 period; all 5 were returned (no additional pages). FamilySearch curated external links for this place and time window returned only 2 results, both predating 1860 — FamilySearch has no curated external links for Schuylkill County specifically within the 1860–1890 window.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deed records, court minutes, naturalization dockets, marriage licenses | In-person or written request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, state-level vital records, colonial and state land records, military records | In-person; some holdings online at PA State Archives portal |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, Miners' Journal microfilm runs, cemetery transcriptions, genealogical files | In-person; contact for hours |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill and Carbon counties) | Written request; check diocesan archive access policy |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers predating Allentown's 1961 erection | Written request |
| NARA Philadelphia Regional Branch | Federal court naturalization records, Civil War pension files | In-person or NARA request |

## Records NOT online
- Triennial Pennsylvania state assessment ledgers (primary census substitute) — physical, Pennsylvania State Archives
- Mine-inspection and accident reports — organized by colliery, not indexed by name; physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- AOH and labor union membership records — physical at local/divisional archives
- Catholic parish baptismal and burial registers beyond the single digitized Church Records volume — contact Diocese of Allentown or Diocese of Philadelphia
- Public school enrollment records — physical at individual school districts
- County court minute books (which record ordinary county business, road maintenance assignments, poor relief payments) — physical at Schuylkill County courthouse

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey identified a specific record loss for Schuylkill County. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction. The FamilySearch Wiki's Schuylkill County Genealogy page and Pennsylvania-specific wiki pages returned only generic content and did not address record losses. The researcher should consult the Schuylkill County Historical Society and the Pennsylvania State Archives directly regarding any known courthouse fires or losses for this county.

## Research tips
- **Distinguish the colliery employment indexes by field.** The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898) covers the lower anthracite field — primarily Luzerne and Lackawanna counties. For Schuylkill County specifically, payroll-derived indexes were not confirmed in tool results; inquire with the Schuylkill County Historical Society about surviving company records for specific collieries. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Use the triennial assessments as your census substitute.** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated residents every three years from 1853, listing occupation and sometimes nativity. These ledgers fill the gaps between federal censuses (1861, 1864, 1867, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1881, 1884, 1887) and can trace a miner's movement between patch towns. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Route Catholic records by diocese carefully.** Schuylkill County Catholic records from the 1860s–1890s fall under Philadelphia (pre-1961). The Diocese of Allentown holds records from 1961 onward. Direct requests to the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives for registers created before Allentown's erection. Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations require a broad court search.** Because declarations of intention could be filed in any court of record before 1906, check the FamilySearch browse-only naturalization volume (DGS 007936750) but also search Common Pleas minute books and NARA federal district court records. The naturalization form often recorded birthplace, year of emigration, and port of arrival — critical for tracing Irish origin.
- **The Miners' Journal is the first newspaper to check.** Its continuous run from 1825 through the target period covers mine accidents, Molly Maguires trials, labor actions, and community vital notices for Irish families in the Schuylkill region. Check the Schuylkill County Historical Society and Chronicling America for available runs.
- **Deed Records are the most searchable land source.** With 22% of DGS 007936752 name-indexed, deed records are the only partially name-searchable volume for Schuylkill County in this survey. Start here for property transactions; the remaining 78% requires browsing.
- **Search adjoining coal counties.** Irish miners moved frequently between patch towns across county lines. The wiki home page for Schuylkill County returned generic content and did not supply a Neighboring Counties table; the researcher should search Carbon, Luzerne, Northumberland, Columbia, Dauphin, Lebanon, and Berks counties for records of the same families. Lackawanna County (formed 1878 from Luzerne) also needs its own locality survey.
- **Records before 1811 are under Berks and Northampton counties.** If tracing family lines before Schuylkill County's formation, search those two parent counties for deeds, court records, and church records.

It names the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule as the starting point ('the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, naming approximately 1,800 grantees'), instructs researchers to contact town clerk offices directly for town-level vital records (citing the FamilySearch Wiki's explicit instruction), recommends using 19th-century town histories to access colonial proprietors' records (citing the Wiki's identification of these as reprinting otherwise-inaccessible records), and flags the critical pitfall that both New Hampshire and New York records must be searched for pre-1777 events because the land-grant controversy created a geographic ambiguity, not a clean temporal split. The guide also identifies the 1790 federal census as the closest population-level record and notes that no statewide civil registration existed before 1857. It recommends Revolutionary War pension files as a source for family relationships and names neighboring jurisdictions (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, New York) to search. The strategy is specific, cites FamilySearch Wiki content, and includes multiple pitfalls (no civil registration, uneven town records, dual-jurisdiction land records, record losses not confirmed).

Here is the locality guide for **pre-statehood Vermont (ca. 1760–March 1791)**:

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Overview

The territory that became Vermont passed through several distinct political phases before statehood:

- **New Hampshire Grants era (1749–1764):** Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued patents for virtually all of present-day Vermont, calling the region the "New Hampshire Grants." Settlers who held Wentworth grants recognized New Hampshire authority.
- **New York claim and disputed period (1764–1777):** The Crown ruled in 1764 that the Connecticut River — not the Hudson — was New Hampshire's western boundary, placing the Grants under New York jurisdiction. New York re-granted land already granted by New Hampshire, creating bitter, sometimes violent conflict between "Yorkers" and settlers loyal to their NH grants. This is the era of Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys.
- **Republic of Vermont (1777–1791):** Vermont declared independence from both colonies in 1777, adopted a constitution (the first in North America to prohibit adult slavery), and governed itself as an unrecognized republic until admitted to the Union on 4 March 1791 as the 14th state.

> **Critical implication:** A single settler in the 1770s may appear in **both** New Hampshire and New York records — under the same parcel of land — depending on which authority that person recognized. Check both colonial archives.

---

### Vital Records

**There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in this period.** Statewide civil vital registration did not begin in Vermont until **1857**.

For pre-statehood vital events, search:

| Record Type | Where to Look |
|---|---|
| Church registers | Individual congregations; Congregational records often deposited at the Vermont Historical Society or denominational archives |
| Town clerk records | Some towns began keeping records from the early 1770s; survival varies widely — contact each town clerk directly |
| Headstone inscriptions | Town and church cemeteries; the Vermont Old Cemetery Association (VOCA) has indexed many |
| Bible records | Published in genealogical journals; the Genealogical Society of Vermont has compiled some |

---

### Land Records — The Most Important Pre-Statehood Source

Land records are the primary evidence for this period. Two parallel systems exist:

**New Hampshire Grant Records**
- Held at the **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management**, Concord, NH
- The **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** is the earliest systematic name list for the future state — it enumerates roughly 1,800 grantees and is an essential starting point

**New York Competing-Grant Records**
- Held at the **New York State Archives**, Albany, NY
- Settlers who accepted New York patents will appear here but not in the NH grant records, and vice versa

**Vermont Town Proprietors' Records**
- Towns granted under NH authority maintained proprietors' records (records of the original township grantees and their lot assignments)
- Many survive in town clerk offices or have been transcribed in 19th-century town histories
- FamilySearch has microfilmed some; search the **FamilySearch Catalog** by town name

**Republic of Vermont Land Records**
- After 1777, the Republic of Vermont's General Assembly re-granted "Yorker" lands
- These records are at the **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)**, Montpelier

---

### Census and Population Lists

No federal census was taken before statehood. Substitute lists include:

| Year | Record | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1771 | New Hampshire Grant Survey Schedule | ~1,800 grantees; most useful pre-statehood name list |
| 1790 | U.S. Federal Census | First federal census taken after Vermont statehood; covers heads of household |
| Various | Town Grand Lists (tax lists) | Some towns kept annual grand lists from the 1770s onward; held at town clerk offices or VSARA |
| Various | Militia musters | Republic of Vermont maintained militia rolls; check VSARA |

---

### Church Records

The dominant denomination in colonial Vermont was **Congregationalist**, reflecting New England migration patterns. Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, and Quaker congregations also formed in this period.

- Congregational records: many deposited at the **Vermont Historical Society** or individual church archives
- FamilySearch has microfilmed selected Vermont church records — search the **FamilySearch Catalog** under "Vermont → [county] → [town] → Church records"
- The **American Congregational Association** library in Boston holds additional records

---

### Probate Records

Vermont's probate court system was established during the Republic of Vermont period (1778 onward), organized by county. Pre-statehood probate records are held at:

- **County probate court offices** (originals)
- **Vermont State Archives** (some transferred)
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many Vermont probate records; check the Catalog

For deaths before the probate court was organized (pre-1778), look to New York or New Hampshire probate courts if the estate was administered under one of those jurisdictions.

---

### Military Records

| Conflict | Repository |
|---|---|
| French and Indian War (1754–1763) | National Archives; Vermont Historical Society; published muster rolls |
| American Revolution — Continental Army | National Archives (fold3.com); *Pension and Bounty Land Warrant Application Files* |
| American Revolution — Vermont militia | VSARA; Vermont Historical Society; published in *Vermont in the Revolution* rosters |
| Republic of Vermont militia (1777–1791) | VSARA |

The **Revolutionary War pension files** (available on Fold3 and FamilySearch) are among the richest sources for pre-statehood biography.

---

### Town Histories

The FamilySearch Wiki specifically calls out **19th-century Vermont town histories** as the best path to colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise inaccessible. These histories routinely transcribe original proprietors' records, town meeting minutes, and early vital records. The Vermont Historical Society holds an extensive collection. Many have been digitized on:

- **Internet Archive (archive.org)**
- **HathiTrust**
- **Google Books**

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA), Montpelier | Land records, legislative records, Republic of Vermont records, some vital records |
| Vermont Historical Society, Barre | Town histories, church records, manuscripts, published genealogies |
| New Hampshire Division of Archives, Concord NH | NH Grant records, 1771 Survey Schedule |
| New York State Archives, Albany NY | NY competing-grant records |
| National Archives (Washington / regional) | Federal census (1790+), military pension files, land bounty warrants |

---

### Research Strategy for Pre-Statehood Ancestors

1. **Identify the town** — Vermont is a "strong towns" state; almost every record set is organized by town, not county. Pinpoint the town before anything else.
2. **Search the 1790 census** and work backward.
3. **Check the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** for your surname.
4. **Pull town land records** — deed grantor/grantee indexes from the town clerk, supplemented by FamilySearch microfilm.
5. **Determine denominational affiliation** and contact the congregation or its archival repository.
6. **Search town grand lists** (tax records) from the 1770s–1790s at VSARA.
7. **Check both NH and NY archives** for land disputes, especially for settlers active 1764–1777.
8. **Read the town history** — nearly every Vermont town has one, and many transcribe pre-1800 records available nowhere else.

---

*This guide was built from the Vermont FamilySearch Wiki place page and reflects FamilySearch's documented record holdings and guidance for this jurisdiction.*

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, c. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted to the Union on 4 March 1791 as the 14th state, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). During the target period the territory passed through three distinct political phases:
  - **1760–1776 (New Hampshire Grants era):** The area had been granted to settlers by New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth beginning in 1749. New York claimed the same territory after 1764 and issued competing grants. No separate Vermont jurisdiction existed; records were created under either New Hampshire or New York authority.
  - **1777–1791 (Republic of Vermont):** Vermont declared independence in 1777 and functioned as an unrecognized independent republic. Its own courts, land records, and town governments operated, but it was recognized by no other government until statehood.
  - **1791 onward:** State of Vermont, 14th state of the Union.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single seat for the territory; governance was at the town level during the Republic period.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** New Hampshire (land grants) and New York (competing colonial claims) before 1777; Republic of Vermont 1777–1791.
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period. The 1790 federal census — taken one year after statehood — is the nearest quantitative snapshot.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, logging, and small-scale trade dominated. Settlement was largely in river valleys.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island) pushing north; some Scots-Irish and smaller groups.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and small Quaker meetings. Anglican presence was limited. No established state church.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (ended 1763) opened the region to rapid English settlement; the "Grants" controversy between New Hampshire grantees and New York claimants produced armed conflict (the Green Mountain Boys, 1770s); American Revolution (1775–1783) — Vermont raised militia but had no formal colonial status; Republic of Vermont declared January 1777; statehood 4 March 1791.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1764, the territory was under New Hampshire's jurisdiction for land-granting purposes.
- After 1764, the British Privy Council ruled in favor of New York's claim, making New York the nominal sovereign — though many settlers continued to hold and defend their New Hampshire grants.
- From 1777, the Republic of Vermont claimed boundaries that at times included portions of present-day New Hampshire and New York (the "Eastern and Western Unions"), though these expansions were short-lived. The final Vermont boundary was settled before statehood.
- **Research implication (geographic split):** Whether a pre-1777 land record was filed under New Hampshire or New York depends on which colony the recorder recognized and on the specific grant. This is not a clean temporal split — both series coexisted. Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the same property or person.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in **1857** — at the state level. This date comes from the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). No statewide registration existed during the pre-statehood period.
- **Town-level records:** Some town clerks began recording births, marriages, and deaths as early as the 1770s, but survival is uneven. The FamilySearch Wiki notes these exist and instructs researchers to consult town clerk offices directly.
- **What exists for 1760–1791:** No civil registration at any level above the individual town. For any event in this period, vital information must be sought in church registers, family Bibles, cemetery inscriptions, and town proprietors' records.
- **Gaps:** Extensive. The majority of pre-statehood vital events were never formally recorded in a civil register. Many early town records were not kept, were lost, or were recorded inconsistently.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below), cemetery inscriptions, family Bible entries, town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page does not list specific denominations; the above reflects the settlement pattern confirmed by the jurisdictional context.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) membership rolls and discipline records. Confirmations were recorded by some churches as a separate dated event years after baptism.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives, denominational archives (e.g., Vermont Congregational Conference records, Baptist state convention), and the Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA). The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page does not name specific depositories for church records for this period — consult VSARA directly for guidance.
- **Language:** English.
- **Importance for this period:** Church records are the primary substitute for absent civil registration. Because no civil vital registration existed in 1760–1791, a church baptism or burial entry may be the only record of a birth or death.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in **1790**, one year after Vermont's statehood. It is the closest documentary snapshot to the pre-statehood population and names heads of household with numerical counts of household members. Vermont appears in the 1790 federal census.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** No federal census before 1790. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Census page was not accessible as a Vermont-specific page in this survey (it resolved to a generic overview). Whether any colonial or Republic-era enumeration survives for Vermont is not confirmed by the tool results in this survey.
- **Tax lists and proprietors' lists** (see Land records below) partially substitute for census-type information.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Vermont is indexed and available with images on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

### The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (unique pre-statehood record)
- This record is specifically highlighted by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) as the **earliest systematic resident list for the future state**.
- Prepared under New York colonial authority in 1771.
- Enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize.
- Each entry lists: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch Wiki does not specify where digital or physical copies are held; consult the Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA) and the New York State Archives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Court records include civil suits and Republic-era legislative/judicial proceedings.
- **Jurisdiction:** During 1777–1791, the Republic of Vermont established its own county courts. Before 1777, probate and court filings went to New Hampshire or New York courts depending on which colony the parties recognized.
- **Where held:** Vermont county probate courts (for post-1777 filings); New Hampshire State Archives and New York State Archives (for pre-1777 filings under those colonies). The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Probate Records page was not accessible as a Vermont-specific page in this survey.
- **Access level:** Physical and microfilm; the FamilySearch external-links tool returned no Vermont-specific probate collections for this period.

### Land records
- **The New Hampshire Grants:** Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants in the region from 1749 into the 1760s. These are the foundational land records for most early Vermont families. Held by the New Hampshire State Archives.
- **New York competing grants:** New York issued patents over the same land from the mid-1760s. Held by the New York State Archives.
- **Republic of Vermont land records:** Vermont began issuing its own grants and recording deeds from 1777. County land records begin with county formation. Held at county clerk offices and VSARA.
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England town grant system — the township as a unit granted to a proprietors' group, then subdivided).
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (see above) is a key land-related record for this period.
- **Town Histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are important substitutes when original proprietors' books are unavailable.
- **Access level:** Largely physical or microfilm. The FamilySearch external-links tool returned no Vermont-specific land record collections for the 1760–1791 window.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (ended 1763), American Revolution (1775–1783). Vermont raised its own militia and supplied troops to the Continental Army.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (filed at the federal level after 1818 and 1832 Acts), bounty land warrants, muster rolls, and Vermont state militia records.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal pension and bounty land files, Continental Army service records); Vermont State Archives (militia records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides access to NARA Revolutionary War pension and service files.
- **Access:** NARA Revolutionary War pension files are partially indexed and available at Fold3 (subscription). State militia records are physical at VSARA.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds associated with each settled township. Denominational cemeteries tied to early churches.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) and BillionGraves provide transcriptions and photographs for many Vermont cemeteries, including early colonial-era stones where they survive.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from this early period are rare; most burial information survives on headstones (where extant) or in church burial registers.
- **Importance:** Headstone inscriptions from the 1770s–1790s can provide birth year, death year, and sometimes family relationships not recorded elsewhere.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspaper, the *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington), began publication in 1781. Coverage was limited and survival is uneven for the pre-statehood years.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Library, Vermont Historical Society, and digital archives. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some early Vermont papers.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land dispute announcements, and occasional vital notices. Coverage of the pre-statehood period is thin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers arrived overland from southern New England, not via international immigration. No seaport is in Vermont.
- **Relevant records:** If ancestors came from overseas before settling in Vermont, passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are sparse and held at NARA) would reflect arrival at ports such as Boston, Providence, or New York.
- **Naturalizations:** Not applicable for native-born colonists; naturalization records for foreign-born individuals who arrived before the Revolution are very limited.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town-level property and poll taxes were assessed from the earliest settlement period. Vermont Republic tax lists begin 1777.
- **Date range:** Some town tax lists survive from the 1770s; statewide consistency improves after 1791.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices, Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name male heads of household and property owners in years between censuses. For the pre-1790 period they are among the best substitutes for missing census-type records.

### Other record types
- **Proprietors' records:** Each town grant was administered by a body of proprietors who kept meeting minutes, division records, and lot assignments. These survive for many towns and name early settlers before any other record type. Held at town clerk offices and sometimes transcribed in town histories.
- **Town histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly identifies 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise hard to access (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best finding aids for locating the history of a specific town.
- **Vermont State Papers:** The Vermont legislature published multi-volume documentary compilations (*State Papers of Vermont*) that include colonial-era grants, petitions, and legislative records relevant to the pre-statehood period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some town vital records (coverage unconfirmed for pre-statehood window by tool results); FamilySearch Catalog for microfilmed county/town records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790 Vermont; some early vital records collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War pension files, service records, bounty land warrants | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions and photographs, including early Vermont burial grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including early Vermont papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: Revolutionary War files, 1790 census originals, federal land patents | Free finding aids; some digital records free, some fee-based |

**Coverage of this survey:** The external_links_search returned 6 resources for Vermont in the 1760–1791 window, all generic national databases. No Vermont-specific curated collections were returned. The FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search were not run in this survey (see Records NOT Online below); the FamilySearch Catalog should be searched directly at the town and county level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA), Montpelier VT | Republic-era and early state land records, tax lists, legislative records, militia records, early vital records | In-person; some records available by written request |
| Vermont Historical Society, Barre VT | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections | In-person; some digital finding aids online |
| New Hampshire State Archives, Concord NH | New Hampshire colonial grant records (Wentworth grants), pre-1764 authority records | In-person; some records online |
| New York State Archives, Albany NY | New York colonial competing grants, pre-1777 court and probate filings for the Grants territory | In-person; some records online |
| Individual town clerk offices (Vermont) | Town vital records from the 1770s onward (survival varies by town), land records post-1777, tax lists, proprietors' records | In-person or mail request; contact each town directly |
| NARA (multiple facilities) | 1790 census; Revolutionary War service and pension records; passenger lists | In-person at regional facility; many records digitized at Ancestry/Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- **Pre-statehood New Hampshire grants** (the Wentworth township grants, 1749–1764): physical at the New Hampshire State Archives; not confirmed as digitized by tool results.
- **New York colonial competing land grants for the Grants territory**: physical at the New York State Archives; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Vermont Republic-era court and probate records (1777–1791)**: held at county courthouses and VSARA; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Town-level tax lists and proprietors' records**: survival and accessibility vary by town; most are physical at town clerk offices; some transcribed in town histories available via WorldCat.
- **Early church registers**: held at individual churches, denominational archives, or VSARA; access varies; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**: the FamilySearch Wiki identifies this record but does not specify a digital copy location; check VSARA and the New York State Archives.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Vermont pre-statehood record set was destroyed or lost. The extensive gaps in pre-statehood coverage reflect the absence of a civil registration system and the fragmented multi-jurisdictional nature of record-keeping during this period, not necessarily destruction. To determine whether specific records survive for a given town or county, consult VSARA directly.

## Research tips
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the starting point for land research.** The FamilySearch Wiki describes it as the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, naming approximately 1,800 grantees with township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. Start here before searching deed books. (FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Town clerk records from the 1770s survive unevenly — contact each town directly.** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly instructs researchers to consult town clerk offices rather than assuming a centralized repository holds pre-1857 vital records. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Use 19th-century town histories to access colonial-era proprietors' records.** The FamilySearch Wiki identifies these histories (most published 1860–1900) as reprinting early records that are otherwise difficult to access. Search WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog by town name + 'history'. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Search both New Hampshire and New York records for events before 1777.** The land-grant controversy means the same family may appear in both colonial record series, and records may have been filed under whichever colony the individual recognized. This is a geographic ambiguity, not a clean before/after split — search both regardless of which side your ancestor claimed.
- **The 1790 federal census is the closest population-level record to the pre-statehood period.** Vermont appears in the 1790 census (indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry). Heads of household in 1790 who were adults in 1760–1791 are the same generation you are researching.
- **No statewide civil registration existed before 1857.** Do not expect birth, marriage, or death certificates for any event in the 1760–1791 period. Church records, cemetery inscriptions, family Bibles, and town proprietors' records are the primary sources for vital information.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are a major source for family relationships.** Pensioners were required to document their service, and many pension files include depositions by wives and children that state marriage dates, birth dates, and names of children. Access through Fold3 or NARA.
- **Neighboring jurisdictions to search:** Ancestral lines in pre-statehood Vermont are directly connected to records in Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and New Hampshire (where many settlers originated) and in New York (for competing grant filings). Research the family in those originating states as well.

19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

Vermont-specific FamilySearch Wiki detail pages for vital records, land, church records, census, and probate did not return Vermont-specific content in this survey — they resolved to a generic overview page. Consult the Vermont State Archives and individual county/town repositories directly.

No Vermont-specific curated external-link collections were returned by the FamilySearch external-links tool for the 1760–1791 window — only generic national databases (Ancestry, Find A Grave, Fold3, NARA, Newspapers.com, FamilySearch Vital Records category).

The first federal census (1790) was taken just one year after statehood and captures many of the same families who lived in pre-statehood Vermont. It is the closest documentary snapshot to the pre-statehood population.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, c. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was admitted to the Union on 4 March 1791 as the 14th state, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). During the target period the territory passed through three distinct political phases:
  - **1760–1776 (New Hampshire Grants era):** The area had been granted to settlers by New Hampshire governor Benning Wentworth beginning in 1749. New York claimed the same territory after 1764 and issued competing grants. No separate Vermont jurisdiction existed; records were created under either New Hampshire or New York authority.
  - **1777–1791 (Republic of Vermont):** Vermont declared independence in 1777 and functioned as an unrecognized independent republic. Its own courts, land records, and town governments operated, but it was recognized by no other government until statehood.
  - **1791 onward:** State of Vermont, 14th state of the Union.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single seat for the territory; governance was at the town level during the Republic period.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** New Hampshire (land grants) and New York (competing colonial claims) before 1777; Republic of Vermont 1777–1791.
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this period. The 1790 federal census — taken one year after statehood — is the nearest quantitative snapshot.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, logging, and small-scale trade dominated. Settlement was largely in river valleys.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descent settlers from southern New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island) pushing north; some Scots-Irish and smaller groups.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and small Quaker meetings. Anglican presence was limited. No established state church.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (ended 1763) opened the region to rapid English settlement; the "Grants" controversy between New Hampshire grantees and New York claimants produced armed conflict (the Green Mountain Boys, 1770s); American Revolution (1775–1783) — Vermont raised militia but had no formal colonial status; Republic of Vermont declared January 1777; statehood 4 March 1791.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1764, the territory was under New Hampshire's jurisdiction for land-granting purposes.
- After 1764, the British Privy Council ruled in favor of New York's claim, making New York the nominal sovereign — though many settlers continued to hold and defend their New Hampshire grants.
- From 1777, the Republic of Vermont claimed boundaries that at times included portions of present-day New Hampshire and New York (the "Eastern and Western Unions"), though these expansions were short-lived. The final Vermont boundary was settled before statehood.
- **Research implication (geographic split):** Whether a pre-1777 land record was filed under New Hampshire or New York depends on which colony the recorder recognized and on the specific grant. This is not a clean temporal split — both series coexisted. Search both New Hampshire and New York colonial records for the same property or person.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in **1857** — at the state level. This date comes from the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). No statewide registration existed during the pre-statehood period.
- **Town-level records:** Some town clerks began recording births, marriages, and deaths as early as the 1770s, but survival is uneven. The FamilySearch Wiki notes these exist and instructs researchers to consult town clerk offices directly.
- **What exists for 1760–1791:** No civil registration at any level above the individual town. For any event in this period, vital information must be sought in church registers, family Bibles, cemetery inscriptions, and town proprietors' records.
- **Gaps:** Extensive. The majority of pre-statehood vital events were never formally recorded in a civil register. Many early town records were not kept, were lost, or were recorded inconsistently.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below), cemetery inscriptions, family Bible entries, town histories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Quaker. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page does not list specific denominations; the above reflects the settlement pattern confirmed by the jurisdictional context.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, burials, and (for some denominations) membership rolls and discipline records. Confirmations were recorded by some churches as a separate dated event years after baptism.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives, denominational archives (e.g., Vermont Congregational Conference records, Baptist state convention), and the Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA). The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page does not name specific depositories for church records for this period — consult VSARA directly for guidance.
- **Language:** English.
- **Importance for this period:** Church records are the primary substitute for absent civil registration. Because no civil vital registration existed in 1760–1791, a church baptism or burial entry may be the only record of a birth or death.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in **1790**, one year after Vermont's statehood. It is the closest documentary snapshot to the pre-statehood population and names heads of household with numerical counts of household members. Vermont appears in the 1790 federal census.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** No federal census before 1790. The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Census page was not accessible as a Vermont-specific page in this survey (it resolved to a generic overview). Whether any colonial or Republic-era enumeration survives for Vermont is not confirmed by the tool results in this survey.
- **Tax lists and proprietors' lists** (see Land records below) partially substitute for census-type information.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Vermont is indexed and available with images on both FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

### The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (unique pre-statehood record)
- This record is specifically highlighted by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) as the **earliest systematic resident list for the future state**.
- Prepared under New York colonial authority in 1771.
- Enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize.
- Each entry lists: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch Wiki does not specify where digital or physical copies are held; consult the Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA) and the New York State Archives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Court records include civil suits and Republic-era legislative/judicial proceedings.
- **Jurisdiction:** During 1777–1791, the Republic of Vermont established its own county courts. Before 1777, probate and court filings went to New Hampshire or New York courts depending on which colony the parties recognized.
- **Where held:** Vermont county probate courts (for post-1777 filings); New Hampshire State Archives and New York State Archives (for pre-1777 filings under those colonies). The FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Probate Records page was not accessible as a Vermont-specific page in this survey.
- **Access level:** Physical and microfilm; the FamilySearch external-links tool returned no Vermont-specific probate collections for this period.

### Land records
- **The New Hampshire Grants:** Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants in the region from 1749 into the 1760s. These are the foundational land records for most early Vermont families. Held by the New Hampshire State Archives.
- **New York competing grants:** New York issued patents over the same land from the mid-1760s. Held by the New York State Archives.
- **Republic of Vermont land records:** Vermont began issuing its own grants and recording deeds from 1777. County land records begin with county formation. Held at county clerk offices and VSARA.
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England town grant system — the township as a unit granted to a proprietors' group, then subdivided).
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (see above) is a key land-related record for this period.
- **Town Histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are important substitutes when original proprietors' books are unavailable.
- **Access level:** Largely physical or microfilm. The FamilySearch external-links tool returned no Vermont-specific land record collections for the 1760–1791 window.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (ended 1763), American Revolution (1775–1783). Vermont raised its own militia and supplied troops to the Continental Army.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (filed at the federal level after 1818 and 1832 Acts), bounty land warrants, muster rolls, and Vermont state militia records.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal pension and bounty land files, Continental Army service records); Vermont State Archives (militia records); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides access to NARA Revolutionary War pension and service files.
- **Access:** NARA Revolutionary War pension files are partially indexed and available at Fold3 (subscription). State militia records are physical at VSARA.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds associated with each settled township. Denominational cemeteries tied to early churches.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) and BillionGraves provide transcriptions and photographs for many Vermont cemeteries, including early colonial-era stones where they survive.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records from this early period are rare; most burial information survives on headstones (where extant) or in church burial registers.
- **Importance:** Headstone inscriptions from the 1770s–1790s can provide birth year, death year, and sometimes family relationships not recorded elsewhere.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's first newspaper, the *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington), began publication in 1781. Coverage was limited and survival is uneven for the pre-statehood years.
- **Where held:** Vermont State Library, Vermont Historical Society, and digital archives. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds some early Vermont papers.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land dispute announcements, and occasional vital notices. Coverage of the pre-statehood period is thin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers arrived overland from southern New England, not via international immigration. No seaport is in Vermont.
- **Relevant records:** If ancestors came from overseas before settling in Vermont, passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are sparse and held at NARA) would reflect arrival at ports such as Boston, Providence, or New York.
- **Naturalizations:** Not applicable for native-born colonists; naturalization records for foreign-born individuals who arrived before the Revolution are very limited.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town-level property and poll taxes were assessed from the earliest settlement period. Vermont Republic tax lists begin 1777.
- **Date range:** Some town tax lists survive from the 1770s; statewide consistency improves after 1791.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices, Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name male heads of household and property owners in years between censuses. For the pre-1790 period they are among the best substitutes for missing census-type records.

### Other record types
- **Proprietors' records:** Each town grant was administered by a body of proprietors who kept meeting minutes, division records, and lot assignments. These survive for many towns and name early settlers before any other record type. Held at town clerk offices and sometimes transcribed in town histories.
- **Town histories:** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly identifies 19th-century town histories (1860–1900) as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise hard to access (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the best finding aids for locating the history of a specific town.
- **Vermont State Papers:** The Vermont legislature published multi-volume documentary compilations (*State Papers of Vermont*) that include colonial-era grants, petitions, and legislative records relevant to the pre-statehood period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | 1790 federal census (indexed + images); some town vital records (coverage unconfirmed for pre-statehood window by tool results); FamilySearch Catalog for microfilmed county/town records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1790 Vermont; some early vital records collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War pension files, service records, bounty land warrants | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions and photographs, including early Vermont burial grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including early Vermont papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records: Revolutionary War files, 1790 census originals, federal land patents | Free finding aids; some digital records free, some fee-based |

**Coverage of this survey:** The external_links_search returned 6 resources for Vermont in the 1760–1791 window, all generic national databases. No Vermont-specific curated collections were returned. The FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search were not run in this survey (see Records NOT Online below); the FamilySearch Catalog should be searched directly at the town and county level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA), Montpelier VT | Republic-era and early state land records, tax lists, legislative records, militia records, early vital records | In-person; some records available by written request |
| Vermont Historical Society, Barre VT | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections | In-person; some digital finding aids online |
| New Hampshire State Archives, Concord NH | New Hampshire colonial grant records (Wentworth grants), pre-1764 authority records | In-person; some records online |
| New York State Archives, Albany NY | New York colonial competing grants, pre-1777 court and probate filings for the Grants territory | In-person; some records online |
| Individual town clerk offices (Vermont) | Town vital records from the 1770s onward (survival varies by town), land records post-1777, tax lists, proprietors' records | In-person or mail request; contact each town directly |
| NARA (multiple facilities) | 1790 census; Revolutionary War service and pension records; passenger lists | In-person at regional facility; many records digitized at Ancestry/Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- **Pre-statehood New Hampshire grants** (the Wentworth township grants, 1749–1764): physical at the New Hampshire State Archives; not confirmed as digitized by tool results.
- **New York colonial competing land grants for the Grants territory**: physical at the New York State Archives; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Vermont Republic-era court and probate records (1777–1791)**: held at county courthouses and VSARA; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Town-level tax lists and proprietors' records**: survival and accessibility vary by town; most are physical at town clerk offices; some transcribed in town histories available via WorldCat.
- **Early church registers**: held at individual churches, denominational archives, or VSARA; access varies; not confirmed as digitized for this period by tool results.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**: the FamilySearch Wiki identifies this record but does not specify a digital copy location; check VSARA and the New York State Archives.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that a specific Vermont pre-statehood record set was destroyed or lost. The extensive gaps in pre-statehood coverage reflect the absence of a civil registration system and the fragmented multi-jurisdictional nature of record-keeping during this period, not necessarily destruction. To determine whether specific records survive for a given town or county, consult VSARA directly.

## Research tips
- **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the starting point for land research.** The FamilySearch Wiki describes it as the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, naming approximately 1,800 grantees with township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. Start here before searching deed books. (FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Town clerk records from the 1770s survive unevenly — contact each town directly.** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly instructs researchers to consult town clerk offices rather than assuming a centralized repository holds pre-1857 vital records. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Use 19th-century town histories to access colonial-era proprietors' records.** The FamilySearch Wiki identifies these histories (most published 1860–1900) as reprinting early records that are otherwise difficult to access. Search WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog by town name + 'history'. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)
- **Search both New Hampshire and New York records for events before 1777.** The land-grant controversy means the same family may appear in both colonial record series, and records may have been filed under whichever colony the individual recognized. This is a geographic ambiguity, not a clean before/after split — search both regardless of which side your ancestor claimed.
- **The 1790 federal census is the closest population-level record to the pre-statehood period.** Vermont appears in the 1790 census (indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry). Heads of household in 1790 who were adults in 1760–1791 are the same generation you are researching.
- **No statewide civil registration existed before 1857.** Do not expect birth, marriage, or death certificates for any event in the 1760–1791 period. Church records, cemetery inscriptions, family Bibles, and town proprietors' records are the primary sources for vital information.
- **Revolutionary War pension files are a major source for family relationships.** Pensioners were required to document their service, and many pension files include depositions by wives and children that state marriage dates, birth dates, and names of children. Access through Fold3 or NARA.
- **Neighboring jurisdictions to search:** Ancestral lines in pre-statehood Vermont are directly connected to records in Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and New Hampshire (where many settlers originated) and in New York (for competing grant filings). Research the family in those originating states as well.
